region: Pelvic girdle, thigh, leg and foot
note: Serial correspondences to forelimb muscles are recorded in `homology.serial`. Following Diogo & Molnar (2014), a listed correspondence is a claim of TOPOLOGICAL equivalence only. It is not a claim of serial homology in the strict (ancestral-duplication) sense, and in several documented cases the two muscles derive from different anlagen.

muscles.name: Puboischiofemoralis internus
muscles.developmental: Somitic; dorsal (extensor) mass of the pelvic limb bud.
synonyms: puboischiofemoralis internus A–D (Prikryl et al. 2009 letter codes, anurans)

consensus.origin: Internal (medial) surface of the pubis and ilium, and the ventral surfaces of the posterior trunk vertebrae.
consensus.insertion: Proximal femur, on or near the trochanter.
consensus.action: Protracts (flexes) and medially rotates the femur; the principal hip protractor of sprawling tetrapods.
consensus.innervation: Femoral nerve (L2–L4) and direct branches of the lumbar plexus.

occurrences.name: Puboischiofemoralis internus
occurrences.attachmentNote: Passes anterior to the ilium to reach the hip. The pubo-ischiac plate is the fused ventral pelvic plate; it is scored here as pubis plus ischium, following the paper's own gloss of the ischium as the plate's posterior portion.
occurrences.origin: Internal (dorsal) face of the pubo-ischiac plate.
occurrences.insertion: Extensively on the femur — the anterior face, extending dorsally and ventrally — anterior to the puboischiofemoralis externus.

occurrences.name: Puboischiofemoralis internus A–D
occurrences.note: Prikryl et al. (2009) letter codes are used deliberately in place of the mammalian-sounding names ('iliacus', 'sartorius', 'pectineus') that earlier authors applied to these muscles, because those names imply homologies that do not hold. The anuran iliacus externus and internus belong to this field. Note the unresolved 'pectineus' — Noble (1922) placed it here, others in the externus.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Discoglossus and Ascaphus, from Prikryl et al.'s review table and descriptions. Iliacus internus and externus, which between them are this record's anuran occurrence. Internus arises on the inner surface of the ilium opposite the anterior acetabulum — variably instead on the anterior rounded margin of the acetabular portion — runs over the anterior acetabular margin and inserts along the proximal anteroventral femur beneath the iliacus externus. Externus arises on the iliac shaft.

occurrences.name: Puboischiofemoralis internus (PIFI 2)
occurrences.attachmentNote:
Reconstructed at Witmer inference level I over a muscular scar on the craniolateral face of the greater trochanter, on the proximolateral tuberosity of the femur, and over the adjacent concavity on the craniolateral side of the trochanter. **The origin is deliberately not scored.** Liparini & Schultz leave it as an unresolved ambiguity between the ventrolateral border of the preacetabular ilium, cranial and ventral to the PIFI 1 origin, and the ventral surfaces of the transverse processes and centra of the last truncal vertebrae — the avian and crocodylian conditions respectively, neither of which they will call ancestral. Recording either would manufacture a decision the authors refuse to make.

Prestosuchus chiniquensis, Liparini & Schultz (2013). Insertion at level I on the proximal portion of a caudomedial crest of the femoral shaft, medial to the distal depression of the fourth trochanter. **Origin unscored for the same reason as the PIFI 2**: level II′, an unresolved choice between the ventral margin of the preacetabular ilium and the medial face of the ilium with the ventral surfaces of the sacral transverse processes. The authors set out why it cannot be settled — if the whole deep dorsal group arose laterally on the ilium in the reptilian and saurian ancestors, then the crocodylian medial origin and the avian preacetabular one are both derived, and whether the shift happened once before the archosaur split or twice afterwards is open. Schachner et al. (2011) put the PIFI 1 of *Poposaurus gracilis* on a medial iliac depression; the same depression is present here **without muscle scars**, and Liparini & Schultz decline to read it as an attachment. They also note their PIFI 1 insertion stays caudomedial, where *Poposaurus* has it craniolateral — a difference that would reverse the muscle's rotational moment from supination to pronation.

occurrences.name: M. iliofemoralis internus + iliotrochantericus cranialis
occurrences.note: = crocodylian puboischiofemoralis internus 1-2. Hip flexors and medial rotators; Allen et al. find hip medial-rotator moment arms roughly doubling along the bird line.

occurrences.name: Iliacus + psoas major (+ sartorius)
occurrences.action: Flexes the hip; the principal hip flexor.
occurrences.note: Diogo & Molnar follow Walker & Homberger (1997) in deriving the mammalian sartorius from the ANTERIOR HEAD of puboischiofemoralis internus — not from the reptilian 'ambiens', as is commonly stated.

parts.name: Sartorius
parts.note: Diogo & Molnar follow Walker & Homberger (1997) in deriving it from the anterior head of this muscle, against the common claim that it comes from the reptilian 'ambiens'.

occurrences.attachmentNote: Iliopsoas: the psoas major head from the ventrolateral bodies and transverse-process bases of the last two or three lumbar vertebrae, the iliacus head from the arcuate line and ventral margin of the ilium, the two fusing before a common insertion on the lesser trochanter and secondarily the femoral neck. The sartorius, which this record's Theria occurrence also carries, runs instead from the iliac wing to the patella and the medial cnemial crest, and its rows are not merged in here.

occurrences.name: Puboischiofemoralis internus
occurrences.action: Protracts the femur; the posterodorsal part also abducts the leg.

parts.name: Anteroventral part
parts.note: Gadow and Kriegler's equivalent of part I in lizards. From most of the dorsal pubis and the epipubic cartilage, interdigitating across the midline with its counterpart.

parts.name: Posterodorsal part
parts.note: Homologous with part III of lizards. From most of the medial ilium, the underside of the first sacral rib and vertebra, and two presacral vertebrae.

occurrences.divisionNote: Two parts often treated as separate muscles. Both converge and unite anterior to the acetabulum before a common insertion, so the division is at the origin only.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Trachemys scripta — Walker (1973) writes *Pseudemys scripta*. **The morphological dorsal surface of the turtle femur faces anteriorly**, which is why a muscle inserting dorsally acts as a protractor; the row records the surface and the note records what that means. In pleurodires, where the ventral girdle is reduced and fused to the shell, much of this origin has spread onto the plastron anterior to the pubis — the same shell-as-attachment pattern as the forelimb.

occurrences.name: Iliopsoas
occurrences.action: Flexes the thigh at the hip; psoas major also flexes the trunk.
occurrences.innervation: Femoral nerve, and direct branches of the ventral rami of L1-L4.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). Iliacus from the iliac fossa, iliac crest and ala of the sacrum; psoas major from the bodies and transverse processes of the lumbar vertebrae; the two join in one tendon onto the lesser trochanter. **The lumbar origin is the change.** In a lizard this muscle is a pelvic muscle taking origin inside the pelvic canal; in a human a whole half of it has climbed onto the vertebral column, which is what lets it flex the trunk as well as the thigh. Psoas minor is scored as a third part and ends on the pelvis rather than the femur — a limb muscle that stopped short of the limb.

occurrences.name: M. puboischiofemoralis internus
occurrences.attachmentNote: Iguana iguana, Russell & Bauer (2008). **Most of this muscle cannot be seen without detaching the pelvis from the vertebral column**: it occupies the anterior edge of the pubic plate and most of the dorsal floor of the girdle, its fibres emerging from inside the girdle beneath the iliopubic ligament. Part 3 from the anterior pubic rim, not encompassing the pubic tubercle, to the femoral trochanter; parts 1 and 2 from the ischial symphysis, the thyroid fenestra rim and the internal ischial wall, inserting together by a broad tendon on the posterodorsal proximal femur where a prominent rugosity marks the site. Russell & Bauer note that Gadow, Romer and Galton each numbered the subdivisions differently and that Walker (1977) renamed them dorsalis/medialis/ventralis; they keep numbers because the degree of subdivision differs between lizards and positional names would assert homologies that do not hold.

occurrences.name: M. pubo-ischio-trochantericus internus
occurrences.innervation: Nervuli ileo-pectinei from the crural plexus.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Sphenodon punctatus, Osawa (1898), *Zur Muskellehre*. Günther's *M. pectineus*, Fürbringer's *ileo-pectineo-trochantericus internus*, Gadow's *pubi-ischio-femoralis internus*, Perrin's *extenseur du femur*. From the inner surface of the pelvis — pubis, ischium and obturator membrane — emerging over the anterior border of the pubis and ilium and running distomedially to the anterior medial surface of the proximal femur. **The femoro-tibialis origin is clamped between this muscle's insertion and the ileo-femoralis**, which is Osawa's way of fixing three attachments against each other rather than against a landmark. A small portion from the dorsal surface of the pubic symphysis crosses onto the extensor side of the thigh and ends in the fascia the pubo-tibialis arises from; Gadow read that slip as a pubic origin of his extensor ilio-tibialis instead.

occurrences.name: Iliopsoas and sartorius
occurrences.action: The sartorius acts chiefly as an extensor of the leg upon the thigh.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Spilocuscus maculatus. The psoas parvus is the larger of the two psoas muscles, as in the great majority of marsupials: from the bodies of six vertebrae — the last thoracic and the anterior five lumbar — ending in a long round tendon on the anterior border of the pubis close to the marsupial bone and immediately in front of the acetabulum. **So the bigger psoas in these animals ends on the girdle, not on the femur.** The iliacus comes off the lower border and iliac fossa of the ilium, blends with the psoas magnus, and inserts on the lesser trochanter and the shaft just below it. The psoas magnus is simple here: from the bodies of the last two lumbar vertebrae and the upper sacrum, blending with the iliacus. The sartorius arises from the anterior superior iliac spine in both animals and **acts chiefly as an extensor of the leg upon the thigh** — Cunningham notes these two are no exception to that marsupial rule, which is a different function from the human muscle of the same name. In the cuscus, whose thigh is held flexed, the sartorius lies at first close against the lower abdominal wall, then expands into an exceedingly thin sheet inserted into the quadriceps expansion on the front of the knee and into the fascia on the inner side of the joint.

occurrences.name: Iliopsoas and sartorius
occurrences.action: The sartorius acts chiefly as an extensor of the leg upon the thigh.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Thylacinus cynocephalus. The psoas parvus is the larger of the two psoas muscles, as in the great majority of marsupials: from the bodies of six vertebrae — the last thoracic and the anterior five lumbar — ending in a long round tendon on the anterior border of the pubis close to the marsupial bone and immediately in front of the acetabulum. **So the bigger psoas in these animals ends on the girdle, not on the femur.** The iliacus comes off the lower border and iliac fossa of the ilium, blends with the psoas magnus, and inserts on the lesser trochanter and the shaft just below it. **The psoas magnus is in two distinct portions here.** The anterior and larger is blended in front with the psoas parvus and springs behind from the bodies and transverse processes of the last two lumbar vertebrae, ending by joining the iliacus; the posterior portion comes off the last lumbar vertebra and the first two pieces of the sacrum and reaches the upper part of the lesser trochanter **independently of the iliacus** — so one psoas has an insertion of its own and the other has not. The sartorius arises from the anterior superior iliac spine in both animals and **acts chiefly as an extensor of the leg upon the thigh** — Cunningham notes these two are no exception to that marsupial rule, which is a different function from the human muscle of the same name. Here it is a thick prismatic muscle inserted entirely in front of the knee, into the quadriceps expansion.

occurrences.name: Iliopsoas and psoas minor
occurrences.divisionNote: **The iliopsoas cannot be divided into psoas major and iliacus in Monotremata.** Gambaryan et al. say so in terms: in therians the two heads are usually separable proximally and fused distally, and here there is no separation at any level. The psoas minor is a distinct muscle that never reaches the limb, and they put it in a lumbar rather than a hind limb group because it does not move the hind limb at all.
occurrences.action: Protracts the femur; the only antagonist of the gluteal and postfemoral mass during the propulsive phase.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Tachyglossus aculeatus, Gambaryan et al. (2002). The iliopsoas from the ventral bodies of the last two lumbar and the first sacral vertebrae and the ventral surface of the ala ossis ilii; the fibres from the vertebral bodies insert by an aponeurosis along the medial edge of the trochanter minor and the dorsal surface of the labium mediale ossis femoris, running down nearly a quarter of the femur, and the fibres from the ilium onto the inner surface of that aponeurosis and further along the labium mediale, covering nearly two-thirds of the femur. The psoas minor from the ventral bodies of the last two thoracic and the first lumbar vertebra and the superficial fascia of the quadratus lumborum, divided into right and left halves by the crura diaphragmatis, to the medial edge of the tuberculum musculi psoas minoris. **The psoas minor is a limb muscle that stops short of the limb** — the same thing the human psoas minor does, here on a tubercle out of all proportion to it. Gambaryan et al.'s lever-arm analysis makes the iliopsoas the sole antagonist of the whole gluteal and postfemoral mass during propulsion.

occurrences.name: Iliopsoas and psoas minor
occurrences.attachmentNote: Ornithorhynchus anatinus, Gambaryan et al. (2002). The iliopsoas from half the ventral surface of the penultimate lumbar vertebra back to the middle of the first sacral, plus the ventral aspect of the ala ossis ilii. It takes the whole cranial surface of the trochanter minor — **displacing the origin of the vastus medialis altogether** — and runs distally over more than half the labium mediale ossis femoris. Gambaryan et al. call this insertion unique among mammals, in which the muscle is normally confined to the trochanter minor. The psoas minor from the ventral bodies of the last three thoracic vertebrae and the first lumbar, and the ventral surfaces of the basal parts of the last two ribs, to the craniodorsal ridge of the tuberculum musculi psoas minoris — a tubercle running to more than half the length of the ilium in this animal.

homology.notes: A stable row across Tetrapoda. Its subdivision in mammals into iliacus, psoas major and sartorius is a derived elaboration.
homology.teaching: The sartorius derivation is a good correction to a widespread textbook claim.

correspondences.note: Topological correspondence only — the pelvic and pectoral internal girdle muscles were not acquired at the same time.
correspondences.caution: Diogo & Molnar (2014) find no clear topological equivalent here. Across every tetrapod clade in their Tables 13-21, including urodeles, they report that not one pelvic or thigh muscle has a clear topological equivalent in the pectoral region or arm, and attribute the lack to phylogenetic constraint on the girdles. This edge records a pairing the literature makes; it is not one that source supports.

muscles.name: Puboischiofemoralis externus
muscles.developmental: Somitic; ventral (flexor) mass.

consensus.origin: External (lateral/ventral) surfaces of the pubis and ischium.
consensus.insertion: Proximal femur, ventrally.
consensus.action: Adducts and laterally rotates the femur.

occurrences.name: Puboischiofemoralis externus
occurrences.note: Deeply blended with the 'pubofemoralis' (= adductor femoris) in Necturus (Walker 1954).
occurrences.attachmentNote: An insertion covering two-thirds of the femoral shaft. Extensive fleshy attachments like this one are why femoral muscle scars in salamanders are poor guides to muscle boundaries.
occurrences.origin: Much of the ventral surface of the pubo-ischiac plate.
occurrences.insertion: Ventral surface of the femur, over nearly two-thirds of the bone's length.

occurrences.name: Puboischiofemoralis externus
occurrences.note: Přikryl et al. (2009) note that the anuran 'pectineus' was identified as puboischiofemoralis EXTERNUS by Hoffmann (1873-78) and Iordansky & Morozov (1994), but as puboischiofemoralis INTERNUS by Noble (1922). The primary literature disagrees about which of the two it is, not merely about what to call it.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Discoglossus and Ascaphus, from Prikryl et al.'s review table and descriptions. Scored from the muscle Prikryl et al. call the pectineus, which Hoffmann and Iordansky & Morozov call the puboischiofemoralis externus — one of the twelve or so anuran names that mean something different in the mammalian literature. Ischium to femur; the review table does not resolve either end further.

occurrences.name: M. obturatorius lateralis + medialis
occurrences.note: = crocodylian puboischiofemoralis externus 1-3.

occurrences.name: Puboischiofemoralis externus
occurrences.note: Reconstructed from the ventral pelvic plate and the trochanteric region; its relative size is one of the variables Bishop & Pierce use to infer posture.

occurrences.name: Obturator externus, quadratus femoris, gemelli
occurrences.action: Laterally rotates the thigh; stabilises the hip.
occurrences.divisionNote: The gemelli are claimed by this field and by the ischiotrochantericus; the dataset records both claims.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Three muscles on one field. Obturator externus from the cranial, ventral and caudal margins of the obturator foramen on the lateral pelvis to the deep trochanteric fossa; quadratus femoris from the caudal lateral ischium to the caudodistal greater trochanter and distolateral fossa; gemelli from the ischial tuberosity and ischial body to the proximal fossa. All three reach the hip joint capsule.

occurrences.name: Obturator externus, quadratus femoris and the gemelli
occurrences.action: Laterally rotate the thigh; obturator externus also adducts it.
occurrences.innervation: Obturator nerve to obturator externus; nerve to quadratus femoris and nerve to obturator internus to the remainder.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). Obturator externus from the external surface of the obturator membrane and both pubic rami to the trochanteric fossa; quadratus femoris from the lateral ischial tuberosity to the quadrate line; the two gemelli from the ischial spine and tuberosity onto the obturator internus tendon. **Three of the four names here are on Diogo & Molnar's list of false friends** — 'obturator externus', 'quadratus femoris' and 'gemellus' are all applied to non-homologous muscles in the anuran literature. The gemelli are the oddity: they do not reach the femur at all, inserting instead on another muscle's tendon.

occurrences.name: M. puboischiofemoralis externus
occurrences.attachmentNote: Iguana iguana, Russell & Bauer (2008). **Divided by where it ends, not where it starts.** Group a has three bellies — a1 from the pubic apron and symphysis, a2 from the symphysis, a3 from the ischiadic symphysis and the posterior thyroid fenestra rim — and they insert on the femoral trochanter in a stratified fashion: a1 anteroventrally, a2 on the trochanter's proximal tip, a3 into the notch between trochanter and articular head. Group b is a single part from the ischiadic symphysis and posterior ischial margin whose broad tendon crosses the ventral proximal femoral condyle to insert on the posterior femur near the articular epiphysis. Russell & Bauer separate a from b because the insertions differ and the two act as complementary synergists, a as protractor and rotator and b supplementing it.

occurrences.name: M. pubo-ischio-femoralis and M. pubo-ischio-trochantericus externus
occurrences.innervation: R. ischio-femoralis of the N. obturatorius, and R. ileo-pectineus from the sacral plexus.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Sphenodon punctatus, Osawa (1898), *Zur Muskellehre*. Gadow's *pubo-ischio-femoralis* is Fürbringer's *adductor longus + pt. magnus*; the second part is Günther's "the principal adductor", Fürbringer's *ileo-pectineo-trochantericus externus* and Gadow's *pubi-ischio-femoralis externus*. The first arises with the puboischiotibialis from the puboischiadic ligament and wraps round the thigh to insert on its posterior surface at about mid-height, between the two origin lines of the femoro-tibialis. The second lies deepest, from the whole ventral surface of the pelvis and the pubic tubercle, to the trochanter major — and Osawa notes its fibre direction changes across the muscle, the ischiadic portion running almost horizontally while the pubic portion becomes progressively steeper.

occurrences.name: Obturator externus and quadratus femoris
occurrences.divisionNote: **This record's synonymy assigns the gemelli here, with the obturator externus and the quadratus femoris; Cunningham assigns them to the obturator internus**, into whose tendon they insert and in whose groove it runs. His rows for them are therefore on `ischiotrochantericus`, and the disagreement is left standing on both records — it is a question about which of two deep hip muscles the gemelli belong to, and this source answers it for one animal by dissection, not for Mammalia by argument.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Spilocuscus maculatus. The obturator externus is an exceedingly powerful fan-shaped muscle with the usual origin, inserted by a broad band-like tendon into the trochanteric fossa below the obturator internus tendon. The quadratus femoris is thick and fleshy, on the same plane as the adductor magnus and quite separate from it here, from the ischial tuberosity to the lower part of the posterior border of the great trochanter and the shaft below it. Cunningham notes it is relatively larger than a human's, with coarser and more oblique fibres. **This record's synonymy assigns the gemelli here, with the obturator externus and the quadratus femoris; Cunningham assigns them to the obturator internus**, into whose tendon they insert and in whose groove it runs. His rows for them are therefore on `ischiotrochantericus`, and the disagreement is left standing on both records — it is a question about which of two deep hip muscles the gemelli belong to, and this source answers it for one animal by dissection, not for Mammalia by argument.

occurrences.name: Obturator externus and quadratus femoris
occurrences.divisionNote: **This record's synonymy assigns the gemelli here, with the obturator externus and the quadratus femoris; Cunningham assigns them to the obturator internus**, into whose tendon they insert and in whose groove it runs. His rows for them are therefore on `ischiotrochantericus`, and the disagreement is left standing on both records — it is a question about which of two deep hip muscles the gemelli belong to, and this source answers it for one animal by dissection, not for Mammalia by argument.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Thylacinus cynocephalus. As in the cuscus, with one difference: **the quadratus femoris is partially fused with the upper border of the adductor magnus** here, where in the cuscus the two are quite separate. The obturator externus is the same powerful fan into the trochanteric fossa. **This record's synonymy assigns the gemelli here, with the obturator externus and the quadratus femoris; Cunningham assigns them to the obturator internus**, into whose tendon they insert and in whose groove it runs. His rows for them are therefore on `ischiotrochantericus`, and the disagreement is left standing on both records — it is a question about which of two deep hip muscles the gemelli belong to, and this source answers it for one animal by dissection, not for Mammalia by argument.

occurrences.name: Deep hip rotators (obturator externus group)
occurrences.divisionNote: Gambaryan et al. group all three in a short postfemoral field together with the caudofemoralis. They describe a single gemellus, not a pair. Its membership is carried as disputed here because the same muscle is claimed by `ischiotrochantericus` on other rows of this dataset; this source does not adjudicate that, and describes no obturator internus at all.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Tachyglossus aculeatus, Gambaryan et al. (2002). Obturator externus from the laterodorsal margin of the obturator foramen, its fibres fanning over the proximal third of the caudal femur and inserting over an almost rectangular area on the medial part of that surface, medial to the adductor brevis. Quadratus femoris by fibres on the dorsal surface of the acetabular branch of the ischium, between the gemellus and the semimembranosus, onto the caudal aspect of the upper trochanter major proximal to the adductor brevis. Gemellus from the acetabular branch of the ischium caudal to the acetabulum, onto the caudal aspect of the upper part of the trochanter major. **The monotremes have no trochanteric fossa.** In therians that fossa takes the gemelli and the obturators; here there is none, and these muscles reach the trochanter's caudal surface instead — which means the single most reliable therian correlate for this muscle field cannot be looked for in a monotreme or in anything bracketed by one.

occurrences.name: Deep hip rotators (obturator externus group)
occurrences.attachmentNote: Ornithorhynchus anatinus, Gambaryan et al. (2002). Obturator externus from the laterodorsal margin of the obturator foramen caudal to the lateral head of the adductor longus, onto the caudal aspect of the trochanter minor proximal to the caudofemoralis. Quadratus femoris from both the dorsal surface and the ventrolateral aspect of the acetabular branch of the ischium, between the gemellus and the semimembranosus anterior, onto the caudal surface of the trochanter major between its rugosities, bordering the adductor brevis medially and the caudofemoralis distally. Gemellus as in the echidna: from the acetabular branch of the ischium caudal to the acetabulum onto the caudal aspect of the upper trochanter major. **The obturator externus has moved to the lesser trochanter in this animal** and to the femoral shaft in the echidna — the same muscle on two different landmarks in two genera of one order, which is worth having in front of a student before they read a single insertion off a fossil.

occurrences.name: Pubo-ischio-femorales externi (PIFE 1, PIFE 2, PIFE 3)
occurrences.attachmentNote: Prestosuchus chiniquensis, Liparini & Schultz (2013). The third head from the lateral surface of the ischium; the first and second from the ventral surface of the pubic apron, the expanded lateral surface of the pubic shaft and the distal concavity of the pubis. Insertion at level I on muscle scars on the caudal tuberosity of the femoral head and the caudomedial concavity of the greater trochanter. **The pubic origin is the weak point and the authors say so**: the pubis of *Prestosuchus* is markedly unlike that of either extant archosaur group, it bears no muscle scars and no specific features along the expanded shaft, so how the muscle was arranged there and whether the first and second heads were separate at all remain undecided. The third head may be homologous with the avian obturatorius lateralis pars dorsalis.

homology.notes: The obturator nerve is the constant marker for this field across Tetrapoda.

correspondences.note: See the reciprocal edge on `ischiotrochantericus`.

correspondences.caution: Diogo & Molnar (2014) find no clear topological equivalent here. Across every tetrapod clade in their Tables 13-21, including urodeles, they report that not one pelvic or thigh muscle has a clear topological equivalent in the pectoral region or arm, and attribute the lack to phylogenetic constraint on the girdles. This edge records a pairing the literature makes; it is not one that source supports.

muscles.name: Iliofemoralis
muscles.developmental: Somitic; dorsal mass.

consensus.insertion: Proximal femur, on or near the greater trochanter.
consensus.action: Abducts the femur; in erect-limbed taxa, the principal hip abductor and pelvic stabiliser during single-limb support.

occurrences.name: Iliofemoralis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Discoglossus and Ascaphus, from Prikryl et al.'s review table and descriptions. Shares its origin on the posterolateral tuber superius with the iliofibularis — the two are slender and closely bound — and inserts on the dorsal surface of the crista femoralis, the crest running posteriorly from the proximal femur. Both ends are on named anuran processes, so this is one of the few thigh muscles here that leaves a correlate at each end.

occurrences.name: Iliofemoralis
occurrences.attachmentNote: From the anterior iliac blade, sharing an intramuscular septum with the puboischiotibialis; the belly wraps the posterior femoral border to insert proximally. Femur abductor, active in swing.

occurrences.name: Iliofemoralis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Crocodylus porosus. Tendinous origin on the central lateral ilium, deep to iliotibialis 2; inserts fleshy onto the DISTAL THIRD of the dorso-lateral femur, between femorotibialis internus and externus, and attaches along most of the femoral length. The femorotibialis internus tendon arising distal and anterior to it is the landmark Klinkhamer et al. use to separate the two. Hip abductor, confirmed by EMG. This is the description `extensor-iliotibialis` was also carrying.

occurrences.name: M. iliofemoralis externus
occurrences.note: Hip abductor.

architecture.note: Values as modelled; maximum isometric force is derived, not measured.

occurrences.name: Iliofemoralis
occurrences.note: Its expansion, tracked through the enlargement of the iliac blade, is central to Bishop & Pierce's argument that erect hindlimb posture was acquired late in the therian stem lineage.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Expansion of the iliac blade along the synapsid stem tracks the enlargement of this field and the shift toward erect posture.

occurrences.name: Gluteus medius + gluteus minimus
occurrences.action: Abduct and medially rotate the thigh; prevent pelvic drop during the stance phase.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Same muscle, same nerve, same attachments — but in a parasagittal limb it becomes the principal pelvic stabiliser during single-limb support.

occurrences.name: Iliofemoralis
occurrences.action: Abducts and protracts the femur.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Trachemys scripta, from Walker (1973). Covers most of the dorsolateral pelvis lateral and posterior to the posterodorsal head of the puboischiofemoralis internus. Extensive origin from the first sacral and one or two presacral vertebrae, **the adjacent carapace**, and most of the lateral surface and anterior border of the ilium, converging onto the dorsal surface of the trochanter major. Most turtles resemble *Pseudemys* in taking some fibres from the vertebrae as well as the ilium.

occurrences.name: Gluteus medius and gluteus minimus
occurrences.action: Abduct the thigh and stabilise the pelvis over the stance limb.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). Medius from the external ilium between the posterior and anterior gluteal lines, minimus between the anterior and inferior lines, both onto the greater trochanter. **This record's whole point is visible here**: the transformation from a modest abductor in a sprawling limb to the principal pelvic stabiliser in a parasagittal one happens with no change of identity, origin, insertion or nerve — the same bone, the same trochanter, the same superior gluteal supply, doing a different job because the limb is held differently. Tensor fasciae latae is scored as a disputed part: it shares the superior gluteal nerve with the other two, but its insertion on the iliotibial tract puts it as easily in the iliotibialis field, and this dataset does not resolve that.

occurrences.name: M. iliofemoralis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Iguana iguana, Russell & Bauer (2008). Fleshy origin from the anterior aspect of the iliac blade, sharing an intermuscular septal origin ventrally with the puboischiotibialis. The belly wraps around the posterior border of the femur and inserts between the origin of the posterior part of the femorotibialis and the insertion of the adductor femoris. **The record's assessment is that this muscle becomes the mammalian gluteus medius and minimus without changing identity, origin, insertion or nerve** — the *Iguana* row is the sprawling-limb end of that claim, and the human row on the same record is the parasagittal one.

occurrences.name: M. ileo-femoralis
occurrences.innervation: R. muscularis brevis of the N. femoralis, and the R. ilio-femoralis of the N. peroneus.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Sphenodon punctatus, Osawa (1898), *Zur Muskellehre*. Günther's *M. iliacus internus*, Fürbringer's *ileo-femoralis (glutaeus medius)* — the name behind this record's gluteus medius and minimus equation. A short muscle covered by the ilio-tibialis and ilio-fibularis, from the lateral surface of the dorsal ilium below the ilio-tibialis origin, inserting on the lateral-posterior surface of the proximal femur between the coccygeo-femoralis longus insertion above and the femoro-tibialis origin below. **The record's claim is that this muscle becomes the mammalian gluteals without changing identity, origin, insertion or nerve**; the tuatara is the sprawling end of that.

occurrences.name: Gluteus medius, minimus and quartus
occurrences.attachmentNote: Spilocuscus maculatus. The medius is a thick fleshy muscle from the short iliac crest, the dorsum of the ilium and its fascia, and the tendinous cord running back from the anterior superior iliac spine, inserted into the summit and outer aspect of the great trochanter. The minimus is a wide thin muscle from the dorsum of the ilium and from the ischium as far back as the gemelli, **almost completely roofing the hip joint**, narrowing to the anterior border of the great trochanter; its anterior border blends with the corresponding margin of the gluteus maximus. Cunningham reports Macalister finding medius and minimus hardly separable in the wombat and *Sarcophilus*, and says that as a rule in Marsupialia they are quite distinct — as they are here. The gluteus quartus is present but very feebly marked, a single delicate slip. The gluteus quartus is carried as a disputed part on Cunningham's own authority: he could not make out its nerve supply with precision in either animal, says in so many words that until that is done its homologies cannot be considered established, and adds that although it is usually grouped with the gluteals it seems more closely related to the extensor muscles. He records it in the wombat, *Sarcophilus*, both kangaroos, the phalanger and the opossum on Macalister, and notes that neither Macalister nor Young found it in the koala.

occurrences.name: Gluteus medius, minimus and quartus
occurrences.attachmentNote: Thylacinus cynocephalus. **The medius is segmented into a superficial and a deep portion, and the deep one sits in a hollow on the under surface of the superficial one** — so at first sight one segment appears to be enclosed within the substance of the other. The superficial part inserts on the outer aspect of the great trochanter, the deep on its summit. Cunningham notes Young found the koala's gluteus medius frequently bilaminar too. The minimus is as in the cuscus: dorsum of the ilium and ischium back as far as the gemelli, roofing the hip joint, converging on the anterior border of the great trochanter. **The gluteus quartus is well developed here** — triangular, by a pointed origin from the acetabular margin close to the reflected tendon of the rectus femoris, expanding over the front of the hip capsule and passing between the vastus externus and vastus internus to insert on the front of the femoral shaft just below the neck. The gluteus quartus is carried as a disputed part on Cunningham's own authority: he could not make out its nerve supply with precision in either animal, says in so many words that until that is done its homologies cannot be considered established, and adds that although it is usually grouped with the gluteals it seems more closely related to the extensor muscles. He records it in the wombat, *Sarcophilus*, both kangaroos, the phalanger and the opossum on Macalister, and notes that neither Macalister nor Young found it in the koala.

occurrences.name: Gluteus medius and gluteus profundus
occurrences.divisionNote: Gambaryan et al. resolve the gluteus medius into proximal, intermediate and distal parts and treat the gluteus profundus as a fourth, separate muscle. Both readings have been in dispute: the distal part of the medius has been called gluteus minimus (Mivart 1866, Westling 1889, Walter 1988) and all three parts have been called gluteus profundus A, B and C (Low 1929), while Meckel, Mivart, Allen, Forster and Walter called the true gluteus profundus the gluteus medius. Gambaryan et al.'s own Table 1 lists the profundus as gluteus minimus, so even within this source the name is not stable.
occurrences.action: Pronates the femur at the hip; the profundus is a tiny muscle wrapped round the rectus femoris origin.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Tachyglossus aculeatus, Gambaryan et al. (2002). A complex pinnate muscle in three parts. The proximal part from the neural spines of the last two lumbar and first two sacral vertebrae and the superficial fascia of the sacrocaudalis dorsalis, by a strong tendon to the top of the trochanter major. The intermediate part from the tuber coxae by a strong medial tendon continuing as a superficial aponeurotic sheet, and by fibres from the ala ossis ilii, along the trochanter major crest. The distal part from the intermediate part's tendinous origin and the medial crest of the ala ossis ilii, by a thick aponeurosis onto the **distal** rugosity of the trochanter tertius — the medial third of the femoral diaphysis. The gluteus profundus is tiny: from close to the iliac tubercle that also gives origin to the rectus femoris, surrounding that muscle cranially, dorsally and caudally, narrowly onto the trochanter major crest deep to the medius. **This is the largest muscle in the echidna's hind limb** at 12.5 per cent of its mass, against 4.2 per cent in the platypus.

occurrences.name: Gluteus medius
occurrences.divisionNote: Three parts, more clearly differentiated than in the echidna. The gluteus profundus, which the echidna has, is absent.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Ornithorhynchus anatinus, Gambaryan et al. (2002). The proximal part from the dorsal half of the ala ossis ilii and the adjacent outer fascia of the sacrocaudalis dorsalis; the intermediate and distal parts from the tendon anchored on the tuber coxae and from the crest of the ala ossis ilii. The three insert in series along the femur: proximal on the upper point of the trochanter major, distal on the **proximal** rugosity of the trochanter tertius, intermediate between them. **The rugosities of the trochanter tertius follow the muscle.** The platypus has the better-developed proximal rugosity and the echidna the distal one, matching where each animal's distal part of the gluteus medius ends — one of the cleanest osteological correlates in this dataset, because the bone records which of two insertions dominated in an animal nobody dissected. The gluteus profundus is not present in this species.

occurrences.name: Ilio-femoralis (IF)
occurrences.attachmentNote: Prestosuchus chiniquensis, Liparini & Schultz (2013). Origin at level II′ on the lateral surface of the ilium, on a smooth area just caudal to the subvertical crest and dorsal to the supra-acetabular crest — level II′ because the authors do not accept that the avian and crocodylian origins are homologous. Insertion at level I over muscular striations on a slightly elevated area of the proximal craniomedial femoral shaft, just distal to the femoral head. **One insertion, so one muscle.** *Tyrannosaurus* has a clearly divided insertion, the iliofemoralis externus on a proximolateral ridge and the iliotrochantericus caudalis on the lesser trochanter; *Prestosuchus* has no homologue of the lesser trochanter and only the one structure, which Liparini & Schultz take as strengthening a single undivided ilio-femoralis in this animal. Its homology is contested in the direction of the PIFI 2: the avian iliotrochantericus cranialis and medialis may belong here rather than there.

homology.notes: Universal in Tetrapoda. The functional transformation — from a modest abductor in a sprawling limb to the principal pelvic stabiliser in a parasagittal one — happens without any change in identity, origin, insertion or nerve.
homology.teaching: The best single muscle for showing that posture change is a change in mechanics, not in anatomy. Same muscle, same nerve, radically different role.
homology.caveat: Leavey et al. (2024), using diceCT on 30 frog species across five locomotor modes, report that bone lengths and pelvic crest sizes are generally NOT reliable predictors of muscle size, and find many-to-one form-function mapping. That is a direct caution against reading muscle proportions off skeletal proportions in fossils, which is the inference osteological correlates are usually recruited for. Correlates locate an attachment; they do not size the muscle that made it.

correspondences.caution: Diogo & Molnar (2014) find no clear topological equivalent here. Across every tetrapod clade in their Tables 13-21, including urodeles, they report that not one pelvic or thigh muscle has a clear topological equivalent in the pectoral region or arm, and attribute the lack to phylogenetic constraint on the girdles. This edge records a pairing the literature makes; it is not one that source supports.

muscles.name: Caudofemoralis
muscles.developmental: Somitic; derived from the caudal axial musculature, not from the limb bud proper.

consensus.origin: Ventrolateral surfaces of the caudal vertebrae and their transverse processes (longus); the posterolateral ilium (brevis).
consensus.insertion: Fourth trochanter of the femur.
consensus.action: The principal femoral retractor of non-mammalian tetrapods — the main propulsive muscle of the hindlimb in sprawling and archosaurian locomotion.
consensus.innervation: Ventral rami of the caudal spinal nerves; inferior gluteal nerve territory in mammals.

occurrences.name: Caudofemoralis
occurrences.attachmentNote: The origin has a countable segmental address — caudals four and five — which is rare in this dataset and is what makes the caudofemoralis tractable in fossils. The insertion is given as the femoral crista ventralis; whether that ridge is the same structure as the amniote fourth trochanter is not settled here, so no landmark is asserted.
occurrences.origin: Transverse processes of the fourth and fifth caudal vertebrae.
occurrences.insertion: Crista ventralis of the femur, by a strong tendon.

occurrences.name: Caudofemoralis longus + brevis
occurrences.action: Primary femoral retractor; drives the propulsive stroke in lizard locomotion.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Longus arises from the proximal third of the tail and caudal vertebrae 4-14, inserting by broad tendon on the femoral trochanter plus a second tendon onto the lateral menisci of the knee; brevis arises from the transverse processes of the four most anterior postsacral vertebrae. Femur retraction and long-axis rotation, active in stance.

occurrences.name: Caudofemoralis
occurrences.note: Inferred from a low, proximodistally elongate fourth trochanter about a quarter of the way down the posteromedial femur, bearing a shallow medial pit. Level I inference. Its modest development relative to the crocodylian condition is the observation that bears on how much of locomotion was still tail-driven in the sphenosuchian grade.

occurrences.name: Caudofemoralis
occurrences.attachmentNote: A rough convexity identified as the fourth trochanter, continuing distally as a faint ridge bearing insertion scars.

occurrences.name: Caudofemoralis longus + brevis
occurrences.note: Large and well developed; inserts on a prominent fourth trochanter. Attachments are deliberately not scored for Alligator mississippiensis: Allen et al. measure this muscle's architecture but give no attachment sites (0.1 origin/insertion mentions per page), and Diogo & Molnar's crocodylian exemplar is Caiman latirostris. The rows this occurrence used to carry were Klinkhamer et al.'s description of Crocodylus porosus and have moved to their own occurrence.

occurrences.name: Caudofemoralis longus + brevis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Crocodylus porosus. Longus is fleshy from the haemal arches of numerous caudal vertebrae BEGINNING AT CAUDAL VERTEBRA 12; brevis has TWO heads, one from the postero-lateral ilium and one from caudal vertebrae 4 and 5, anterior to the longus origin — so both muscles take caudal vertebrae and the caudal row is shared, where the block used to read longus-from-vertebrae and brevis-from-ilium as though each had one head. Both insert by tendon on the proximo-ventral femur at the fourth trochanter. The second insertion row is the longus' ACCESSORY TENDON onto the ventro-distal femur at the tibial condyle, together with gastrocnemius externus; scored on the condyles because that is as fine as skeleton.json resolves. The longus is the largest muscle in the animal's body. Allen et al. is no longer cited here: it measures architecture and gives no attachment sites, and it is the Alligator source that used to hold this row on the wrong animal.

occurrences.name: M. caudofemoralis pars caudalis + pars pelvica
occurrences.note: Greatly reduced with the shortening of the tail to the pygostyle and the shift to a knee-driven, femur-held-horizontal gait. Its reduction is a defining event in the theropod–bird locomotor transition. Allen et al. (2021) split the avian muscle into pars caudalis (= crocodylian caudofemoralis longus) and pars pelvica (= brevis). Its leverage declines across several nodes along the bird line.

architecture.note: Values as modelled; maximum isometric force is derived, not measured.

occurrences.name: Caudofemoralis
occurrences.note: Progressive reduction along the synapsid stem, tracked through the reduction of the fourth trochanter.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Progressive reduction of the fourth trochanter along the synapsid stem tracks the loss of tail-driven femoral retraction.

occurrences.note: Galictis cuja. Ercoli et al. state it flatly: 'M. gluteofemoralis (m. caudofemoralis) — this muscle is absent.' A carnivoran with a long, well-muscled tail, where a persistent gluteofemoralis would be least surprising, and it is not there; they read the absence as a derived condition acquired within some mustelid clades. In THREE HIND LIMBS the caudal portion of the gluteus superficialis divided into one or more extra bellies, which they suggest 'could be a remnant of this muscle' — a second candidate remnant, and one that disagrees with the proposal that the piriformis is the remnant. The paper gives no denominator for those three limbs, and this note previously said 'three of six', which the paper does not support: its methods name three specimens plus a fourth for additional observations, and its largest stated count anywhere is 'in four legs'. This row read `variable` until an audit caught it — that was the clade's answer written onto one animal, which is the error the rollup exists to prevent. Theria computes `variable` on its own if another therian disagrees.

occurrences.name: Piriformis
occurrences.action: Laterally rotates the extended thigh; abducts the flexed thigh.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). Anterior surface of the sacrum to the upper border of the greater trochanter. **Scored on a proposed correspondence, and the proposal is about a lost tail.** This record tracks the fourth trochanter, which is what makes it the most reliably reconstructed hindlimb muscle in fossils; the human femur has no fourth trochanter and the human tail is a coccyx, so what survives is a short sacrum-to-trochanter muscle that has kept the topology and lost the lever. Birds and anurans reduced the same muscle independently, for the same reason.

occurrences.name: M. caudifemoralis longus and brevis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Iguana iguana, Russell & Bauer (2008). Longus accrues heads from the fourth to the fourteenth caudal vertebra, from the haemal arches and transverse processes; brevis from the transverse processes and centra of the four anteriormost postsacral vertebrae. **The division is by vertebral type, not by position** — Russell & Bauer point out the brevis is associated with the pygals, which lack haemal arches, and the longus with the true caudals, which have them. Both insert on the femoral trochanter. The longus also sends a supplementary tendon at right angles that runs ventral and parallel to the femur, accompanied by the femoral nerve, artery and vein, to insert on the ventral surface of the knee-joint meniscus — a tail muscle with an attachment on the knee.

occurrences.name: M. coccygeo-femoralis brevis and longus
occurrences.innervation: Rami musculares of the first postsacral nerve; the brevis chiefly from a branch of the N. pudendus externus.
occurrences.attachmentNote:
Sphenodon punctatus, Osawa (1898), *Zur Muskellehre*. Brevis is Gadow's *caudi-ilio-femoralis* and Fürbringer's *coccygeo-femoralis brevis s. pyriformis* — the name behind this record's proposed homology with the mammalian piriformis. It arises from the ventral surface of the transverse processes of six anterior caudal vertebrae and joins the origin tendon of the ischio-tibialis posticus. Longus arises from the root of the transverse processes and the haemal arches of the eight anterior caudals and inserts by a thick tendon on the trochanter major.

**The longus also sends a tendon to the knee**, a narrow strand running distad to the knee joint capsule and the lateral side of the fibular femoral epicondyle — the crural tendon Russell & Bauer describe in *Iguana* as reaching the meniscus. Osawa corrects Gadow twice here: the two muscles do not merge, and the innervation is postsacral rather than presacral or sacral.

occurrences.name: Pyriformis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Thylacinus cynocephalus. **Identical in both of Cunningham's two animals**: a strongly marked triangular muscle lying on the posterior part of the gluteus minimus behind the gluteus medius, from the lower surface and outer margin of the sacrum, inserted by a rounded tendon into the posterior part of the summit of the great trochanter. It lands on this record because this dataset already carries the piriformis as the proposed mammalian caudofemoralis, and the human row here is scored the same way. **But Cunningham describes a second candidate in the same two animals** — the agitator caudae, which actually reaches the caudal vertebrae and the posterior femur, and which he groups with the gluteus maximus. Both cannot be the caudofemoralis, and nothing in this source settles which is; the disagreement is recorded on both records rather than resolved on either. Macalister found the piriformis indistinguishable from the gluteus medius in *Phalangista*.

occurrences.name: Pyriformis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Spilocuscus maculatus. **Identical in both of Cunningham's two animals**: a strongly marked triangular muscle lying on the posterior part of the gluteus minimus behind the gluteus medius, from the lower surface and outer margin of the sacrum, inserted by a rounded tendon into the posterior part of the summit of the great trochanter. It lands on this record because this dataset already carries the piriformis as the proposed mammalian caudofemoralis, and the human row here is scored the same way. **But Cunningham describes a second candidate in the same two animals** — the agitator caudae, which actually reaches the caudal vertebrae and the posterior femur, and which he groups with the gluteus maximus. Both cannot be the caudofemoralis, and nothing in this source settles which is; the disagreement is recorded on both records rather than resolved on either. Macalister found the piriformis indistinguishable from the gluteus medius in *Phalangista*.

occurrences.name: Caudofemoralis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Tachyglossus aculeatus, Gambaryan et al. (2002). By an aponeurosis on the superficial fascia of the sacrocaudalis dorsalis at the level of the transverse processes of the first two caudal vertebrae, to an aponeurosis on the **proximal** rugosity of the trochanter tertius. **The monotremes keep a caudofemoralis and have no piriformis** — the therian muscle usually read as this one's derivative is absent in both genera, and what Coues (1870) called a piriformis here is the gluteus superficialis. So this is a tail-to-femur retractor still doing its own job in a mammal, in an animal whose femoral retraction is only about fifteen degrees. It is a small muscle, 1.8 per cent of hind limb mass.
occurrences.action: Retracts the femur.

occurrences.name: Caudofemoralis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Ornithorhynchus anatinus, Gambaryan et al. (2002). By fibres on the fascia lying between the sacrocaudalis ventralis and dorsalis at the level of the transverse processes of the first caudal vertebra, inserting by muscle fibres over a rather large area on the caudal aspect of the proximal rugosity of the trochanter tertius. **Where the caudofemoralis lands is the comparative point.** In archosaurs it takes the fourth trochanter, which is the best single fossil-muscle landmark in the vertebrate skeleton and is lost in Theria; here it has arrived on a third trochanter instead. At 0.6 per cent of hind limb mass this is the smallest it gets in either monotreme.

occurrences.name: Caudofemoralis (pars caudi-femoralis + pars ilio-femoralis)
occurrences.attachmentNote: *Grus americana*, Fisher & Goodman (1955); anconal and palmar are dorsal and ventral in their usage. **M. caudofemoralis.** The pars caudi-femoralis arises from the most ventral tip of the pygostyle as a tendon which courses latero-ventrad to pass through the ischial notch; immediately it forms a narrow, thin band of fleshy muscle. The pars ilio-fem. comes fleshy in its anterior two-thirds from a line along the most ventral part of the posterior iliac crest deep to the origins of Mm. extens. ilio-fib. and flex. cruris lat. The posterior third to half is aponeurotic (fig. 31). Insertion.—Pars caudi-fem. when present inserts tendinously on the outer face of the femur some 4 or 5 centimeters from the proximal end of the femur. This is an insertion distinct from that of the pars ilio-fem., even in th *Insertion.* Pars caudi-fem. when present inserts tendinously on the outer face of the femur some 4 or 5 centimeters from the proximal end of the femur. This is an insertion distinct from that of the pars ilio-fem., even in that instance shown in figure 30, in which there was some fleshy fusion of the bellies of the three parts. The pars ilio-fem. inserts widely and fleshily some 2 to 4 centimeters distad from the proximal end of the femur and on its postero-lateral surface; this insertion is anterior and partly proximal to that of M. flex. ischio-fem. and posterior to the in- sertion of M. piriformis (figs. 30, 31). In that specimen in which pars caudi-fem. was absent, pars ilio-fem. had its insertion 1

occurrences.name: Caudofemorales (CFL, CFB)
occurrences.attachmentNote: Prestosuchus chiniquensis, Liparini & Schultz (2013). The brevis from the caudolateral surface and the postacetabular medial fossa of the ilium together with the first caudal vertebrae; the longus from the more posterior caudals, running by comparison with extant archosaurs from about the third to the fifteenth. **Those vertebrae are not preserved in the specimen**, so the extent of the longus origin is inferred from living animals rather than observed, and the row records the caudal series without a count. Insertion at level I on muscle scars on the fourth trochanter, with the longus continuing onto the adjacent distal impression.

homology.notes: Presence and size track the fourth trochanter directly, making this the most reliably reconstructed hindlimb muscle in fossils. Its independent reduction in birds and in mammals accompanies two separate shifts away from tail-driven femoral retraction. Anurans are a third such reduction and the most complete: with the tail lost and the caudal series replaced by the urostyle, the muscle's origin has no vertebrae to arise from.
homology.teaching: The single best fossil-muscle example: a bony landmark (the fourth trochanter) that reads directly as muscle presence, size and locomotor mode across 300 million years.
homology.caveat: Leavey et al. (2024), using diceCT on 30 frog species across five locomotor modes, report that bone lengths and pelvic crest sizes are generally NOT reliable predictors of muscle size, and find many-to-one form-function mapping. That is a direct caution against reading muscle proportions off skeletal proportions in fossils, which is the inference osteological correlates are usually recruited for. Correlates locate an attachment; they do not size the muscle that made it.

correspondences.note: No forelimb counterpart. The caudofemoralis is a clean falsification of any expectation of one-to-one fore/hindlimb correspondence. Diogo & Molnar (2014) report that no pelvic or thigh muscle has a clear topological equivalent in the pectoral region or arm in any tetrapod clade they examine, which is the general result this particular absence sits under.

muscles.name: Extensor iliotibialis / iliotibialis
muscles.developmental: Somitic; dorsal mass.

consensus.insertion: Tibia, via the knee extensor apparatus.
consensus.action: Extends the knee; protracts the femur.

occurrences.name: Extensor iliotibialis
occurrences.note: Single-headed in Taricha, against the two heads (pars anterior and posterior) usual in Cryptobranchus, Necturus, Salamandra, Pseudoeurycea, Ambystoma and Dicamptodon. The split tracks limb robustness rather than habitat or phylogeny: slender-limbed salamanders (Amphiuma, Typhlomolge, Bolitoglossa, Taricha) have one head, robust-limbed ones two, and aquatic and terrestrial species occur in both groups. Smith (1927) reported two heads in the congener Taricha granulosa, so the character may vary within the genus.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Crosses both hip and knee. Recorded with a single head in Taricha; the tibial insertion is on the anterior proximal tibia, which the paper calls the spine and which may or may not be the cnemial crest of amniotes — left unasserted.
occurrences.origin: Lateral surface of the ilium above the acetabulum.
occurrences.insertion: Spine of the tibia, by a long strong tendon.

occurrences.name: Extensor iliotibialis A/B
occurrences.note: Diogo & Molnar use letter codes rather than the mammalian names ('gluteus maximus', 'tensor fasciae latae') applied by earlier authors, because those homologies do not hold. Přikryl et al. (2009) list the anuran muscle as 'glutaeus maximus (iliotibialis)'. It is NOT homologous with the mammalian gluteus maximus — one of the twelve false-friend names Diogo & Molnar (2014) identify.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Discoglossus and Ascaphus, from Prikryl et al.'s review table and descriptions. Cruralis and glutaeus maximus, this record's anuran A/B pair. Cruralis runs from the ilium to the knee aponeurosis; glutaeus maximus from the dorsolateral tuber superius onto the fascia of the distal cruralis rather than onto bone. Prikryl et al. note the glutaeus maximus origin is the one marked on their pelvic figure — it is a scoreable correlate.

occurrences.name: Iliotibialis (+ femorotibialis, + 'ambiens')
occurrences.attachmentNote: Scored from Zaaf et al.'s tables for Eublepharis macularius, with the Gekko gecko differences noted where they bear on the attachment. The whole knee-extensor field this record covers in lizards: iliotibialis from the lateral ilium by a broad aponeurosis, 'ambiens' aponeurotically from the pubis and proximoventral femur, femorotibialis from the femoral shaft by four bellies surrounding it. All three converge tendinously on the lateral surface of the tibial condyle.

occurrences.name: Iliotibialis 1 and 2
occurrences.attachmentNote: Rugosities on the dorsal surface of the supraacetabular crest. Godoy et al. note the surface is unusually extensively rugose in P. sera, implying a larger attachment area than in comparable notosuchians.

occurrences.name: Iliotibialis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Crocodylus porosus. Three parts, and all three insert by tendon on the PROXIMO-ANTERIOR TIBIA: IT1 fleshy from the antero-lateral ilium, IT2 by tendon from the central lateral ilium between IT1 and IT3, IT3 fleshy from the postero-lateral ilium. IT2 is the largest and forms almost the whole dorsolateral face of the thigh. All three are knee extensors, which is what a tibial insertion is for, and EMG confirms it for IT2.

occurrences.name: M. iliotibialis cranialis + lateralis
occurrences.note: = crocodylian iliotibialis 1-3.

architecture.note: Values as modelled; maximum isometric force is derived, not measured.

occurrences.name: Rectus femoris + tensor fasciae latae
occurrences.action: Extends the knee; flexes the hip.
occurrences.innervation: Femoral nerve; superior gluteal nerve (tensor fasciae latae).
occurrences.attachmentNote: Galictis cuja. Rectus femoris from the quadriceps tuberosity of the ilium and the cranial hip capsule to the anterodorsal patellar margin; tensor fasciae latae from a small area of the iliac wing, inserting not on bone but through the fascia lata onto gluteus superficialis, biceps femoris, sartorius and the crural fascia.

occurrences.name: Iliotibialis (+ femorotibialis, + 'ambiens')
occurrences.attachmentNote: Gekko gecko, from the differences column of Zaaf et al.'s tables. Zaaf et al. examined this muscle in both geckos and record no difference, so the Eublepharis rows stand for Gekko too. A blank in a differences column is an observation of sameness, not a gap, and scoring it as a row is what lets the clade rollup say the two species AGREE rather than say nothing.

occurrences.name: Iliotibialis
occurrences.action: Extends the shank; also abducts and possibly retracts the femur.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Trachemys scripta, from Walker (1973). Band-shaped, its main origin on the posterodorsal corner of the ilium dorsal to the iliofibularis origin, plus a **second tendinous head in *Pseudemys*** from the anterior border of the ilium. Sitting high on the ilium it can abduct and retract the femur as well as extend the shank.

occurrences.name: Rectus femoris
occurrences.action: Extends the knee and flexes the hip.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). Straight head from the anterior inferior iliac spine, reflected head from above the acetabular rim, to the patella and the tibial tuberosity through the patellar ligament. **The rectus femoris is why the quadriceps is a composite of two different ancestral muscles**: it comes from this record and the three vasti come from the femorotibialis, which is exactly why the rectus crosses the hip and the vasti do not. Read the two rows together — one human muscle group, two homology groups, and the joint each part spans is the tell. The urodele end of this record is actively disputed: Kardong derives femorotibialis, iliotibialis and 'ambiens' from three separate salamander muscles, Gadow, Walker and Diogo & Molnar from one.

occurrences.name: M. iliotibialis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Iguana iguana, Russell & Bauer (2008). Largely by a broad aponeurosis from the lateral surface of the ilium, its anteriormost portion taking fleshy origin from the girdle instead, inserting with the femorotibialis by a common tendon onto the cnemial crest. **The patella is embedded in that tendon** — Russell & Bauer give Currey's (1984) reason, that the sesamoid keeps the moment arm large at every joint angle. This muscle is the dorsalmost part of the functional 'quadriceps' of lizards, but Russell & Bauer are explicit that the complex is not a developmental unit: this record and `femorotibialis` and `ambiens` are three different things acting together, which is exactly the composite the human quadriceps also is.

occurrences.name: M. ileo-tibialis and M. pubo-tibialis, heads of the M. extensor triceps
occurrences.innervation: Rr. ileo-tibialis and pubo-tibialis of the N. cruralis; the proximal ileo-tibialis also from the N. peroneus communis.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Sphenodon punctatus, Osawa (1898), *Zur Muskellehre*. Osawa's *M. extensor triceps* is Günther's extensor cruris quadriceps and Fürbringer's *pubo-ileo-bifemoro-tibialis s. quadriceps femoris*, and he is explicit that it has **three** heads, not four. Two are scored here: the lateral *ileo-tibialis* by a broad tendon from the lateral ilium above the ileo-femoralis origin, and the medial *pubo-tibialis* from the base of the pubic tubercle with the pubo-tibialis posticus and from the hip joint capsule. Gadow called the medial head the *ambiens* — which is this dataset's separate record — so the tuatara's 'quadriceps' contains a muscle another author names elsewhere. All three heads unite distally and insert through a **partly cartilaginous ligamentum patellare** on the anterior head of the tibia. The third head is scored on `femorotibialis`.

occurrences.name: Rectus femoris
occurrences.attachmentNote: Spilocuscus maculatus. **A double origin**, of which the reflected head is much the larger; the other head, though quite distinct, is a very slender tendon. **Neither animal has an osseous patella.** The parts of the quadriceps, with the sartorius, unite instead into an exceedingly dense tendinous expansion in front of the knee — so tough and knife-resistant that Cunningham likened its consistence to fibrocartilage, and in the wombat, he reports, it apparently becomes cartilage outright. `skeleton.json` scores the patella present in Theria, which is a clade statement; these are two animals inside that clade without one, and the fact is recorded here rather than used to flip the clade. Cunningham reports two heads in the koala (Young) and in *Perameles lagotis* (Owen), against Macalister's single head from the anterior inferior iliac spine in the brushtail possum, opossum, wombat, Tasmanian devil and both kangaroos — so a two-headed rectus is the minority condition among marsupials and both of Cunningham's animals have it.

occurrences.name: Rectus femoris
occurrences.attachmentNote: Thylacinus cynocephalus. A double origin, and here **the straight head is enormous** — Cunningham says it recalls the long head of the triceps in the fore limb of the same animal, which he had described taking nearly the whole axillary border of the scapula. It arises by a thin aponeurosis along the entire lower border of the ilium, from the reflected tendon behind to the anterior superior spine in front, and that aponeurosis gives place to a thick fleshy triangular belly joining the reflected head. The reflected head is strongly marked too. **Neither animal has an osseous patella.** The parts of the quadriceps, with the sartorius, unite instead into an exceedingly dense tendinous expansion in front of the knee — so tough and knife-resistant that Cunningham likened its consistence to fibrocartilage, and in the wombat, he reports, it apparently becomes cartilage outright. `skeleton.json` scores the patella present in Theria, which is a clade statement; these are two animals inside that clade without one, and the fact is recorded here rather than used to flip the clade.

occurrences.name: Rectus femoris
occurrences.attachmentNote: Tachyglossus aculeatus, Gambaryan et al. (2002). From a strong tendon on a tuberosity of the ilium very close to the acetabulum, the tendon continuing as a superficial sheet over the proximal third of the muscle; the distal part is again covered by a tendinous sheet reaching the upper point of the patella, with muscle fibres still traceable under the covering. **Distinctly separate from the vasti here**, where in the platypus it is fused with them — and the tiny gluteus profundus wraps round this muscle's origin on three sides, which is how that muscle is identified.

occurrences.name: Rectus femoris
occurrences.attachmentNote: Ornithorhynchus anatinus, Gambaryan et al. (2002). From the same iliac tuberosity as in the echidna, but its distal part is fused with the vastus lateralis and vastus medialis, all three inserting together on the proximal half of the inner surface of the patella.

occurrences.name: Extensor ilio-tibialis lateralis + anterior
occurrences.attachmentNote: *Grus americana*, Fisher & Goodman (1955); anconal and palmar are dorsal and ventral in their usage. **M. extensor ilio-tibialis lateralis.** —A broad, double aponeurotic sheet covers the entire ilial re- gion and forms a common origin for Mm. extens. ilio-tib. lat. and ant. M. extens. ilio-fib. also takes origin from the deeper part of this apo- neurosis. The deep part of the sheet is very fibrous, almost tendinous; 76 MUSCLES OF THE LEG 77 bands of fibers radiate anteriorly, dorso-anteriorly, and dorsally from the antitrochanteric region to form strengthening bands in the origin. Anteriorly the aponeurosis covers Mm. glut. prof. and piriformis; pos- teriorly it hides the proximal part of M. extens. ilio-fib. The ultimate attach *Insertion.* Just above the knee, the anterior fleshy part of this muscle joins the posterior edge of M. extens. ilio-tib. ant. to form a common, diamond-shaped sheet of insertion. M. vastus lat. fuses strongly with the deep surface of this sheet, which sheet in turn is a major component of the patellar tendon. It is quite noticeable that the anterior part of the sheet inserts on the patellar tendon; the posterior portion of the apo- neurosis sends strong fibers of connective tissue directly to the rotular crest and to the anterior surface of the outer cnemial crest, in addition to its patellar contribution. **M. extensor ilio-tibialis anterior.** Superficially the origin is aponeurotic from the anterior part of the iliac crest, anterior to, but continuous with, the origin of M. extens. ilio-tib. lat. (figs. 22, 25). The origin extends medially, by aponeurosis, to the neural crests of the posterior lumbar vertebrae. There is fleshy origin from the entire width of the ilial blade antero-dorsal to the origin of M. glut. prof. (fig. 29). In G. canadensis the origin is similar to the aponeurotic origin just described; we did not find the primary origin to be from the anterior end of the ilium as did Hudson (1937). 78 THE MYOLOGY OF THE WHOOPING CRANE *Insertion.* The fleshy insertion on the medial side of the patellar ten- don is covered medially by the most proximal fleshy head of origin of the pars interna of M. gastroc. On the lateral surface of the knee the apo- neurosis of insertion is superficially continuous with that of M. extens. ilio-tib. lat., but there is a round tendon here which apparently forms the main lateral insertion of M. extens. ilio-tib. ant. This tendon runs through the patellar tendon, deep to, and sometimes fused with, the inserting tendon of M. femoritib. int., and inserts on the base of the inner cnemial crest just medial to the rotular crest.

occurrences.name: Ilio-tibialis (IT)
occurrences.attachmentNote: Prestosuchus chiniquensis, Liparini & Schultz (2013). **Both ends at level I.** Muscle scars on the dorsal crest and the subtriangular rugosity of the ilium carry the first head, and the dorsolateral crest carries the second and third together; insertion on the cnemial crest through the common knee extensor tendon. *Prestosuchus* shows no osteological structure dividing the second head from the third, and Liparini & Schultz leave them undivided where Schachner et al. (2011) restore three separate heads in *Poposaurus* on parsimony alone. Function: the group as a whole a knee extensor, but its preacetabular portion capable of acting as a hip flexor.

homology.notes: The urodele/reptile correspondence is actively disputed. Kardong (2002) derives the reptilian femorotibialis, iliotibialis and 'ambiens' from three distinct salamander muscles; Gadow (1882), Walker (1954) and Diogo & Molnar derive all three from a single salamander extensor iliotibialis. The dissections in Diogo & Molnar (2014) support the latter.
homology.openQuestion: One salamander muscle or three? The answer changes how many separate acquisitions are needed in the reptile lineage.
homology.caveat: Leavey et al. (2024), using diceCT on 30 frog species across five locomotor modes, report that bone lengths and pelvic crest sizes are generally NOT reliable predictors of muscle size, and find many-to-one form-function mapping. That is a direct caution against reading muscle proportions off skeletal proportions in fossils, which is the inference osteological correlates are usually recruited for. Correlates locate an attachment; they do not size the muscle that made it.

correspondences.note: Both are the principal extensor of the second limb joint, but the correspondence is functional and topological, not developmental.
correspondences.caution: Diogo & Molnar (2014) find no clear topological equivalent here. Across every tetrapod clade in their Tables 13-21, including urodeles, they report that not one pelvic or thigh muscle has a clear topological equivalent in the pectoral region or arm, and attribute the lack to phylogenetic constraint on the girdles. This edge records a pairing the literature makes; it is not one that source supports.

muscles.name: Iliofibularis
muscles.developmental: Somitic; dorsal (extensor) mass.

consensus.origin: Lateral surface of the ilium, posterior to the iliofemoralis origin.
consensus.insertion: Proximal fibula, via a broad tendon.
consensus.action: Extends the hip and flexes the knee; stabilises the femur during the stance phase.

occurrences.name: M. iliofibularis
occurrences.note: Tomańska et al. (2025) report it stabilising the pelvic region and femur during movement in Varanus komodoensis, allowing hip abduction. Dick & Clemente (2016) include it among the major varanid locomotor muscles.

occurrences.name: M. iliofibularis
occurrences.note: Its insertion marks the iliofibular tubercle on the fibular shaft, which Pereyra et al. (2024) use as the landmark for the fibularis longus origin.

occurrences.name: M. iliofibularis
occurrences.note: Name retained across the crocodylian–avian transition. Allen et al. (2021) find knee-flexor leverage declining relative to knee extensors along the bird line, which is the leverage change underlying the shift from hip-driven to knee-driven propulsion.

architecture.note: Values as modelled; maximum isometric force is derived, not measured.

occurrences.name: iliofibularis
occurrences.note: Present in anurans under the same name; Přikryl et al. (2009) describe it attaching to the knee aponeurosis, partly covering the head of the fibula.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Discoglossus and Ascaphus, from Prikryl et al.'s review table and descriptions. The dorsal member of the iliofibularis/iliofemoralis pair, sharing their origin on the tuber superius. Its distal half is exposed and attaches into the knee aponeurosis, in part covering the head of the fibula — so the fibular attachment is by way of the aponeurosis rather than directly onto bone.

occurrences.name: Iliofibularis
occurrences.action: Elevates the femur and flexes the knee.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Runs parallel to the extensor iliotibialis but slightly deeper and posterior, crossing both hip and knee. The insertion is the site the iliofibular tubercle marks in taxa that have one; no landmark is asserted here because the paper does not name a tubercle.
occurrences.origin: External face of the ilium, just posterior to the extensor iliotibialis.
occurrences.insertion: Posterior side of the proximal end of the fibula, by a tendon.

occurrences.name: M. iliofibularis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Iguana iguana, Russell & Bauer (2008). Fleshy origin from the posteroventral margin of the ilium, the cylindrical belly not tapering as it descends, giving rise to a wide flat tendon as it passes between the peroneus longus and the femoral gastrocnemius to attach to the expanded blade-like part of the proximal fibular shaft. One of the simplest rows in the hindlimb and one of the most useful, because the muscle is what the iliofibular trochanter of archosaurs is read from.

occurrences.name: M. ileo-fibularis
occurrences.innervation: N. ileo-fibularis of the N. peroneus communis.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Sphenodon punctatus, Osawa (1898), *Zur Muskellehre*. Fürbringer's *ileo-fibularis s. glutaeus maximus* — another mammalian name on a lepidosaur muscle. A slender muscle on the lateral thigh between the ilio-tibialis and the ischio-tibialis posticus, **covering the N. peroneus communis from outside**, from the lateral surface of the ilium below the ileo-femoralis origin to the lateral surface of the proximal second quarter of the fibula.

occurrences.name: Extensor ilio-fibularis
occurrences.attachmentNote: *Grus americana*, Fisher & Goodman (1955); anconal and palmar are dorsal and ventral in their usage. **M. extensor ilio-fibularis.** There is fleshy origin from a narrow line on the posterior iliac crest from the antitrochanteric region to the anterior edge of the origin of M. flex. cruris lat. (figs. 22, 29). Lateral to the head of the femur there is an aponeurotic origin that covers the posterior edge of M. piriformis; in this same region there is very close attachment to the deep aponeurotic origin of M. extens. ilio-tib. lat. Insertion —The heavy inserting tendon passes through the character- istic tendinous loop, the proximal medial end of which is attached to the proximal end of the external femoral condyle (fig. 33) and the distal lateral end to the most lateral proximal part of the flexor attachment area on the *Insertion.* The heavy inserting tendon passes through the character- istic tendinous loop, the proximal medial end of which is attached to the proximal end of the external femoral condyle (fig. 33) and the distal lateral end to the most lateral proximal part of the flexor attachment area on the femur. The third arm of this loop, as described by Hudson (1937:25 and fig. 3), is not present as such.
