In its place is a strong vin- culum which is 2 centimeters wide and passes to the tendinous origin of the several flexor muscles posterior to the knee (fig. 33); this vinculum is in part covered laterally by M. flex. perf. et perf. dig. II. We found MUSCLES OF THE LEG

occurrences.name: Ilio-fibularis (ILFB)
occurrences.attachmentNote: Prestosuchus chiniquensis, Liparini & Schultz (2013). Origin at level II′ on the lateral surface of the postacetabular ilium, with no osteological structure marking where; insertion at level I on the iliofibular tubercle, which is as secure as this reconstruction gets — the same prominent tubercle carries the muscle in birds, crocodylians, *Tyrannosaurus* and *Poposaurus*. The uncertainty is all at the iliac end: *Prestosuchus* has a crest running the whole dorsal and dorsolateral margin of the ilium with a rugose oval area caudally, and the authors state they could not determine whether that crest carries the ilio-tibialis group alone, as in crocodylians, or shares it with the ilio-fibularis, as in birds. They also reject the ridge Carrano & Hutchinson use in *Tyrannosaurus* to divide iliofemoralis from iliofibularis: no living archosaur supports a vertical ridge doing that.

homology.notes: One of the muscles whose name survives unchanged from crocodylians to birds in Allen et al.'s (2021) table. Its correspondence with the mammalian biceps femoris is proposed but not settled — Diogo & Molnar (2014) treat the hamstring group as deriving from the ischioflexorius field rather than from a single iliofibularis.
homology.openQuestion: Is the amniote iliofibularis the homologue of the mammalian biceps femoris, or does the hamstring group derive wholesale from the ischioflexorius field?
homology.teaching: A muscle spanning hip and knee whose declining leverage is measurable along the bird line — a case where a function claim rests on geometry, not on presence or absence.

correspondences.note: Diogo & Molnar (2014) report that no pelvic or thigh muscle has a clear topological equivalent in the pectoral region or arm in any tetrapod clade they examine, which is the general result this particular absence sits under.

muscles.name: Femorotibialis
muscles.developmental: Somitic; dorsal mass.
synonyms: vastus lateralis + vastus medialis + vastus intermedius (mammals)

consensus.insertion: Tibia, via the knee extensor apparatus.
consensus.action: Extends the knee. Because it does not cross the hip, it is a pure knee extensor.

occurrences.note: Not separated from the extensor iliotibialis in salamanders under the Gadow/Walker/Diogo & Molnar reading.

occurrences.name: Femorotibialis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Fleshy origin along the entire femoral shaft; joins the iliotibialis tendon to insert on the cnemial crest. Knee extensor, active in both stance and swing.

occurrences.name: Femorotibialis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Crocodylus porosus. Externus arises fleshy about a third of the way down the dorsal femur and inserts on the proximo-lateral cnemial crest; internus arises by tendon on the dorso-proximal femur, distal and anterior to iliofemoralis, and joins the same tendon at insertion.

occurrences.name: M. femorotibialis lateralis + medialis
occurrences.note: = crocodylian femorotibialis externus and internus.

architecture.note: Values as modelled; maximum isometric force is derived, not measured.

occurrences.name: Vastus lateralis, medialis and intermedius
occurrences.action: Extend the knee.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Galictis cuja. The three vasti, all femoral in origin and patellar in insertion — which is the character that separates them from the rectus femoris head of the same complex. Vastus lateralis from the cranioproximal femur medial to the greater trochanter base, to the lateral patellar margin and proximolateral tibia; vastus medialis from the craniomedial femoral neck and diaphysis to the medial and mediodistal patella.

occurrences.name: Femorotibialis (vasti medialis, internus and externus)
occurrences.action: Extends the shank.

parts.name: Vastus medialis
parts.note: Arises from and covers the morphological dorsal surface of the femur.

parts.name: Vastus internus
parts.note: From the distal border of the trochanter minor and the anteroventral femur.

parts.name: Vastus externus
parts.note: From the distal border of the trochanter major and the posteroventral femur.

occurrences.divisionNote: Trifurcate at its origin in *Pseudemys*, each part called a vastus. **The two other thigh muscles run between them**: the iliofemoralis insertion passes between the origins of vasti externus and medialis, and the puboischiofemoralis internus insertion separates medialis from internus. The three-way split is carved by what crosses it.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Trachemys scripta, from Walker (1973). The deepest and most massive part of the knee-extensor complex; all three vasti converge to form the greater part of the patellar tendon.

occurrences.name: Vastus lateralis, medialis and intermedius
occurrences.action: Extend the knee; articularis genu retracts the suprapatellar bursa.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). Three vasti from the anterior, lateral and medial femoral shaft and the two lips of the linea aspera, onto the patella. **One of the least contested correspondences in the hindlimb** — a femur-to-tibia extensor that never crosses the hip, in every tetrapod that has one. Articularis genu is scored as a fourth part: it is a few fibres of vastus intermedius that stop at the knee capsule instead of reaching the patella, and it is the smallest thing in this dataset that still counts as a muscle.

occurrences.name: M. femorotibialis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Iguana iguana, Russell & Bauer (2008). The most massive part of the 'quadriceps', investing the entire femoral shaft by folding from its origin and taking origin from virtually the whole length of it, diverging posteriorly into two masses that reconverge onto the iliotibialis insertion tendon. **A thin slender proximal tendon of origin arises next to the ischiotrochantericus tendon**, which Russell & Bauer read as indicating a primitive physical association with the ischial part of the girdle — a femoral muscle keeping a trace of a pelvic origin. Femur to tibia without crossing the hip, which is what distinguishes it from the rectus femoris in the mammalian complex.

occurrences.name: M. femoro-tibialis, deep head of the M. extensor triceps
occurrences.innervation: R. femoro-tibialis of the N. cruralis.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Sphenodon punctatus, Osawa (1898), *Zur Muskellehre*. Gadow's name; Fürbringer's *femoro-tibialis externus + internus*, Perrin's *tête profonde*. From the entire extensor surface of the femur from the neck to the distal end, and from the lateral and posterior surfaces of its distal half. **Its origin is interlocked with three other muscles**: on the front the origin digitation is clasped between the pubo-ischio-trochantericus internus and the ileo-femoralis, while on the back the insertions of the ileo-femoralis and ischio-femoralis are wedged between its two origin lines. Femur to tibia without crossing the hip, which is what separates it from the iliotibialis heads in every column on this record.

occurrences.name: Vasti, crureus and subcrureus
occurrences.attachmentNote: Spilocuscus maculatus. The vastus externus is the most strongly developed and **the only part even partially separable from the others**; the vastus internus and the crureus are intimately blended with each other. There is a very distinct subcrureus here, where the thylacine has no trace of one. They end in the dense patellar expansion described on `extensor-iliotibialis`, there being no bony patella in this animal.

occurrences.name: Vasti and crureus
occurrences.attachmentNote: Thylacinus cynocephalus. As in the cuscus — vastus externus strongest and alone partially separable, vastus internus and crureus intimately blended — but **with no trace of a subcrureus**. The gluteus quartus of this animal passes down between the vastus externus and the vastus internus to reach the femoral shaft.

occurrences.name: Vastus lateralis and vastus medialis
occurrences.divisionNote: Two vasti, not three: Gambaryan et al. describe no vastus intermedius in either monotreme.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Tachyglossus aculeatus, Gambaryan et al. (2002). Vastus lateralis from the lateral half of the cranial surface of the femur medial to the gluteus medius insertion, narrowing distally to fuse with the medialis. Vastus medialis from the dorsal aspect of the trochanter minor lateral to the iliopsoas insertion, broadening as it runs distally, the two fusing to insert by fibres on the proximal half of the patella. **Note the plane.** Gambaryan et al. warn at the outset that the cranial surface of the monotreme femur faces dorsally and the caudal surface ventrally, so 'cranial surface of the femur' here is not the plane a reader of therian myology will picture.

occurrences.name: Vastus lateralis and vastus medialis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Ornithorhynchus anatinus, Gambaryan et al. (2002). Vastus lateralis from the proximal half of the femur above the gluteus medius insertion. **The vastus medialis is totally replaced by the iliopsoas** over the cranial surface of the proximal half of the femur — the knee extensor has lost its origin to a hip flexor whose insertion Gambaryan et al. call unique among mammals. The two vasti and the rectus femoris fuse to insert on the proximal half of the inner surface of the patella. At 0.8 per cent of hind limb mass against the echidna's 3.9 per cent, the medialis is the muscle that pays for that.

occurrences.name: Femoritibialis externus
occurrences.attachmentNote: *Grus americana*, Fisher & Goodman (1955); anconal and palmar are dorsal and ventral in their usage. **M. femoritibialis externus.** The origin is widely fleshy from the lateral face of the femur, extending proximally from the proximal end of the external condylar crest to approximately the middle of the length of the femur. Proximally the origin is on the lateral face of the femur, but it is on the anterior surface distally. The deep part of the distal half of the origin is aponeu- rotic from the lateral edge of the popliteal region (fig. 31). Insertion—Part of the insertion is on the patellar tendon, but the anterior two-thirds of the insertion forms a separate tendon to the disto- lateral tip of the outer cnemial crest of the tibiotarsus. Just before the patellar component fuses with the patellar tendon, M. flex. pe *Insertion.* Part of the insertion is on the patellar tendon, but the anterior two-thirds of the insertion forms a separate tendon to the disto- lateral tip of the outer cnemial crest of the tibiotarsus. Just before the patellar component fuses with the patellar tendon, M. flex. perf. et perf. dig. II takes part of its origin from the deep side of this component. Mm. obturator externus and internus These muscles (fig. 32) are as described by Fisher (1946:671) for the Black Vulture, except that no tibial innervation was found for M. obt. int. See figure 28, nos. 17 and 18, for the innervation in the Whooping Crane. Hudson (1937:28) stated that M. obt. ext. had two distinct parts in **Scored on `tibia` rather than `tibiotarsus`**: the cnemial crest is a tibial landmark, and `fusedFrom` is deliberately not containment in this schema, so the crest is not reachable through the compound bone. That is the convention the other avian rows already use.

occurrences.name: Femoro-tibialis (FMT)
occurrences.attachmentNote: Prestosuchus chiniquensis, Liparini & Schultz (2013). Origin at level I′ over the medial, cranial and lateral surfaces of the femoral shaft; insertion at level I on the cnemial crest, by the extensor tendon it shares with the ambiens and ilio-tibialis. The three rows record the three surfaces, not three muscles: the authors say the group was possibly divided into two or three portions — lateralis, intermedius and internus in the extant nomenclature — and decline to fix the number, so no `parts` are asserted. Inferred function is knee extension, and the muscle is placed in the stance phase of the stride with the caudofemorales, flexor cruris and adductores.

homology.notes: The femorotibialis → vasti correspondence is one of the least contested in the hindlimb. Together with the rectus femoris (from extensor iliotibialis) it forms the mammalian quadriceps — a composite of two different ancestral muscles, which is why the rectus femoris crosses the hip and the vasti do not.
homology.teaching: Explains a fact students memorise without understanding: why one of the four quadriceps heads flexes the hip and three do not. They are not four parts of one muscle; they are two muscles.

correspondences.caution: Diogo & Molnar (2014) find no clear topological equivalent here. Across every tetrapod clade in their Tables 13-21, including urodeles, they report that not one pelvic or thigh muscle has a clear topological equivalent in the pectoral region or arm, and attribute the lack to phylogenetic constraint on the girdles. This edge records a pairing the literature makes; it is not one that source supports.

muscles.name: 'Ambiens'
muscles.developmental: Somitic; dorsal mass. Romer (1942) and Jones (1979) emphasise that it is a DORSAL muscle despite its ventral position.

consensus.insertion: Tibia (and in some archosaurs, via the digital flexor tendons).
consensus.action: Protracts the femur and extends the knee.

occurrences.note: Not present as a separate muscle; part of the undivided extensor iliotibialis.

occurrences.name: 'Ambiens'
occurrences.note: Reptiles may have both an 'ambiens' and a 'pubifemoralis'; the two names are sometimes used as synonyms (Russell & Bauer 2008), which is a persistent source of confusion.
occurrences.attachmentNote: In Varanus komodoensis the muscle has dorsal and ventral heads; the dorsal attaches to the ventral edge of the acetabulum and the ventral lies anteriorly, both converging on the femur at the intertrochanteric fossa.

occurrences.name: 'Ambiens'
occurrences.attachmentNote: Crocodylus porosus. Tendinous origin on the proximo-lateral pubis, inserting by a long tendon on the proximo-anterior tibia AT THE CNEMIAL CREST — the crest is named in the source, so it is scored rather than left at the bone. Knee extensor and hip flexor, knee extension confirmed by EMG. Klinkhamer et al. found only a SINGLE HEAD, against two in Alligator mississippiensis, but they attribute that to the sub-adult age of their specimens and of the Caiman latirostris in the earlier study that found the same — NOT to a species difference. Recorded here as an observation and explicitly not as a Crocodylus porosus character.

occurrences.name: M. ambiens
occurrences.note: In birds the ambiens tendon famously passes to the digital flexors, an arrangement once invoked (incorrectly) as an automatic perching mechanism. Hip flexor and knee extensor; the name is retained across the transition.

architecture.note: Values as modelled; maximum isometric force is derived, not measured.

occurrences.note: Diogo & Molnar reject the classical derivation of the mammalian sartorius from the 'ambiens'; they derive the sartorius from the anterior head of puboischiofemoralis internus (Walker & Homberger 1997).

occurrences.name: 'Ambiens'
occurrences.action: Adducts and protracts the thigh, and extends the shank.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Trachemys scripta, from Walker (1973). A weak muscle from the posterior part of the base of the lateral pubic process and the adjacent puboischiadic ligament, onto the patellar tendon. It crosses the hip as well as the knee. **With the thigh in its normal turtle position — morphological dorsal surface directed anteriorly — the ambiens lies along its anteroventral border**, which is not where a reader importing the lizard arrangement would look for it.

occurrences.note: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). **Absent, and the note is about the muscle it is not.** The classical equation makes the amniote 'ambiens' the mammalian sartorius, and Diogo & Molnar reject it: the diagnostic is that the 'ambiens' is a DORSAL muscle sitting in a ventral position, which the sartorius is not. Gest's sartorius runs from the anterior superior iliac spine to the medial tibia through the pes anserinus, on the femoral nerve, and this dataset gives it no home rather than give it a wrong one. The same rejection is why 'tensor fasciae latae' appears on Diogo & Molnar's list of false-friend names.

occurrences.name: 'Ambiens'
occurrences.attachmentNote: Iguana iguana, Russell & Bauer (2008). The smallest and anteriormost part of the 'quadriceps' complex, arising by a bifurcated tendon — the broader branch onto the pubis immediately anterior to the acetabulum, the slender posterior branch passing ventral to the femoral head to attach in the intertrochanteric notch and spread along the ventral acetabular rim, so that **part of the muscle's origin becomes part of the hip joint capsule**. It contributes the anterior portion of the 'quadriceps' tendon. The record's name is quoted because the diagnostic point is that this is a dorsal muscle sitting in a ventral position; Diogo & Molnar reject the classical equation with the mammalian sartorius, which is why the human row on this record is scored absent.

occurrences.name: Ambiens (AMB)
occurrences.attachmentNote:
Prestosuchus chiniquensis, Liparini & Schultz (2013). **Both ends at level I** — the strongest reconstruction in the paper, and one of only two muscles scoring level I at the origin. Muscular scars on the dorsal tubercle, dorsal crest, lateral crest and cranial tubercle of the pubis, and on the iliac peduncle where it contacts the pubis; insertion on the cnemial crest by the knee extensor tendon shared with the femoro-tibialis and ilio-tibialis. In both extant archosaur groups a secondary tendon perforates that extensor tendon — in birds to reach the tendon of origin of the digital flexors and gastrocnemius lateralis, in crocodylians to reach the gastrocnemius lateralis itself — and the reconstruction carries that perforating portion over.

Prestosuchus chiniquensis, Liparini & Schultz (2013). A second ambiens head, at level II′, from the proximal medial surface of the pubis over the pubo-ischiadic plate. **It has no bony insertion and none is scored**: like its counterpart in extant lepidosaurs and crocodylians it inserts on the femoro-tibialis, muscle to muscle, and an empty insertion here is the accurate record of that. Carrano & Hutchinson treat the two-headed ambiens as a crocodylian autapomorphy with no avian homologue, and reconstruct it in neither *Tyrannosaurus* nor *Poposaurus*; Liparini & Schultz restore it here on the argument that the crocodylian condition is plesiomorphic and matched in lepidosaurs. **It is one of the two muscles this paper adds to the pseudosuchian stem that the bird-line reconstructions do not carry.**

homology.notes: The critical diagnostic is that the 'ambiens' is a DORSAL muscle sitting in a ventral position. The amphibian 'pubifemoralis', which looks superficially similar in dorsal view, is a deep VENTRAL muscle and corresponds instead to the reptilian adductor femoris. Diogo & Molnar make this call explicitly and reject the ambiens→sartorius derivation.
homology.teaching: A worked example of using mass assignment (dorsal vs ventral) rather than position to settle a homology dispute.

correspondences.note: Diogo & Molnar (2014) report that no pelvic or thigh muscle has a clear topological equivalent in the pectoral region or arm in any tetrapod clade they examine, which is the general result this particular absence sits under.

muscles.name: Adductor femoris
muscles.developmental: Somitic; deep ventral mass.
synonyms: adductor magnus + adductor longus + adductor brevis (mammals)

consensus.origin: Ventral surface of the pelvic girdle (pubis and ischium).
consensus.insertion: Ventral surface of the femur.
consensus.action: Adducts and retracts the femur.
consensus.innervation: Obturator nerve (with a sciatic contribution to the adductor magnus in mammals).

occurrences.name: 'Pubifemoralis'
occurrences.note: Diogo & Molnar's dissections support the amphibian 'pubifemoralis' = reptilian adductor femoris, against the alternative that it corresponds to the 'ambiens'. Both are deep ventral muscles lying just dorsal to the pubotibialis and running from the ventral girdle to the ventral femur; the 'ambiens' is dorsal.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Recorded as m. pubifemoralis. The three ventral pelvis-to-femur muscles are separated by their sequence along the femur rather than by distinct attachment sites — internus anterior, pubifemoralis next, externus posterior.
occurrences.origin: Anterior and ventral surface of the pubo-ischiac plate, anterior to the puboischiofemoralis externus.
occurrences.insertion: Ventral face of the femur, anterior and distal to the puboischiofemoralis externus but posterior to the puboischiofemoralis internus.

occurrences.name: Adductor femoris
occurrences.attachmentNote: From the puboischiadic ligament to the ventral femoral shaft; adducts and protracts the femur, active in both stance and swing.

occurrences.name: Adductor femoris
occurrences.attachmentNote: Fleshy at the ventrolateral ischium, tendinous at the ventromedial femur.

occurrences.name: M. puboischiofemoralis medialis + lateralis
occurrences.note: = crocodylian adductor femoris 1 and 2 respectively.

occurrences.name: Adductor magnus, longus and brevis
occurrences.action: Adduct and extend the thigh.
occurrences.innervation: Obturator nerve; the hamstring part of adductor magnus by the tibial division of the sciatic nerve.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Galictis cuja. Adductor magnus and adductor brevis share a small origin on the caudal ramus of the pubis and the ischial ramus. Magnus inserts on the distal caudal femur in two areas just proximal to the condyles, sharing fibres with semimembranosus; brevis on the proximal third of the lateral femur. Adductor longus lies between pectineus and magnus and its origin is not scored here.

occurrences.name: Adductor magnus, longus, brevis and minimus
occurrences.action: Adduct the thigh; the ischiocondylar part of adductor magnus extends it.
occurrences.innervation: Obturator nerve, both divisions; the ischiocondylar part of adductor magnus by the tibial nerve, and pectineus by the femoral nerve.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). Four adductors from the pubic rami and the ischial tuberosity onto the linea aspera, plus pectineus from the pecten of the pubis to the pectineal line. **The nerve supply is split three ways across one mass** and each split means something: the ischiocondylar part of adductor magnus takes the tibial nerve because it belongs functionally with the hamstrings, and pectineus takes the femoral nerve — and 'pectineus' is another name on Diogo & Molnar's false-friends list. This record also resolves the first of their two contested amphibian muscles: the 'pubifemoralis' is this, not the 'ambiens' it superficially resembles in dorsal view.

occurrences.name: M. adductor femoris
occurrences.attachmentNote: Iguana iguana, Russell & Bauer (2008). A thick triangular muscle from the puboischiadic ligament — ligament, not bone — narrowing to insert along the ventral femoral shaft over about its middle third, between the two divergent components of the femorotibialis and in close association with the iliofemoralis insertion. Diogo & Molnar resolve the amphibian 'pubifemoralis' as this muscle rather than as the 'ambiens' it superficially resembles in dorsal view, which is the other of their two contested ventral pelvic cases.

occurrences.name: Triceps adductor and pectineus
occurrences.attachmentNote: Thylacinus cynocephalus. **Three strata as in a human, and Cunningham's point is that the human names misdescribe them**: the adductor longus is the shortest muscle, the brevis the bulkiest, the magnus the longest. The longus takes a pointed origin from the base of the marsupial bone and expands to the middle third of the posterior femur, fused with the brevis beneath it. The brevis has a wide origin from the pubic arch and the front of the ischial tuberosity and runs from the lesser trochanter down to the medial condyle. The magnus comes off the ischial tuberosity under the semimembranosus and gracilis, less bulky than the brevis but reaching lower — the posterior shaft in its lower two-thirds and, by fleshy fibres, the inner side of the medial condyle. **Both the brevis and the magnus are perforated by the femoral artery** as it passes back into the popliteal space. The pectineus in this animal springs entirely from the cartilaginous nodule that represents the marsupial bone and inserts just below the lesser trochanter.

occurrences.name: Triceps adductor and pectineus
occurrences.divisionNote: The adductor longus is absent, on the evidence of the obturator nerve lying superficial to the adductor brevis.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Spilocuscus maculatus. **Only two adductors — the brevis and the magnus — and Cunningham identifies the missing one by a nerve**: the obturator nerve lies on the superficial aspect of the adductor brevis, which it could not do if the adductor longus were there in front of it. The brevis is much the larger, hiding the magnus completely from the front, with a curved origin from the base of the marsupial bone and the margin of the pubic symphysis under the gracilis, the same insertion as the thylacine's, and the same perforation by the femoral artery. The magnus is a thick fleshy strap from the pubic arch and the ischial tuberosity to the lower third of the posterior femur, and **it is not perforated by the artery**; the two separate easily. The pectineus is better marked than the thylacine's: a small pointed origin from the anterior margin of the pubis and slightly from the outer and lower angle of the large marsupial bone, expanding to a linear insertion on the middle third of the posterior femur in front of the adductor brevis. Cunningham reports the group varying widely across Marsupialia — three distinct portions in the wallaby and giant kangaroo, brevis and magnus partly or wholly blended in the opossum, *Sarcophilus*, wombat and *Phalangista*.

occurrences.name: Pectineus, adductor longus, magnus and brevis
occurrences.divisionNote: **Gambaryan et al. separate magnus from brevis on insertion, not origin**, because the two have so often been confused: the brevis insertion is the most lateral and often takes the lateral edge of the trochanteric crest, while the magnus runs down the caudal femur and works medially towards the labium mediale or the medial epicondyle. They agree with everyone else that the adductor longus is fixed by its origin beside the pectineus.
occurrences.action: Adduct the femur; pronate it through their insertions on the medial epicondyle.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Tachyglossus aculeatus, Gambaryan et al. (2002). Pectineus by an aponeurosis on the tuberculum musculi psoas minoris lateral to the gracilis anterior, curving ventrally to the cranial edge of the proximal half of the pubis, and inserting by aponeurosis on the medial third of the labium mediale ossis femoris. Adductor longus from the epipubis lateral to the gracilis anterior — nearly half the ventral surface of that bone — and along the symphysis to the proximal third of the caudal edge of the ischium; insertion broad, from the medial third of the labium mediale nearly to the distal end of the medial epicondyle, passing beneath the medial collateral ligament. Adductor magnus aponeurotically from the ischial tuberosity cranial to the semimembranosus anterior and from the first half of the caudal edge of the ischium, its most caudal fibres onto the caudal femur between the gastrocnemius medialis origin and the adductor longus insertion, joining the adductor longus tendon at the medial epicondyle. Adductor brevis from the ventral surfaces of the symphysial branches of ischium and pubis, between the other adductors and the obturator foramen, by a narrow aponeurosis onto a rugosity between the quadratus femoris and obturator externus insertions. **In the echidna the medial epicondyle is elongated medially**, which lengthens the adductors' lever arms — the reason Gambaryan et al. count them among the pronators of a femur that barely retracts.

occurrences.name: Pectineus, adductor longus, magnus and brevis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Ornithorhynchus anatinus, Gambaryan et al. (2002). Pectineus by fibres on the dorsomedial surface of the tuberculum musculi psoas minoris caudal to the gracilis anterior, reaching the base of the tubercle and extending to the pubis–epipubis joint, inserting tendinously on the caudal aspect of the labium mediale ossis femoris over its medial fifth. Adductor longus in two distinct heads, from the medial and lateral edges of a rugosity of the pubis close to the pubis–epipubis joint and taking no part of the symphysial branch; the medial head's aponeurosis reaches the distal third of the labium mediale and the dorsal surface of the medial epicondyle, and the lateral head inserts by fibres on the medial head's tendinous sheet. Adductor magnus by a thin aponeurosis fused with the aponeurotic origin of the semimembranosus anterior, inserting along the labium mediale to the ventral surface of the medial epicondyle. Adductor brevis from the symphysial branches of ischium and pubis between the medial edge of the obturator foramen and the other two adductors, along the medial edge of the caudal surface of the trochanter major. **Gambaryan et al. use this animal's adductor brevis as the model from which the therian patterns can be derived**: move its origin from the cranial edge of the obturator foramen onto the ischial tuberosity and you have the marsupial, insectivore and rodent arrangement; keep only the cranial part of the origin and put the proximal adductor magnus insertion lateral to that of the brevis and you have the human one, which they attribute to erect posture since other primates do it differently.

occurrences.name: Adductor superficialis + adductor profundus
occurrences.attachmentNote: *Grus americana*, Fisher & Goodman (1955); anconal and palmar are dorsal and ventral in their usage. **M. adductor superficialis.** Fleshy from the most ventral edge of the ischium, starting | centimeter posterior to the acetabulum and continuing caudad for one- half the length of the ischium. On the inner side the origin is aponeurotic a s ° = 5 c 8 o *Insertion.* The insertion is usually entirely fleshy on the postero- internal edge of the femur distad from the level of insertion of pars caudi-fem. of M. caudofem. to the most posterior part of the origin of M. femoritib. ext. in the popliteal area. In lateral view the distal part of the insertion is covered by M. femoritib. ext., and the proximal part by the ventral part of M. caudofem. **M. adductor profundus.** This starts 1 centimeter posterior to the acetabulum, im- mediately deep to M. add. superf., and continues caudad to within 4 centimeters of the posterior tip of the pubis. The anterior half is mixed fleshy and tendinous superficially, but is entirely tendinous on the medial side from the ventral edge of the ischium and the fascia between the ischium and the pubis. The posterior half of the origin is primarily from the outer face and ventral edge of the pubis, the posterior third being completely tendinous. Most of the fleshy fibers of the posterior part of the muscle arise from the lateral surface of this tendon. Insertion.—The insertion, laterally fleshy and medially tendinous, starts 5 *Insertion.* The insertion, laterally fleshy and medially tendinous, starts 5.0 centimeters from the proximal end of the femur and extends distally on this bone to the popliteal region. The medial tendinous part of the insertion extends to the internal femoral condyle along a narrow line medial to the popliteal region. Thus the insertion lies on the mid-posterior surface of the femur, bordered medially by the origin of M. femoritib. int. and laterally by the insertion of M. add. superf.

occurrences.name: Adductores femores (ADD 1, ADD 2)
occurrences.attachmentNote: Prestosuchus chiniquensis, Liparini & Schultz (2013). Two heads at the pelvis, one insertion at the femur. The first arises on the cranial border of the ischium at a proximal cranioventral keel; the second on the caudolateral surface of the ischial shaft with no specific osteological correlate, which is why the origin is level II′ and rests on the crocodylian and lepidosaur condition being the most parsimonious. The insertion is level I on a single slightly elevated area of the caudal and caudodistal femoral shaft — **the authors state explicitly that they could not distinguish separate insertion sites for the two heads**, so one insertion row is the whole of what they claim.

homology.notes: Diogo & Molnar note that almost all amphibian–reptile ventral pelvic/thigh homologies are straightforward and consensual, with exactly two exceptions: the amphibian 'pubifemoralis' and 'ischiofemoralis'. They resolve both — pubifemoralis = adductor femoris, ischiofemoralis = ischiotrochantericus.

correspondences.caution: Diogo & Molnar (2014) find no clear topological equivalent here. Across every tetrapod clade in their Tables 13-21, including urodeles, they report that not one pelvic or thigh muscle has a clear topological equivalent in the pectoral region or arm, and attribute the lack to phylogenetic constraint on the girdles. This edge records a pairing the literature makes; it is not one that source supports.

muscles.name: Ischiotrochantericus
muscles.developmental: Somitic; ventral mass.

consensus.insertion: Trochanteric region of the proximal femur.
consensus.action: Laterally rotates the femur; stabilises the hip.
consensus.innervation: Sacral plexus branches; nerve to obturator internus in mammals.

occurrences.name: 'Ischiofemoralis'
occurrences.note: Most authors (and Diogo & Molnar) hold that the amphibian 'ischiofemoralis' corresponds to the reptilian ischiotrochantericus; Gadow (1882) was a minority voice for adductor femoris. Walker (1954, p. 94) defends the ischiotrochantericus reading.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Recorded as m. ischiofemoralis, and the passage that fixes the plate's composition: the paper equates the ischium with the plate's posterior portion, which is what licenses scoring the plate as pubis plus ischium throughout.
occurrences.origin: Lateral border of the ischium — the posterior portion of the pubo-ischiac plate.
occurrences.insertion: Posterior face of the head of the femur.

occurrences.name: Ischiotrochantericus
occurrences.attachmentNote: Scored from Zaaf et al.'s tables for Eublepharis macularius, with the Gekko gecko differences noted where they bear on the attachment. From the ischial tuberosity onto the proximal edge of the trochanter; in Gekko onto its distal edge.

occurrences.name: M. ischiofemoralis
occurrences.note: Hip extensor and lateral rotator.

occurrences.name: Obturator internus (+ gemelli)
occurrences.action: Laterally rotates the extended thigh; abducts the flexed thigh.
occurrences.divisionNote: The gemelli are claimed by this field and by the puboischiofemoralis externus; the dataset records both claims.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Obturator internus from the medial surface of the obturator foramen, turning over the dorsal margin of the ischium to reach the proximal trochanteric fossa. Frequently divided into two bellies near the origin and partially fused there with the gemelli, which this dataset assigns to the puboischiofemoralis externus — the membership dispute the parts list records.

occurrences.name: Ischiotrochantericus
occurrences.attachmentNote: Gekko gecko, from the differences column of Zaaf et al.'s tables. Inserts on the **distal** edge of the trochanter, against the proximal edge in Eublepharis.

occurrences.name: Obturator internus
occurrences.action: Laterally rotates the thigh.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). Internal surface of the obturator membrane and the margin of the obturator foramen, turning through a right angle around the lesser sciatic notch to the medial greater trochanter. **The obturator internus equation is one half of a pair Diogo & Molnar resolved**: of all the amphibian-to-reptile ventral pelvic homologies they found only two contested, the 'pubifemoralis' and the 'ischiofemoralis', and they resolve the second as this muscle. Note that obturator internus and obturator externus arise from the two faces of the same membrane and belong to different homology groups.

occurrences.name: M. ischiotrochantericus
occurrences.attachmentNote: Iguana iguana, Russell & Bauer (2008). From the ischial tuberosity and the dorsal surface of the posterior angle of the ischium, tapering to a strap-shaped tendon that passes behind the ilioischiadic junction to insert on the dorsal aspect of the proximal femur just distal to the joint capsule. Diogo & Molnar resolve this as the amphibian 'ischiofemoralis' and propose the mammalian obturator internus as its homolog — one of only two contested amphibian-to-reptile ventral pelvic correspondences they found.

occurrences.name: M. ischio-trochantericus
occurrences.innervation: Nervuli ileo-pectinei longi et breves from the sacral plexus.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Sphenodon punctatus, Osawa (1898), *Zur Muskellehre*. Günther's *M. quadratus femoris*, Fürbringer's *pubo-ischio-femoralis brevis* (his obturator externus + quadratus femoris in part), Gadow's *pubi-ischio-femoralis posterior*, Perrin's *rotateur inverse du femur* — **five names, four of them borrowed from mammalian muscles that are not this one**, which is what this dataset's false-friend list is about. A small muscle chiefly from the inner surface of the tuber ischii, also from its caudal border and a little of its outer surface, inserting beside the pubo-ischio-trochantericus externus on the trochanter minor and reinforcing the joint capsule. Diogo & Molnar resolve this record as the amphibian 'ischiofemoralis' and propose the mammalian obturator internus.

occurrences.name: Obturator internus and the gemelli
occurrences.attachmentNote: Spilocuscus maculatus. The obturator internus tendon plays in the lesser sciatic notch in both animals, but **the encrusting cartilage there is not raised into ridges**, so the tendon shows none of the longitudinal furrows that are so characteristic of the same muscle in a human. It inserts with the obturator externus into the bottom of a deep recess between the great trochanter and the femoral neck. Strongly developed here, where it is comparatively feeble in the thylacine. **The gemelli are enormously developed** and inseparable except at their origin — the superior from the ischium in front of the lesser sciatic notch, the inferior from the ischial tuberosity. The obturator internus tendon lies in a groove in their substance and they insert into that tendon, which is why Cunningham files them with this muscle rather than with the quadratus femoris. The nerve to the quadratus femoris passes down through their substance.

occurrences.name: Obturator internus and the gemelli
occurrences.attachmentNote: Thylacinus cynocephalus. The obturator internus tendon plays in the lesser sciatic notch in both animals, but **the encrusting cartilage there is not raised into ridges**, so the tendon shows none of the longitudinal furrows that are so characteristic of the same muscle in a human. It inserts with the obturator externus into the bottom of a deep recess between the great trochanter and the femoral neck. Comparatively feeble here. **The gemelli are more strongly marked still than the cuscus's, and each is itself segmented into a superficial and a deep part**; they fuse towards their insertion, which goes partly into the obturator internus tendon but chiefly straight into the recess between the great trochanter and the neck — so in this animal the gemelli reach bone on their own account. Cunningham uses a nerve to map them: the nerve to the quadratus femoris passes between the two segments of the gemellus superior but under cover of both parts of the gemellus inferior.

occurrences.name: Flexor ischiofemoralis
occurrences.attachmentNote: *Grus americana*, Fisher & Goodman (1955); anconal and palmar are dorsal and ventral in their usage. **M. flexor ischiofemoralis.** Fleshy from virtually the entire lateral surface of the ischium posteriorly from the ilio-ischiatic fenestra to a point just beneath the widest extension of the posterior iliac crest. At its caudal end the origin may be limited by the tendon of origin of pars caudi-fem. of M. caudo- fem. Insertion.—Tendinous on the postero-lateral part of the femur, some 3 centimeters distad, and posterior to and between the insertions of the two parts of M. caudofem. (fig. 31). *Insertion.* Tendinous on the postero-lateral part of the femur, some 3 centimeters distad, and posterior to and between the insertions of the two parts of M. caudofem. (fig. 31).

occurrences.name: Ischio-trochantericus (ISTR)
occurrences.attachmentNote: Prestosuchus chiniquensis, Liparini & Schultz (2013). Origin at level II′ from the medial surface of the ischium, on the proximal dorsocaudal keel — level II′ because **no osteological structure could be tied to it**, and the reconstruction rests on the medial origin being shared by extant lepidosaurs and crocodylians. Insertion at level I on muscle scars at the distal base of the greater trochanter, on the caudodistal crest of the caudolateral tuberosity of the femur. Liparini & Schultz note the attachment sites are effectively the same in *Prestosuchus*, *Tyrannosaurus* and *Poposaurus*, and that the two other animals have the better evidence: both show muscle scars on the medial ischium that this specimen does not.

homology.notes: One of the two contested amphibian ventral pelvic muscles resolved by Diogo & Molnar (the other being 'pubifemoralis').

correspondences.note: The gemelli are claimed by this record and by `puboischiofemoralis-externus`, and this dataset records both claims rather than settling them. Cunningham (1882) puts them here by dissection in the thylacine and the cuscus; Gambaryan et al. (2002) group a single gemellus with the obturator externus field in the monotremes. A question about which of two deep hip muscles the gemelli belong to, answered for individual animals by dissection and not for Mammalia by argument.

correspondences.caution: Diogo & Molnar (2014) find no clear topological equivalent here. Across every tetrapod clade in their Tables 13-21, including urodeles, they report that not one pelvic or thigh muscle has a clear topological equivalent in the pectoral region or arm, and attribute the lack to phylogenetic constraint on the girdles. This edge records a pairing the literature makes; it is not one that source supports.

muscles.name: Puboischiotibialis
muscles.developmental: Somitic; ventral mass.
synonyms: puboischiotibialis sensu Mivart 1869 and Iordansky & Morozov 1994

consensus.origin: Ventral pelvic girdle — pubis and ischium.
consensus.insertion: Medial surface of the proximal tibia.
consensus.action: Adducts the thigh and flexes the knee.

occurrences.name: Puboischiotibialis
occurrences.attachmentNote: The most superficial muscle over the pelvis in ventral view, divided into proximal and distal sections by a tendinous inscription at about the level of the acetabulum. Francis (1934) and Mivart (1869) describe it as an undivided sheet in Salamandra and Cryptobranchus, so the inscription is not general to salamanders.
occurrences.divisionNote: Divided into proximal and distal sections by a tendinous inscription at about the level of the acetabulum in Taricha. Francis (1934) and Mivart (1869) describe it as an undivided sheet in Salamandra and Cryptobranchus, so the inscription is not general to salamanders.
occurrences.origin: Pubo-ischiac plate, lateral to the midline.
occurrences.insertion: Anterior surface of the tibia.

occurrences.name: Gracilis major + gracilis minor
occurrences.note: Two heads in anurans versus one in mammals. Both derive from the puboischiotibialis, but via different heads — so the anuran and mammalian 'gracilis' are not straightforwardly equivalent. The anuran gracilis major is Mivart's and Iordansky & Morozov's puboischiotibialis (Přikryl et al. 2009).
occurrences.attachmentNote: Discoglossus and Ascaphus, from Prikryl et al.'s review table and descriptions. Gracilis major and gracilis minor, both ischium to knee aponeurosis. Mivart and Iordansky & Morozov call the major one the puboischiotibialis, which is this record's name.

occurrences.name: Puboischiotibialis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Scored from Zaaf et al.'s tables for Eublepharis macularius, with the Gekko gecko differences noted where they bear on the attachment. From the pubic tubercle and both pelvic ligaments, tendinously onto the proximal tibial shaft. Two of its three origins are ligament rather than bone, which is why it leaves little for a fossil reconstruction to find.

occurrences.name: Gracilis
occurrences.action: Adducts the thigh; flexes and medially rotates the leg.
occurrences.divisionNote: One head, against two in anurans (Prikryl et al. 2009).
occurrences.attachmentNote: Gracilis: a band from the ventral pelvic symphysis, fusing cranially with the insertion of the abdominal muscles, to the craniomedial tibia just proximal to the semitendinosus insertion.

occurrences.name: Puboischiotibialis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Gekko gecko, from the differences column of Zaaf et al.'s tables. Zaaf et al. examined this muscle in both geckos and record no difference, so the Eublepharis rows stand for Gekko too. A blank in a differences column is an observation of sameness, not a gap, and scoring it as a row is what lets the clade rollup say the two species AGREE rather than say nothing.

occurrences.name: Gracilis
occurrences.action: Adducts the thigh and flexes the knee.
occurrences.innervation: Anterior division of the obturator nerve.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). Pubic symphysis and inferior pubic ramus to the medial surface of the tibia through the pes anserinus. **This is the single most important human row in the hindlimb.** Diogo & Molnar single out the gracilis as the one muscle for which the last common ancestor of tetrapods probably had a directly corresponding individual muscle in the modern human sense — everything else in the human hindlimb is a subdivision or a recombination of something that was not a discrete muscle. If a reader wants one row that shows what a one-to-one homology looks like against a whole limb of composites, it is this one.

occurrences.name: M. puboischiotibialis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Iguana iguana, Russell & Bauer (2008). The most superficial muscle of the ventral thigh, arising aponeurotically in front and fleshily behind from the ischiopubic ligament, inserting by a tendon on the proximomesial tibial shaft and joined posteriorly by a slip of the flexor tibialis internus. **Developmentally three muscles, indistinguishable in the adult** — Russell & Bauer identify the thicker fleshy posterior part, applied to the skin in the region of the femoral pores, as puboischiotibialis 3, with 1 and 2 fused as the thinner aponeurotic anterior part. This record is the one Diogo & Molnar single out as the single muscle for which the tetrapod ancestor probably had a direct one-to-one counterpart in the modern human sense; the lizard shows it already partly compounded.

occurrences.name: M. pubo-ischio-tibialis
occurrences.innervation: R. pubo-ischio-tibialis of the N. obturatorius.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Sphenodon punctatus, Osawa (1898), *Zur Muskellehre*. Fürbringer's *ischio-pubo-tibialis s. M. gracilis*, Gadow's *pubi-ischio-tibialis*, Perrin's *adducteur de la jambe*. A broad muscle incompletely separated from the ischio-tibialis posticus, from the ventral pelvic surface at the puboischiadic ligament and the ischiopubic symphysis, running down the medial thigh to the medial side of the proximal tibia. **This is the record Diogo & Molnar single out** as the one muscle for which the tetrapod ancestor probably had a directly corresponding individual muscle in the modern human sense — and Osawa flags that Günther's *M. gracilis* probably corresponds to the pubo-tibialis posticus instead, quoting Günther's own description to show it does not fit this muscle at all.

occurrences.name: Gracilis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Spilocuscus maculatus. **Neither animal's gracilis is attached to the marsupial bone**, though its origin from the side of the pubic symphysis reaches as high as that bone's antero-inferior angle. Cunningham sets this against Macalister, who says he found the gracilis attached to the epipubic bone in every marsupial he examined; Young does not mention such an attachment in the koala. Two animals against a generalisation, recorded as two animals. A powerful broad band with an extensive insertion into the anterior sharp ridge of the tibia in its middle third — much the longer of the two insertions.

occurrences.name: Gracilis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Thylacinus cynocephalus. **Neither animal's gracilis is attached to the marsupial bone**, though its origin from the side of the pubic symphysis reaches as high as that bone's antero-inferior angle. Cunningham sets this against Macalister, who says he found the gracilis attached to the epipubic bone in every marsupial he examined; Young does not mention such an attachment in the koala. Two animals against a generalisation, recorded as two animals. A much more limited insertion than the cuscus's: the subcutaneous surface of the tibia a short distance below the medial tuberosity.

occurrences.name: Gracilis anterior and gracilis posterior
occurrences.attachmentNote: Tachyglossus aculeatus, Gambaryan et al. (2002). Gracilis anterior from the tuberculum musculi psoas minoris and the cranial edge of the pubis, onto the proximal fifth of the medial edge of the tibia, the patellar ligament and the cranial surface of the patella. Gracilis posterior from the ventral half of the caudal edge of the ischium, its origin passing along the whole symphysis onto the proximal third of the epipubis, and inserting on the second quarter of the tibial crest lateral to the medial collateral ligament. **The echidna's gracilis is unique among mammals** on Gambaryan et al.'s reading, because that insertion stays lateral to the collateral ligament where in the platypus and in therians generally the distal part of the anterior division passes medial to it.
occurrences.action: Adducts the thigh and extends the leg.

occurrences.name: Gracilis anterior and gracilis posterior
occurrences.divisionNote: The gracilis posterior is in three parts here and undivided in the echidna. Its posterior and intermediate parts share one insertion tendon with the cutaneus maximus and the semitendinosus pars vertebralis.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Ornithorhynchus anatinus, Gambaryan et al. (2002). Gracilis anterior from the tuberculum musculi psoas minoris dorsocaudal to the psoas minor and cranial to the pectineus, inserting along the medial broadening of the tibial crest, the medial side of the patellar ligament and the medial edge of the patella. Gracilis posterior in three parts: pars anterior from the craniomedial edge of the epipubis — two-thirds of that bone's length and over half its width — passing onto the cranial third of the symphysis; pars posterior from the caudal third of the symphysis and the caudal three-fifths of the ischium; pars intermedia from what is left of the symphysis and from the outer fasciae of the other two. The posterior and intermediate parts share a tendon with the cutaneus maximus and the semitendinosus pars vertebralis, ending on the tibia at two-thirds of its length; the anterior part inserts as a narrow strip beginning a quarter of the way down the tibia. **Unlike the echidna, the distal insertion of the pars anterior lies medial to the medial collateral ligament**, which Gambaryan et al. call the characteristically mammalian arrangement.

occurrences.name: Pubo-ischio-tibialis (PIT)
occurrences.attachmentNote: Prestosuchus chiniquensis, Liparini & Schultz (2013). Both ends at level II. Origin on muscle scars over the cranioventral border of the obturator process of the ischium — the row carries the ischium and the cranial side, since the obturator process is not a separate element here — and insertion on the craniomedial fossa of the proximal half of the tibia, by the tendon it shares with the first and second flexores tibiales interni. **Among living archosaurs this muscle survives only in Crocodylia.** Carrano & Hutchinson found nothing to support it in *Tyrannosaurus*, and Liparini & Schultz read its presence here plus its absence there as placing the loss on the avemetatarsalian line before theropods — which makes this row a datum about where a muscle disappeared, not only about where it attached.

homology.notes: Diogo & Molnar single out the gracilis as the one muscle for which the last common ancestor of tetrapods probably had a directly corresponding individual muscle in the modern human sense — the muscles printed in bold in their Table 1. Every other human hindlimb muscle is a subdivision or recombination.
homology.teaching: A one-line answer to 'which of my leg muscles would a salamander recognise?' — essentially just the gracilis.

correspondences.note: Diogo & Molnar (2014) report that no pelvic or thigh muscle has a clear topological equivalent in the pectoral region or arm in any tetrapod clade they examine, which is the general result this particular absence sits under.

muscles.name: Ischioflexorius / flexor tibialis
muscles.developmental: Somitic; ventral mass.
synonyms: semitendinosus + semimembranosus + biceps femoris (mammals — the hamstrings)

consensus.insertion: Proximal tibia and/or fibula; in some taxa continuing to the tarsus.
consensus.action: Flexes the knee and retracts (extends) the hip.

occurrences.name: Ischioflexorius
occurrences.attachmentNote: Runs from the pelvis to the sole without a bony insertion — the longest muscle chain in the hindlimb, and one whose action cannot be read from any single joint.
occurrences.note: Only the distal section is fully separable from the puboischiotibialis in Taricha; the proximal section is incompletely divided from it and resists mechanical separation. Pseudoeurycea, Bolitoglossa, Paramesotriton and Onychodactylus share this. The character does not follow salamander phylogeny and must have arisen or been lost more than once.
occurrences.origin: Posterior and lateral edge of the ischium, behind the puboischiotibialis.
occurrences.insertion: Plantar aponeurosis overlying the flexor primordialis communis.

occurrences.name: 'Semitendinosus'
occurrences.note: A false-friend name. The anuran 'semitendinosus' is not homologous to the mammalian muscle of that name. Přikryl et al. (2009) record that the anuran 'semimembranosus' was called ischioflexorius by Hoffmann and caudalipuboischiotibialis by Francis, while the anuran 'semitendinosus' was called ischioflexorius by Mivart and puboischiotibialis by Hoffmann. Two muscles, four names, two of them shared — which is what Diogo & Molnar mean by false friends.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Discoglossus and Ascaphus, from Prikryl et al.'s review table and descriptions. Semitendinosus from the ischium to the knee aponeurosis, and semimembranosus — which Hoffmann calls the ischioflexorius, this record's own name — from the pars ascendens ilii and adjacent ischium onto the posterior knee capsule and the posterior proximal head of the tibiofibula. The semimembranosus is divided proximally by a tendinous inscription.

occurrences.name: Flexor tibialis externus + internus
occurrences.attachmentNote: Scored from Zaaf et al.'s tables for Eublepharis macularius, with the Gekko gecko differences noted where they bear on the attachment. Flexor tibialis externus from the ilioischiadic ligament and flexor tibialis internus from that ligament and the ischial tuberosity, both onto the proximal tibia. Gekko adds a further part to each, the internus tendons meeting at the interarticular area of the knee.

occurrences.name: Flexor tibialis externus + internus
occurrences.attachmentNote: Crocodylus porosus. Flexor tibialis internus is FOUR-part here, against three in some Alligator and Caiman latirostris accounts: FTI1 from the postero-lateral ischium to the proximo-medial tibia by a long tendon shared with puboischiotibialis; FTI2 fleshy from the postero-ventral ilium, the largest of the four; FTI3 from the proximo-lateral ischium; FTI4 a small thin muscle from the latero-ventral ilium near the ischium, joining the common tendon. The tibial insertion is the internus'. Flexor tibialis EXTERNUS is named in this record but its insertion is deliberately unscored: it arises by tendon from the postero-lateral ilium and ends, by a long tendon shared with gastrocnemius externus, IN THE PES at the proximal tarsus — not on the tibia.

occurrences.name: M. flexor cruris medialis + flexor cruris lateralis pars pelvica
occurrences.note: = crocodylian flexor tibialis internus 3 and flexor tibialis externus. Crocodylian flexor tibialis internus 1 is LOST between Avialae and Aves — one of the few outright losses in their table.

occurrences.name: Semitendinosus, semimembranosus, biceps femoris
occurrences.action: Extend the hip and flex the knee.
occurrences.innervation: Tibial division of the sciatic nerve; the short head of biceps femoris by the common fibular division.

nerves.note: Only the short head of biceps femoris. It is the one hamstring on the dorsal division, which is why the muscle's nerve and its ventral-mass identity disagree here — a real exception, not a scoring error.

occurrences.attachmentNote: Galictis cuja. The hamstring field, and the origins are what make it one field: biceps femoris from the dorsal ischial tuberosity, semitendinosus from the ischial tuberosity AND the tail — its caudal belly fleshy from the transverse process of caudal vertebra 2 and aponeurotic from C1 and C3 — semimembranosus from the caudal ramus of the ischium. Ercoli et al. read that RESTRICTED caudal origin as a derived mustelid condition, so the row is scored as C1–C3 rather than as a broad caudal sheet. The caudal-vertebral head is the one worth noting — a thigh muscle taking origin from the tail. Insertions run to the tibia in all three, with semimembranosus also on the medial femoral epicondyle and biceps femoris on the lateral.

occurrences.name: Flexor tibialis externus + internus
occurrences.attachmentNote: Gekko gecko, from the differences column of Zaaf et al.'s tables. Zaaf et al. examined this muscle in both geckos and record no difference, so the Eublepharis rows stand for Gekko too. A blank in a differences column is an observation of sameness, not a gap, and scoring it as a row is what lets the clade rollup say the two species AGREE rather than say nothing.

occurrences.name: Hamstrings
occurrences.action: Extend the thigh and flex the knee.
occurrences.innervation: Tibial division of the sciatic nerve; the short head of biceps femoris by the common fibular division.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). All three from the ischial tuberosity, with a second head of biceps femoris from the lateral lip of the linea aspera, to the fibular head and the two tibial condyles. **The group derives from this field and the head-by-head correspondences are not settled** — Diogo & Molnar reject the classical claim of Gregory & Camp, Romer and Haines that the mammalian tenuissimus is the caudal head of biceps femoris, and follow Jones in deriving it from a dorsal tail-region muscle instead. The human row is therefore the mammalian outcome of the split, not a key to it. The short head of biceps femoris has a different nerve from the rest of the muscle it is named part of, which is the sort of thing that makes the split hard to read.

occurrences.name: M. flexor tibialis internus and externus
occurrences.attachmentNote: Iguana iguana, Russell & Bauer (2008). Internus part 2 from the perineal region and the anterior ilioischiadic ligament, its deep portion from the posteroventral ischium, inserting on the mesial and proximolateral tibia; part 1 from the ilioischiadic ligament, inserting in common with the puboischiotibialis. Externus has a single belly from the same ligament. **The externus tendon bifurcates and one branch never reaches the tibia at all**: it follows the lateral border of the femorotibial gastrocnemius, receives fibres from it, and contributes to the plantar aponeurosis. Russell & Bauer read those connections as relicts of the developmental stage in which thigh and crural muscles are one undifferentiated mass — a muscle that still shows where the limb was divided.

occurrences.name: M. ischio-tibialis posticus
occurrences.innervation: Nn. ischio-tibiales from the sacral plexus.
occurrences.attachmentNote:
Sphenodon punctatus, Osawa (1898), *Zur Muskellehre*. **Osawa lists eight names for this one mass**, and they are the hamstring names: Günther's great flexor cruris (semimembranosus, semitendinosus), the slender portion of it (biceps) and its adductor branch; Fürbringer's ileo-ischio-tibialis proprius, pubo-ischio-tibialis sublimis posterior and profundus; Gadow's flexor tibialis externus and internus. From the outer surface of the tuber ischii and its medial region, from the caudal fascia, and directly from the end tendon of the coccygeo-femoralis brevis, inserting across the whole posterior and part of the medial and lateral aspects of the proximal tibia and onto an oblique band between tibia and lateral femoral condyle.

Osawa says the mass cannot well be divided further, but that in one specimen he could separate a lateral and a medial portion by which side of the tibial head they reached. That is exactly this record's assessment — the hamstring group derives from this field but the head-by-head correspondences are not settled — observed directly in one animal.

occurrences.name: Biceps, semitendinosus and semimembranosus
occurrences.attachmentNote: Spilocuscus maculatus. **The biceps has no femoral head at all**, so Cunningham remarks the name is inappropriate: the biceps proper rises by a narrow pointed origin from the ischial tuberosity in common with the semitendinosus and fans out into the fascia on the outer leg from the external femoral condyle in front to the external malleolus behind. Its second part is caudal, and Cunningham says **it had not been noticed in any marsupial before** — a long ribbon from the transverse processes of the first two caudal vertebrae, in the plane of the gluteus medius and under the agitator caudae, running down between the ischial tuberosity and the great trochanter superficial to the biceps proper. Opposite the back of the knee it gives a slip to the semitendinosus and splits: the fibular division fuses with the biceps proper into the outer crural fascia, the longer tibial division ends in an aponeurosis on the inner subcutaneous surface of the tibia about its middle, lower than the semitendinosus and slightly overlapped by the gracilis. The semitendinosus takes the ischial tuberosity and inserts on the inner tibia about its middle, completely under the gracilis; **Cunningham found no tendinous intersection in it, which he says is the usual marsupial condition.** The semimembranosus ends in a round tendon passing under the cord-like medial collateral ligament to the side of the tibia's anterior tuberosity, so it is a rotator of the leg as well as a flexor.

occurrences.name: Biceps, semitendinosus and semimembranosus
occurrences.attachmentNote: Thylacinus cynocephalus. **The biceps is in three parts here**, tied together by numerous fleshy slips passing from one to another. The biceps proper is more massive than the cuscus's and far less expanded, reaching only the fascia over the outer knee and the upper third of the leg. The superficial caudal division answers to the cuscus's caudal part: from the transverse processes of the second and third caudal vertebrae, giving a slip to the semitendinosus and then dividing — the larger tibial portion, reinforced by a slip *from* the semitendinosus, going down with it to the middle of the inner tibial surface, the fibular portion, reinforced by a long slender slip from the biceps proper, into the outer crural fascia. The deep caudal portion is **Haughton's bicipiti accessorius**, a long narrow slip from the transverse process of the first caudal vertebra that passes under the biceps proper and emerges at its posterior border to reach the fibular crural fascia; Macalister found it in *Sarcophilus* and absent in five other marsupials, Young asserted it in the opossum and denied it in the koala. Cunningham's reading of all this caudal recruitment is functional: the divisions exist **to associate the movements of the heavy tail with those of the hind limb**. The semitendinosus inserts much higher than the cuscus's and below the gracilis rather than under it, and is crossed by a faint tendinous intersection — which Cunningham calls a rare thing in a marsupial.

occurrences.name: Semitendinosus, semimembranosus and biceps femoris
occurrences.divisionNote: The semitendinosus has two heads with widely separated insertions, which is why the vertebral head has repeatedly been mistaken for another muscle: Meckel, Mivart and Manners-Smith called it the gluteus maximus, Appleton and Low the flexor cruris, Pearson and Jouffroy et al. the crurococcygeus. Gambaryan et al. place it here, in the long postfemoral group. In therians the two heads usually join into one belly; some insectivores keep them separate, as here.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Tachyglossus aculeatus, Gambaryan et al. (2002). The semitendinosus pars vertebralis from the neural spines of sacral I to caudal III, then over the fascia of the sacrocaudalis dorsalis to the prezygapophysis of caudal IV and the transverse processes of caudals IV–VI; its cranial bundles end on the fascia over the distal shin and its caudal fibres on the dorsal surface of that fascia, curving medially into a tendon distomedial to the gracilis posterior. The pars ischiadica from the ischial tuberosity together with the semimembranosus anterior and from that muscle's aponeurotic sheet, inserting deep and lateral to the gracilis posterior. Semimembranosus posterior from the anterior border of the aponeurosis shared with the pars ischiadica, by a thin tendon onto the tibia distolateral to the semimembranosus anterior; semimembranosus anterior from that same tendinous sheet onto the tibia caudal and proximal to the medial collateral ligament, not passing under it. Biceps femoris from the dorsocaudal edge of the ischial tuberosity by a broad aponeurosis onto the tibia, its thick cranial part reaching the lateral edge of the patella, the lateral surface of the patellar ligament and the lateral aspect of the tibial crest, the thinner remainder onto the fascial sheets between the long extensors of the foot. **In one specimen the semimembranosus posterior of the left side weighed twenty times less than its fellow on the right**, which Gambaryan et al. read as a muscle capable of reducing to nothing — an observation about individual variation of the kind most descriptive myology does not record. **Neither monotreme has any connection between the biceps femoris and the Achilles tendon**, which they call characteristic of therians.

occurrences.name: Semitendinosus, semimembranosus and biceps femoris
occurrences.action: Flex the knee; the semitendinosus pars vertebralis rotates the first and fifth metatarsals about their long axes so that the web spreads.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Ornithorhynchus anatinus, Gambaryan et al. (2002). **The semitendinosus pars vertebralis is the largest muscle in this animal's hind limb** — 16.3 per cent of its whole hind limb mass, against 4.6 per cent in the echidna — and it is the muscle that opens the web. It arises from the neural spine of the last lumbar vertebra, over the fascia erectoris spinae onto the whole laterodorsal surface of the tuber coxae, caudally from the neural spine of caudal III over the fascia of the sacrocaudalis dorsalis to the prezygapophysis of caudal IV and the transverse processes of caudals III and IV, and further over the fascia of the sacrocaudalis ventralis to the haemal arch between caudals IV and V. All of that converges on one strong tendon running to the lateroplantar foot, which broadens over the lateral aspect of the foot and **inserts on the dorsolateral edge of the fifth metatarsal and the dorsomedial edge of the first**. Gambaryan et al.'s point is mechanical: contracting it turns both marginal metatarsals about their long axes, and the web then unfolds by itself under water pressure. A tendinous sheet splits off to the caudomedial surface of the gracilis posterior tendon and an aponeurosis onto the medial third of the tibia. The pars ischiadica from the ischial tuberosity mediocranial to the biceps femoris and from the cranial end of the semimembranosus posterior's tendinous sheet, onto the caudal tibia. Semimembranosus posterior from the ischial tuberosity cranial to the semitendinosus, onto the proximal third of the caudal tibia near its medial edge; semimembranosus anterior from the ischial tuberosity, passing onto the symphysial branch of the pubis lateral to the gracilis posterior, onto the very proximal end of the caudal tibia. Biceps femoris from the dorsocaudal edge of the ischial tuberosity, its aponeurosis onto the lateral edge of the patella and the outer fascia of the vastus lateralis, then curving over the tibialis cranialis onto the tibial crest — **the echidna's aponeurosis does not curve over that muscle**, and its connections to the fascia between the long extensors are strong where the platypus's are extremely weak.

occurrences.name: Flexor cruris lateralis + flexor cruris medialis
occurrences.attachmentNote: *Grus americana*, Fisher & Goodman (1955); anconal and palmar are dorsal and ventral in their usage. **M. flexor cruris lateralis.** The origin is fleshy from the posterior 2 centimeters of the posterior iliac crest deep to the origin of M. extens. ilio-fib. and just dorsal to the tendon of pars caudi-fem. of M. caudofem. (figs. 22, 25, 29). Other origin in this region takes place by means of fascia overlying the origin of M. flex. cruris. med., the disto-lateral and dorsal surfaces of the pubis, and the body wall dorsal to the pubis. The proximal accessory head arises fleshily from a 3-centimeter-long line in the proximal part of the popliteal region. Farther distally the origin (probably of the distal accessory segment) becomes aponeurotic and tendinous from the medial surface of the internal condyle of the femur. *Insertion.* The tendon coming from the raphe at the junction of the main and proximal accessory heads usually inserts on the wide tendon of insertion of M. flex. cruris med. at the surface of the shank musculature. As described previously, the tendon of the distal accessory head inserts on the posterior surface of the pars media of M. gastroc., posterior to 84 THE MYOLOGY OF THE WHOOPING CRANE 2? ast rib to M. ext. ilio-tib. ant. to thigh mm. **M. flexor cruris medialis.** Fleshy from the ventro-posterior corner of the ischium, from the fascia between the pubis and ischium, and from the entire lateral face of the pubis posterior to the adductor muscles and extending to within 2 centimeters of the caudal end of the pubis (fig. 22). There is strong fascial connection throughout the fleshy origin. Insertion.—As the muscle passes to the tibial musculature a thin, wide, and strong inserting tendon is produced. Almost immediately the tendon of the main and proximal accessory heads of M. flex. cruris lat. inserts on this wide tendon; in one instance only a vinculum formed this connection between the tendons. The combined tendons then pass into the shank musculat *Insertion.* As the muscle passes to the tibial musculature a thin, wide, and strong inserting tendon is produced. Almost immediately the tendon of the main and proximal accessory heads of M. flex. cruris lat. inserts on this wide tendon; in one instance only a vinculum formed this connection between the tendons. occurrences.name: Flexor cruris (FTE, FTI 3 + FTI 4)
occurrences.attachmentNote:
Prestosuchus chiniquensis, Liparini & Schultz (2013). Two portions reconstructed: a lateral one, the flexor tibialis externus, arising caudally from the lateral surface of the postacetabular ilium, and a medial one, the third and fourth flexores tibiales interni, from the dorsal tubercle of the ischium. Both insert at level I on the proximocaudal tuberosity of the tibia, **combined in a single tendon** — which is why one insertion row carries both. The same osteological features supporting the medial portion here were the ones Carrano & Hutchinson used in *Tyrannosaurus*.

Prestosuchus chiniquensis, Liparini & Schultz (2013). The second head at level II′ on the lateral surface of the postacetabular ilium; the first at level II, running mediolaterally from the distal tubercle of the ischium along muscle scars on the distal caudomedial ischial surface to the distal caudodorsal groove. The pair insert on the craniomedial fossa of the tibia by a tendon **shared with the pubo-ischio-tibialis**, which is scored on its own record with the same insertion. Carrano & Hutchinson did not reconstruct the second head in *Tyrannosaurus* for want of muscle scars on the caudal postacetabular ilium; the scars are present here.

homology.notes: The hamstring group derives from this field, but the correspondences head-by-head are not settled. Diogo & Molnar reject the classical claim (Gregory & Camp 1918; Romer 1922; Haines 1935) that the mammalian tenuissimus is the caudal head of biceps femoris; following Jones (1979) they derive tenuissimus from a dorsal tail-region muscle homologous with the reptilian 'flexor cruris tarsi dorsalis'.
homology.caveat: Leavey et al. (2024), using diceCT on 30 frog species across five locomotor modes, report that bone lengths and pelvic crest sizes are generally NOT reliable predictors of muscle size, and find many-to-one form-function mapping. That is a direct caution against reading muscle proportions off skeletal proportions in fossils, which is the inference osteological correlates are usually recruited for. Correlates locate an attachment; they do not size the muscle that made it.

correspondences.note: Frequently asserted; the two are innervated by different divisions and derive from opposite masses (hamstrings ventral, triceps dorsal). This correspondence should be treated as functional analogy.
correspondences.caution: Diogo & Molnar (2014) find no clear topological equivalent here. Across every tetrapod clade in their Tables 13-21, including urodeles, they report that not one pelvic or thigh muscle has a clear topological equivalent in the pectoral region or arm, and attribute the lack to phylogenetic constraint on the girdles. This edge records a pairing the literature makes; it is not one that source supports.

muscles.name: Gluteus maximus
muscles.developmental: Somitic; dorsal mass.

consensus.origin: Posterior ilium, sacrum, coccyx and sacrotuberous ligament.
consensus.insertion: Gluteal tuberosity of the femur and the iliotibial tract.
consensus.action: Extends and laterally rotates the hip; principal muscle of the erect-posture power stroke.

occurrences.name: Gluteus maximus
occurrences.note: Diogo & Molnar note innervation differences between humans and rats: the human gluteus maximus is supplied by the inferior gluteal nerve alone, the rat muscle by that nerve plus the inferior branch of the superior gluteal nerve. One of several cases where innervation differs between mammals for muscles otherwise treated as identical.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Gluteus superficialis: an aponeurotic head from the iliac crest and fleshy and tendinous fibres from the sacrocaudal aponeurosis over the first two caudal vertebrae, inserting on the lateral greater trochanter and onto the insertions of gluteus medius and tensor fasciae latae.

occurrences.note: The enlargement of this field along the synapsid stem is part of the erect-posture transition documented by Bishop & Pierce.
occurrences.name: Gluteal (dorsal iliac) mass
Gluteus maximus
occurrences.action: Extends and laterally rotates the thigh.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). Posterior gluteal line, the posterior sacrum and coccyx and the sacrotuberous ligament; upper fibres to the iliotibial tract, lowermost to the gluteal tuberosity. **The human muscle is what this record is for**, and its name is one of the clearest false friends in Diogo & Molnar's list: the anuran literature applies 'gluteus maximus' to a muscle that is not this one. It is a mammalian differentiation out of the dorsal iliac field, not an inherited muscle, which is why the record has no reptile or bird rows to compare it against.

occurrences.name: Superficial gluteal sheet
occurrences.divisionNote: The tensor fasciae femoris is not separable from the gluteus maximus in this animal — the two are one thin layer — and is listed as a part only because Cunningham traced a superior gluteal twig into its fibres. This dataset otherwise carries the tensor fasciae latae as a disputed part of `iliofemoralis`, where the human row puts it.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Spilocuscus maculatus. Three muscles in one plane, superficial to everything else in the gluteal region, arising in a continuous line from the anterior superior iliac spine in front to the fourth caudal vertebra behind. The two posterior ones, only partly separated from each other, are the agitator caudae: the smaller anterior portion from the fascia over the hinder sacrum and the first caudal vertebra, the wider posterior portion from the fascia over the second caudal vertebra and the transverse processes of the third, fourth and fifth — both inserted along a continuous line on the posterior femur from the root of the great trochanter almost to the external condyle. The anterior muscle is **the gluteus maximus and the tensor fasciae femoris combined, and Cunningham proves the second component by its nerve**: a twig of the superior gluteal nerve traced into the anterior fibres. It arises from the fascia over the last lumbar vertebra and the sacrum, from the fascia over the meso-gluteus, and from a tendinous cord an inch and a half long running back from the anterior superior iliac spine — a cord that gives origin by its upper border to all three gluteals and by its lower border to the sartorius and the obliquus internus, and which Cunningham says **cannot be the homologue of the inguinal ligament**, because the aponeurosis of the external oblique has no connection with it. Its insertion is the outer aspect of the root of the great trochanter and slightly the shaft below.
