In front it winds round the anterior border of the meso-gluteus and fuses with the gluteus minimus, so the superficial and deep gluteals enclose the middle one on every side but the back. **The agitator caudae is the row's problem and it is left as one.** It arises from the caudal vertebrae and their transverse processes and inserts on the posterior femur — which are the attachments of a caudofemoralis, not of a gluteus maximus. Cunningham groups it here on plane and nerve: it lies in the superficial gluteal sheet with the others, and all the factors representing the human gluteus maximus in this animal share one special nerve from the sacral plexus. His grouping is what is scored; the attachment-based reading, which would put it on `caudofemoralis` alongside the piriformis, is recorded here rather than acted on. Note that Cunningham *also* describes a piriformis in both animals, so the two candidates are not the same muscle.

occurrences.name: Gluteus maximus and agitator caudae
occurrences.attachmentNote: Thylacinus cynocephalus. **Every muscle in this animal's gluteal region tends to segment**, and the gluteus maximus does it twice over: two portions one behind the other, each split again into a superficial and a deep part. The anterior portion is the gluteus maximus proper and lies wholly behind the meso-gluteus — its superficial segment a thin sheet from the fascia on the dorsum of the sacrum to the back of the great trochanter, its deep segment narrower but fleshier, from the side of the sacrum in its posterior half and the same fascia, emerging from under its fellow near the trochanter to reach the posterior femur just below it. The posterior portion is the agitator caudae: superficial segment from the fascia over the first three caudal vertebrae, deep segment a very narrow band from the transverse process of the second, uniting after a short independent course to insert on the posterior femur below the deep segment of the gluteus maximus. All four factors are supplied by one special nerve from the sacral plexus. **There is apparently no trace of a tensor fasciae femoris in this animal**, which the cuscus has fused into its gluteus maximus. **The agitator caudae is the row's problem and it is left as one.** It arises from the caudal vertebrae and their transverse processes and inserts on the posterior femur — which are the attachments of a caudofemoralis, not of a gluteus maximus. Cunningham groups it here on plane and nerve: it lies in the superficial gluteal sheet with the others, and all the factors representing the human gluteus maximus in this animal share one special nerve from the sacral plexus. His grouping is what is scored; the attachment-based reading, which would put it on `caudofemoralis` alongside the piriformis, is recorded here rather than acted on. Note that Cunningham *also* describes a piriformis in both animals, so the two candidates are not the same muscle.

occurrences.name: Gluteus superficialis
occurrences.action: Pronates the femur at the hip rather than retracting it.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Tachyglossus aculeatus, Gambaryan et al. (2002). From an aponeurosis stretched between the neural spines of sacral vertebrae II and IV; at the level of the third sacral spine it dips below the aponeurosis of the semitendinosus pars vertebralis to reach the caudal surface of the **distal** rugosity of the trochanter tertius, just distal to the caudofemoralis insertion. **The origin is much reduced compared with therians**, so the muscle overlays only the most caudal fibres of the gluteus medius rather than forming a broad superficial sheet. Gambaryan et al.'s lever-arm analysis has it shortening during femoral retraction rather than lengthening, which is their argument that its work is pronation of the femur and not retraction — the movement that in this animal replaces the femoral retraction other tetrapods use to propel themselves. It is 3.0 per cent of the hind limb muscle mass here.

occurrences.name: Gluteus superficialis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Ornithorhynchus anatinus, Gambaryan et al. (2002). From an aponeurosis running from the caudal third of the spinous process of sacral vertebra II to the cranial half of that of sacral vertebra IV, and additionally from the prezygapophysis of the last sacral vertebra; the insertion is the same as in the echidna. **Coues (1870) described this muscle as the piriformis**, which Gambaryan et al. call an error — the piriformis proper arises on the ventral surfaces of the sacral vertebrae and inserts on the top of the trochanter major deep to the gluteus medius, and **it is absent in both monotremes**. The muscle that occupies the piriformis position in a therian pelvis is on the `caudofemoralis` record, which the monotremes retain in full. At 1.8 per cent of hind limb muscle mass this is a smaller muscle than the echidna's.

homology.notes: A mammalian differentiation from the dorsal iliac field. Its name is applied to non-homologous muscles in the anuran literature — one of the clearest cases in Diogo & Molnar's list of false-friend names ('tensor fasciae latae', 'gluteus maximus', 'gemellus', 'obturator externus', 'quadratus femoris', 'obturator internus', 'pectineus', 'adductor longus', 'iliacus', 'sartorius', 'semitendinosus', 'adductor magnus' — none homologous in anurans to the human muscles of the same name).
homology.teaching: The anchor for the false-friend-names lesson. Twelve human muscle names are applied to non-homologous anuran muscles.

correspondences.caution: Diogo & Molnar (2014) find no clear topological equivalent here. Across every tetrapod clade in their Tables 13-21, including urodeles, they report that not one pelvic or thigh muscle has a clear topological equivalent in the pectoral region or arm, and attribute the lack to phylogenetic constraint on the girdles. This edge records a pairing the literature makes; it is not one that source supports.

muscles.name: Gastrocnemius
muscles.developmental: Somitic; ventral (flexor) mass of the crus.

consensus.origin: Distal femur, by medial and lateral heads (and from the tibia in some taxa).
consensus.insertion: Calcaneum/fibulare, via the Achilles tendon.
consensus.action: Plantarflexes the ankle; flexes the knee.

occurrences.name: Gastrocnemius
occurrences.note: Walthall & Ashley-Ross describe no discrete gastrocnemius in Taricha. The flexor primordialis communis occupies the position and takes the femoral epicondylar origin that the amniote gastrocnemius takes, and the paper treats it as one muscle. Recorded here without changing the presence state, since other sources score a gastrocnemius in Caudata; what this source shows is that the boundary between the two is a division that not every author makes.

occurrences.name: Gastrocnemius
occurrences.attachmentNote: From the ventral proximal tibia and the distal ventral tibial crest, by a broad aponeurosis onto the proximolateral margins of the first three phalanges — not onto a calcaneum, unlike the mammalian condition.

occurrences.name: Gastrocnemius
occurrences.attachmentNote: Externus arises by a tendon shared with the caudofemoralis longus and from the posterolateral femoral epicondyle, which bears a scattered striated surface; internus from the proximoposterior tibia. Both insert on the calcaneum by a broad tendon.

occurrences.name: M. gastrocnemius
occurrences.note: Ankle plantarflexor.

architecture.note: Values as modelled; maximum isometric force is derived, not measured.

occurrences.name: Gastrocnemius
occurrences.action: Plantarflexes the foot; flexes the knee.
occurrences.note: Kardong (2002) derived the mammalian gastrocnemius from the femorotibial ('internal') head; Diogo & Molnar discuss and qualify this.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Galictis cuja. Lateral head by a strong tendon from the lateral femoral epicondyle and the lateral sesamoid of the knee, medial head from the medial epicondyle, both also from the caudal femoral diaphysis and the knee capsule. Inserts on the caudodorsal calcaneal tubercle, its tendon fusing with those of flexor digitorum superficialis and soleus to form the calcaneal tendon.

occurrences.name: Triceps surae and plantaris
occurrences.action: Plantarflexes the foot; gastrocnemius also flexes the knee.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). Gastrocnemius from above the two femoral condyles, soleus from the fibular head and the soleal line of the tibia, plantaris from above the lateral condyle, all to the dorsum of the calcaneus through the calcaneal tendon. **Femoral and tibial origins at once**, which is what this record says varies: head count and the femoral-versus-tibial origin are the two variables across Tetrapoda, and a human has both states in one muscle group. In anurans the same muscle is the principal jump-propulsion muscle and is hypertrophied past everything else in the leg.

occurrences.name: M. femorotibial gastrocnemius and M. femoral gastrocnemius
occurrences.attachmentNote:
Iguana iguana, Russell & Bauer (2008). **Nine tendons of origin between the two muscles, and the insertion is not on the ankle.** The femorotibial gastrocnemius arises by six tendons — two into the knee joint capsule and meniscus, one from the pubotibialis motor tendon, a bifid one from the distal femur, one from the proximal tibial process and one from the tibial shaft — and its motor tendon runs past the tarsus to insert on the proximolateral margin of the first phalanx of digit V and the proximal ends of the succeeding phalanges. The femoral gastrocnemius arises from the lateral femoral epicondyle, the posterior knee capsule and the iliofibularis insertion tendon, its deep head inserting on the lateral and mesial plantar tubercles of metatarsal V.

There is no calcaneal tendon here. Instead the aponeuroses give off four **tie tendons** linking the two muscles to the flexor digitorum brevis of digit I, the astragalocalcaneum, the peroneus longus tendon and the superficial digital tendons. The deep femoral gastrocnemius fibres lie in series with the flexores digitores breves of digits II and III along a common inscription, making an effectively digastric arrangement across two records. A muscle that reaches the toes.

occurrences.name: M. gastrocnemius
occurrences.innervation: Rr. gastrocnemii of the N. tibialis lateralis and medialis.
occurrences.attachmentNote:
Sphenodon punctatus, Osawa (1898), *Zur Muskellehre*. Two heads, each with its own synonymy: caput tibiale is Fürbringer's *epitrochleo-tibio-metatarsalis ventralis s. gemellus internus* and **Günther's *M. soleus***; caput femorale is Fürbringer's *epitrochleo-metatarsalis ventralis fibularis s. gemellus externus* and Günther's gastrocnemius. The tibial head is itself two-headed, its stronger head from the posterior and fibular surface of the tibial neck and its thin tendinous second head from the end tendon of the ischio-tibialis posticus lateralis.

**There is no calcaneal tendon: both heads end in the plantar aponeurosis.** The tibial head's aponeurosis goes to the proximal tarsal and the fibular border of metatarsal V and the base of the fifth toe's proximal phalanx; the femoral head splits at the ankle into a superficial aponeurotic sheet forming a second layer of the plantar aponeurosis and a deep fleshy part that ends in a transverse tendinous arch **which gives origin to the flexor digitorum communis sublimis** — so one muscle's insertion is the next muscle's origin, in series.

occurrences.name: Gastrocnemius, soleus and plantaris
occurrences.attachmentNote: Thylacinus cynocephalus. Two very large heads. **The outer head arises in part from a large sesamoid bone on the back of the head of the fibula**, and from a powerful ligament binding that bone to the back of the lateral femoral condyle; a second, tendinous slip comes off the outer aspect of the lateral condyle itself, and the external popliteal nerve passes forward between the two. The inner head takes not only the back of the medial condyle but the whole breadth of the popliteal surface of the femur at that level. The heads join almost at once and the tendo Achillis reaches the lower part of the back of the calcaneum. **There is no separate soleus in either animal, and Cunningham argues it is inside the outer head of the gastrocnemius.** His evidence is that head's fibular origin — a calf muscle taking the fibula is doing what a soleus does — and he answers the objection that the plantaris lies deep to it by pointing out that the plantaris is subjacent only to the *inner* part of the compound muscle, not to the outer part that represents the soleus. So the missing muscle is not to be looked for among the deep flexors of the calf. The plantaris arises in common with the outer head and stays fused to its under surface for some distance, then runs down beside the tendo Achillis, expands at the heel, passes **superficial** to that tendon into the sole and spreads out as a plantar fascia dividing into three slips for the index, medius and annularis — each slip forking to embrace the metatarsophalangeal joint and attaching to the ligaments around it, and the fascia nowhere attached to the muscles beneath.

occurrences.name: Gastrocnemius, soleus and plantaris
occurrences.attachmentNote: Spilocuscus maculatus. **The two heads are separate along their whole length** — the muscle is two distinct factors here. The inner head comes off the back of the medial condyle only, takes no fibres from the popliteal surface, and half-way down the leg gives place to a narrow tendon with an insertion of its own into the back of the calcaneum. The outer head is as in the thylacine but for two things: no tendinous slip to the outer aspect of the lateral condyle, and **an origin from the posterior aspect of the fibula in its upper two-thirds**, through the intermuscular septum between it and the peronei. It inserts by a strong tendon into the calcaneal tuber under the inner head's tendon. **There is no separate soleus in either animal, and Cunningham argues it is inside the outer head of the gastrocnemius.** His evidence is that head's fibular origin — a calf muscle taking the fibula is doing what a soleus does — and he answers the objection that the plantaris lies deep to it by pointing out that the plantaris is subjacent only to the *inner* part of the compound muscle, not to the outer part that represents the soleus. So the missing muscle is not to be looked for among the deep flexors of the calf. The plantaris is large and quite distinct from the compound soleo-gastrocnemius, arising from the sesamoid bone at the head of the fibula and passing over the calcaneal tuber to insert into **a plate of cartilage in the sole that replaces the plantar fascia and takes the place of the true heel** — attached internally to a sesamoid gliding on the internal cuneiform and giving origin to some short muscles of the hallux, externally to the under surface of the cuboid where it gives origin to some short muscles of the minimus, and prolonged forward as fascial slips to the roots of the digits. Cunningham reports the plantaris almost invariably present in marsupials and absent in the wombat.

occurrences.name: Gastrocnemius lateralis and gastrocnemius medialis
occurrences.divisionNote: **Mivart and Westling called the lateral head a soleus in this animal**, on the strength of its insertion tendon lying deep to the medial head's rather than superficial to it. Gambaryan et al. follow Meckel and keep it as the gastrocnemius lateralis despite that topography, because the platypus and the therians agree in the other arrangement and the echidna is the odd one.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Tachyglossus aculeatus, Gambaryan et al. (2002). Gastrocnemius lateralis by fibres on the proximal extremities of the lateral aspects of both the cranial and caudal surfaces of the processus parafibularis, its flat tendon lying **deep** to the medial head's; gastrocnemius medialis from above the medial femoral condyle, also anchored by a thick tendinous guy on the proximal tibia. The two tendons fuse at the calcaneus and insert on the tuber calcanei close to its apex.
occurrences.action: Extends the ankle.

occurrences.name: Gastrocnemius lateralis and gastrocnemius medialis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Ornithorhynchus anatinus, Gambaryan et al. (2002). Gastrocnemius lateralis by fibres on a thickening of the caudal surface of the proximal processus parafibularis and the ligamentum parafibulopatellae, its aponeurosis anchoring on a distal prominence of that process. Gastrocnemius medialis as in the echidna, with some fibres from the proximal tibia. **Here the lateral head's tendon lies superficial to the medial head's before joining it** — the therian arrangement, and the reason Gambaryan et al. decline to call the echidna's lateral head a soleus. The common tendon inserts on the middle of the top of the tuber calcanei, between the tubercles bordering the groove that carries the flexor digitorum fibularis. The lateral head is 3.9 per cent of hind limb mass here against 1.2 per cent in the echidna.

occurrences.name: Gastrocnemius
occurrences.attachmentNote: *Grus americana*, Fisher & Goodman (1955); anconal and palmar are dorsal and ventral in their usage. **M. gastrocnemius.** This origin is separated from that of the pars media by the inserting tendon of M. extens. ilio-fib. and by N. peroneus. The primary origin is tendinous from the flexor attachment on the external surface of the distal end of the femur. There is also tendinous and some fleshy origin from the lateral femoritibial ligaments and from the underlying tendons of origin of other flexor muscles. Pars interna Lying on the medial and anterior surfaces of the shank, this heavy and wide muscle, the largest of the three gastrocnemius components, is super- ficial to M. per. longus (figs. 25, 26). Proximally its fleshy belly curves around the anterior surface of the pat

homology.notes: Universal across Tetrapoda. Head count and the femoral versus tibial origin vary. In anurans it is the principal jump-propulsion muscle and is hypertrophied relative to every other muscle of the leg.

correspondences.note: The crural and antebrachial flexor masses correspond as fields, but muscle-for-muscle mapping within them is unreliable.
correspondences.caution: Diogo & Molnar (2014) give the gastrocnemius no forelimb equivalent in Table 14 — the cell is blank for Timon, Rattus and Homo alike. This edge is not theirs.

muscles.name: Tibialis anterior
muscles.developmental: Somitic; dorsal (extensor) mass of the crus.

consensus.origin: Proximal tibia and the interosseous membrane.
consensus.insertion: Medial tarsals and the base of metatarsal I.
consensus.action: Dorsiflexes the ankle; inverts the foot.

occurrences.name: Extensor cruris tibialis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Recorded as m. extensor cruris tibialis. Visible from both ventral and dorsal views as it fans from the femoral epicondyle across the anterior face of the tibia — three rows for one muscle on one bone, because it wraps.
occurrences.origin: Tibial (medial) epicondyle of the femur.
occurrences.insertion: Extensively on the anterodorsal and anteroventral faces of the tibia.

occurrences.name: Tibialis anterior
occurrences.attachmentNote: Scored from Zaaf et al.'s tables for Eublepharis macularius, with the Gekko gecko differences noted where they bear on the attachment. From the entire anterior surface of the tibia, tendinously onto digit I. In Gekko the tendon also contributes to the lateral digital tendon.

occurrences.name: Tibialis anterior
occurrences.attachmentNote: From the proximomedial tibia to the dorsolateral proximal metatarsals I-II; the metatarsal bases carry coarse rugosities marking the insertion.

occurrences.name: Tibialis cranialis (classical) / extensor digitorum longus (Hattori & Tsuihiji 2021)
occurrences.note: Which avian muscle this record corresponds to is exactly what Hattori & Tsuihiji (2021) dispute. Scored uncertain rather than picking a side.

architecture.note: Values as modelled; maximum isometric force is derived, not measured.

occurrences.name: Tibialis anterior
occurrences.action: Dorsiflexes and inverts the foot.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Tibialis cranialis from the craniolateral proximal quarter of the tibia including the lateral condyle and the lateral margin of the cnemial crest, from the proximal interosseous membrane, and by a second tendinous head from the cranial head of the fibula. Inserts on the medial aspect of the ventral tubercle at the base of metatarsal I.

occurrences.name: Tibialis anterior
occurrences.attachmentNote: Gekko gecko, from the differences column of Zaaf et al.'s tables. The insertion tendon additionally contributes to the lateral digital tendon, which Eublepharis's does not.

occurrences.name: Tibialis anterior
occurrences.origin: Broad area on the shaft of the tibia — the proximal two-thirds of the dorsal surface and the distal two-thirds of the ventral aspect.
occurrences.insertion: Medial margin of metatarsal I.
occurrences.attachmentNote:
Iguana iguana. The two squamates differ here and the difference is scored rather than averaged: the iguana's dorsal origin stops short of the distal tibia and the monitor's does not.

Iguana iguana, Russell & Bauer (2008). Russell & Bauer refine the insertion Hattori & Tsuihiji (2021) scored from correlates. Origin at its most proximal from the anteromesial head of the tibia, then from the anterior and dorsal faces of the shaft, ceasing to take dorsal origin near the distal end but continuing anteriorly to the tibia's distalmost extremity. **The insertion is threefold and all of it is on metatarsal I**: a fleshy proximolateral attachment, a broad tendon onto the base, and a slender tendon running along the mesial border as far as the metatarsophalangeal joint capsule.

occurrences.name: Tibialis anterior
occurrences.origin: Broad area on the shaft of the tibia, the dorsal surface origin continuing to the distal end of the bone.
occurrences.insertion: Medial margin of metatarsal I.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Varanus indicus. Against Iguana, the dorsal origin runs the whole length of the tibia.

occurrences.name: Tibialis anterior
occurrences.origin: Dorsomedial margin of the tibia, marked on the bone by a rugose longitudinal sulcus.
occurrences.insertion: Proximomedial end of metatarsal I, marked by a tubercle.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Chelydra serpentina. Both ends leave a correlate — a sulcus at the origin and a tubercle at the insertion — which is what makes this muscle reconstructable in a fossil turtle.

occurrences.name: Tibialis anterior
occurrences.origin: Proximal-most portion of the dorsal aspect of the tibia, marked with surface rugosity that broadens proximodistally on the lateral side.
occurrences.insertion: Bulge on the dorsal aspect of each of metatarsals I and II.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Paleosuchus palpebrosus.

occurrences.name: Tibialis anterior
occurrences.origin: Proximal-most portion of the dorsal aspect of the tibia, marked by distinct rugosity.
occurrences.insertion: Bulge on the dorsal aspect of each of metatarsals I and II.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Crocodylus porosus. Hattori & Tsuihiji describe this animal together with its clade-mate and record no difference between the two for this muscle. A blank in a comparison is an observation of sameness, which is why both carry rows rather than one standing for the clade.

occurrences.name: Extensor digitorum longus
occurrences.origin: Broad surface between the cranial and lateral cnemial crests and the dorsolateral aspect of the tibial shaft, tapering distally.
occurrences.insertion: Processes on the proximodorsal lips of the phalanges of digits II-IV.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Gallus gallus. The other half of the revision: Hattori & Tsuihiji put the avian m. extensor digitorum longus HERE, with the non-avian tibialis anterior, on the strength of the shared tibial origin. Note what that does to the shared cnemial crests — under their scheme both anterior tibial muscles take them in birds, the tibialis cranialis on the crests' expansions and this one on the surface between them.

occurrences.name: Extensor digitorum longus
occurrences.origin: Broad surface between the cranial and lateral cnemial crests and the dorsolateral tibial shaft.
occurrences.insertion: Processes on the proximodorsal lips of the phalanges of digits II-IV.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Grus japonensis. Hattori & Tsuihiji describe this animal together with its clade-mate and record no difference between the two for this muscle. A blank in a comparison is an observation of sameness, which is why both carry rows rather than one standing for the clade.

occurrences.name: Tibialis anterior
occurrences.action: Dorsiflexes and inverts the foot.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). Lateral tibial condyle and the upper lateral tibial surface to the medial cuneiform and the first metatarsal — the preaxial dorsiflexor, unchanged in position from the amphibian extensor cruris tibialis and reaching the same first-digit side of the foot. The medial cuneiform is scored as `distal-tarsals`.

occurrences.name: M. tibialis anticus
occurrences.innervation: R. muscularis of the N. peroneus profundus medialis.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Sphenodon punctatus, Osawa (1898), *Zur Muskellehre*. Fürbringer's *tibio-metatarsalis longus*, Perrin's *extenseur du premier metatarsien*. It covers almost the whole anterior and medial surface of the tibia except the medial face of the proximal third, its origin line crossing the long axis of the bone at an acute angle, and inserts along **the entire medial side of metatarsal I**. The preaxial dorsiflexor in the same position as in every other column here.

occurrences.name: Tibialis anticus
occurrences.attachmentNote: Spilocuscus maculatus. Very powerful in both animals, from the lateral tuberosity and outer surface of the tibial shaft and from the interosseous membrane. Here it inserts into the plantar aspect of the internal cuneiform and the base of the first metatarsal — **the hallux**, where the thylacine's goes to the index.

occurrences.name: Tibialis anticus
occurrences.attachmentNote: Thylacinus cynocephalus. Very powerful, with the same tibial and interosseous origin as the cuscus's, but **inserted into the base of the metatarsal of the index** rather than onto the medial side of the foot — the muscle has shifted one digit laterally in an animal whose hallux is reduced.

occurrences.name: Tibialis cranialis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Tachyglossus aculeatus, Gambaryan et al. (2002). From the cranial surface of the tibia distal to the knee-joint bursa, over about a quarter of the bone's length, becoming a flat tendon a third of the way up the shin which dips under the tendon of the extensor hallucis longus; both pass together under the transverse ligament to insert on the dorsomedial aspect of the distal end of the entocuneiform (tarsale I). **The distal tibia here is the insertion of the cutaneus maximus**, which forms a dense connective sheet fused to the periosteum, and the long extensor tendons run through that thickening rather than lying in synovial sheaths as they normally do.
occurrences.action: Flexes the ankle; contributes to rotation of the foot about its long axis.

occurrences.name: Tibialis cranialis
occurrences.divisionNote: Two heads in the platypus, one in the echidna. The superficial head arises from the patella and the parafibular process, the deep from the proximal tibia.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Ornithorhynchus anatinus, Gambaryan et al. (2002). The superficial head from the lateral edge of the patella, then over the ligamentum patelloparafibularis onto the top of the hooked broadening of the processus parafibularis; the deep head from the proximal extremity of the tibia over about a third of it from the fibular articulation. Both become one flat tendon over the distal third of the shin, running beside the extensor hallucis longus tendon under the transverse ligament, to the dorsomedial aspect of the distal end of the entocuneiform. **This muscle is nearly twice the echidna's** — 1.5 against 0.8 per cent of hind limb mass — because in the platypus it is one of the three muscles that turn the foot about its long axis during swimming, along with the peroneus longus and the extensor hallucis longus.
occurrences.action: Flexes the ankle; rotates the foot about its long axis during swimming.

occurrences.name: Tibialis anterior
occurrences.attachmentNote: *Grus americana*, Fisher & Goodman (1955); anconal and palmar are dorsal and ventral in their usage. **M. tibialis anterior.** The pinnate nature of this muscle seemingly comes about through the fusion anteriorly of the edges of the two heads of origin. The anterior head arises fleshily from the antero-lateral surface of the tibio- tarsus between the two cnemial crests, sometimes by tendon from the most proximal antero-lateral corner of the fibular head, and tendinous from the edge of the rotular crest. The femoral head takes tendinous origin from the usual position on the disto-anterior face of the external femoral condyle. This head is unusually well developed proximally; 94 THE MYOLOGY OF THE WHOOPING CRANE fleshy fibers surround the tendon of origin to within less than a centimeter of *Insertion.* tThe calcified tendon is formed between the bellies of the two parts of the muscle, approximately in the middle of the shank, and lies on the mid-anterior surface. Just above the tibial condyles the tendon passes through a wide, tendinous loop across the tendinal groove, and continues distally on to the tarsometatarsus where it attaches to the usual tubercle on the mid-anterior face of this bone. **Scored on `tibia` rather than `tibiotarsus`**: the cnemial crest is a tibial landmark, and `fusedFrom` is deliberately not containment in this schema, so the crest is not reachable through the compound bone. That is the convention the other avian rows already use.

homology.notes: Hattori & Tsuihiji (2021) propose that the classical homologies of the two anterior tibial muscles are swapped: on their reading the avian m. tibialis cranialis is homologous with the NON-AVIAN m. extensor digitorum longus, and the avian m. extensor digitorum longus with the non-avian m. tibialis anterior. Their argument is that this requires no drastic change in attachment sites between avian and non-avian homologues, whereas the classical scheme does. The classical scheme descends from Romer (1923-27) and, they note, had been used uncritically by palaeontologists for a century. Their method weights morphological and functional congruence over innervation, on the grounds that nerve-muscle specificity is itself variable across taxa — which is the reverse of the priority used elsewhere in this dataset, and worth noting as a genuine methodological disagreement rather than a detail. Allen et al. (2021) independently adopt the revised scheme in their crocodylian-to-avian homology table, equating the crocodylian extensor digitorum longus with the avian m. tibialis cranialis. That is a second line of support for Hattori & Tsuihiji's reading against the classical one, from authors working on moment arms rather than on homology, so the agreement is not circular.
homology.openQuestion: Is the avian tibialis cranialis the homologue of the non-avian tibialis anterior (Romer's scheme, followed by most of the literature) or of the non-avian extensor digitorum longus (Hattori & Tsuihiji 2021)? The two schemes imply different attachment histories across the archosaur stem, so fossil muscle reconstruction in theropods depends on which is right.

correspondences.note: Stated by Diogo & Molnar (2014) Table 13 as a "clear topological correspondence"; their forelimb name for it is the extensor antebrachii et carpi radialis, in Timon.

muscles.name: Extensor digitorum longus (pes)
muscles.developmental: Somitic; dorsal mass of the crus.

consensus.origin: Lateral tibial condyle, proximal fibula and the interosseous membrane.
consensus.insertion: Dorsal aponeuroses of the digits.
consensus.action: Extends the toes; dorsiflexes the ankle.

occurrences.name: Extensor digitorum longus
occurrences.attachmentNote: Thin, lying on the dorsal crus between the extensor tarsi tibialis and the extensor cruris et tarsi fibularis. Unlike its forelimb counterpart it stops at the metatarsals rather than reaching the phalanges.
occurrences.origin: Lateral epicondyle of the femur, anterior to the extensor cruris et tarsi fibularis; sometimes a few fibres from the tibial spine.
occurrences.insertion: Bases of the metatarsals, by many small tendons.

occurrences.name: Extensor digitorum longus
occurrences.note: From the lateral femoral extensor fossa and condyle to the proximodorsal metatarsals III-IV.
occurrences.attachmentNote: From the lateral femoral extensor fossa and lateral condyle onto the proximodorsal metatarsals III-IV, which bear a smooth bump at the insertion. Note that this is a femoral origin, not a tibial one — relevant to the Hattori & Tsuihiji (2021) dispute over which anterior tibial muscle is which.

occurrences.name: Extensor digitorum longus
occurrences.note: See the tibialis anterior record: which avian muscle is the homologue is disputed.

architecture.note: Values as modelled; maximum isometric force is derived, not measured.

occurrences.name: Extensor digitorum longus
occurrences.note: In humans the fibularis tertius derives from the extensor digitorum longus anlage (Lewis 1910). In rats the fibularis digiti quinti derives from the extensor digiti quinti anlage. The two are therefore NOT homologous, despite both being called a 'fibularis' and both being innervated by the deep fibular nerve.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Femoral, not tibial, in origin — from the lateral condyle of the femur and the aponeurosis over tibialis cranialis — so it crosses the knee as well as the ankle. Four flat tendons to the distal phalanges of digits II–V, fused en route with the tendons of extensor digitorum brevis and, on digit V, extensor digitorum lateralis.

occurrences.name: Extensor digitorum longus
occurrences.origin: Dorsomedial aspect of the lateral distal condyle of the femur.
occurrences.insertion: Metatarsals II and III by two tendons, each passing the lateral aspect of the proximal shaft to the tubercle on its lateroplantar aspect.
occurrences.attachmentNote:
Iguana iguana. This is the muscle Hattori & Tsuihiji standardise as m. tibialis cranialis, and its avian member is the point of the paper: on their reading the bird's m. tibialis cranialis belongs on THIS record and not on `tibialis-anterior`, where the classical scheme puts it.

Iguana iguana, Russell & Bauer (2008). Russell & Bauer add the proximal end of a row Hattori & Tsuihiji (2021) had scored from the osteological correlates. Origin from the dorsomesial aspect of the lateral femoral epicondyle by a long cylindrical tendon that passes deep to the knee joint capsule ligaments and the 'quadriceps' tendon, remaining discernible inside the belly for its proximal third and continuing to give fibre origin from within the muscle. Two tendons of insertion arise at about the distal extremity of the astragalocalcaneum, passing either side of the origin of the extensor digitorum brevis of digit III, to the dorsolateral proximal shafts of metatarsals II and III.

occurrences.name: Extensor digitorum longus
occurrences.origin: Dorsomedial aspect of the lateral distal condyle of the femur.
occurrences.insertion: Metatarsals II and III by two tendons, onto the tubercle on the lateroplantar aspect of each proximal shaft.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Varanus indicus. Hattori & Tsuihiji describe this animal together with its clade-mate and record no difference between the two for this muscle. A blank in a comparison is an observation of sameness, which is why both carry rows rather than one standing for the clade.

occurrences.name: Extensor digitorum communis
occurrences.origin: Dorsal aspect of the lateral distal condyle of the femur.
occurrences.insertion: Lateral sides of metatarsals I-IV and the proximodorsal lip of phalanx I-2.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Chelydra serpentina. The widest insertion of any sauropsid on this record — all four metatarsals — and turtles vary in it: Gadow (1882) put the insertion on the proximal phalanges of digits I-IV instead, and Ribbing (1938) found the Emys condition scored here. This is the muscle Hattori & Tsuihiji standardise as m. tibialis cranialis, and its avian member is the point of the paper: on their reading the bird's m. tibialis cranialis belongs on THIS record and not on `tibialis-anterior`, where the classical scheme puts it.

occurrences.name: Extensor digitorum longus
occurrences.origin: Dorsal aspect of the femur just proximal to the lateral distal condyle.
occurrences.insertion: Tubercle on the medial margin of the proximal shaft of each of metatarsals II-IV, merging at the medial-most site with the tibialis anterior.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Paleosuchus palpebrosus. An MT I insertion is reported by Gadow (1882), Ribbing (1909, 1938) and Cong et al. (1998) and was not found here. This is the muscle Hattori & Tsuihiji standardise as m. tibialis cranialis, and its avian member is the point of the paper: on their reading the bird's m. tibialis cranialis belongs on THIS record and not on `tibialis-anterior`, where the classical scheme puts it.

occurrences.name: Extensor digitorum longus
occurrences.origin: Dorsal aspect of the femur just proximal to the lateral distal condyle.
occurrences.insertion: Tubercle on the medial margin of the proximal shaft of each of metatarsals II-IV.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Crocodylus porosus. Hattori & Tsuihiji describe this animal together with its clade-mate and record no difference between the two for this muscle. A blank in a comparison is an observation of sameness, which is why both carry rows rather than one standing for the clade.

occurrences.name: Tibialis cranialis
occurrences.origin: Distal extremity of the lateral distal condyle of the femur, at the fovea tendinis m. tibialis cranialis, plus the lateral expansion of the cranial cnemial crest and the dorsoventral expansion of the lateral cnemial crest of the tibia.
occurrences.insertion: Tubercles on the dorsal aspect of the proximal tarsometatarsus — the tuberositas m. tibialis cranialis.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Gallus gallus. **The row the homology revision turns on.** Hattori & Tsuihiji place the avian m. tibialis cranialis here, with the non-avian extensor digitorum longus, because the femoral origin is conserved across all four clades and the avian tuberositas on the tarsometatarsus sits where metatarsals II and III would have been. The classical scheme instead pairs it with `tibialis-anterior`, which requires the extensor digitorum longus origin to cross the knee joint and the tibialis cranialis to lose its MT I insertion. The tibial origin, on the two cnemial crests, is the avian addition. Two of the fifteen orphan correlates in GAPS §3 close on this row.

occurrences.name: Tibialis cranialis
occurrences.origin: Distal extremity of the lateral distal condyle of the femur and the cranial and lateral cnemial crests of the tibia.
occurrences.insertion: Tubercles on the dorsal aspect of the proximal tarsometatarsus.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Grus japonensis. Hattori & Tsuihiji describe this animal together with its clade-mate and record no difference between the two for this muscle. A blank in a comparison is an observation of sameness, which is why both carry rows rather than one standing for the clade.

occurrences.name: Extensor digitorum longus and extensor hallucis longus
occurrences.action: Extend the toes and dorsiflex the foot.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). Extensor digitorum longus from the lateral tibial condyle, the anterior fibula and the interosseous membrane to the extensor expansions of the lateral four toes; extensor hallucis longus from the middle fibula to the distal phalanx of the hallux. **Fibularis tertius is scored here as a disputed part rather than with the fibularis group**, and the reason is its nerve: Diogo & Molnar make the point that fibularis tertius and fibularis digiti quinti are supplied by the DEEP fibular nerve, with the extensors, not by the superficial fibular nerve that supplies the true fibularis muscles. The name groups it with the peronei; the innervation groups it here.

occurrences.name: M. extensor digitorum communis longus
occurrences.innervation: R. muscularis of the N. peroneus profundus medialis.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Sphenodon punctatus, Osawa (1898), *Zur Muskellehre*. Gadow's *extensor longus digitorum*, Fürbringer's *epicondylo-metatarsalis dorsalis longus*. By a thin tendon from the anterior surface of the fibular femoral condyle, fused there with the knee joint capsule, running between the tibialis anticus and the peroneus and splitting near the dorsum of the foot into two slips to the fibular sides of the bases of metatarsals II and III. **In one of Osawa's specimens there was a third slip, to metatarsal IV** — a within-species difference recorded as such, and the same two-versus-three variation Russell & Bauer met in *Iguana*.

occurrences.name: Extensor longus digitorum and extensor longus hallucis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Spilocuscus maculatus. Three well-defined muscles on the front of the leg — tibialis anticus, extensor longus hallucis, extensor longus digitorum — in the same relative positions as in a human. **The extensor longus hallucis is well developed here and absent altogether in the thylacine**: from the anterior prominence of the head of the fibula, the inner border of the fibula in its upper half and the interosseous membrane, emerging between the tibialis anticus and the long digital extensor, its tendon reaching the ungual phalanx of the hallux. Macalister reports it inserting by two tendons, to hallux and index, in the wallaby, opossum and phalanger. The digital extensor has a very limited origin — the anterior prominence of the fibular head, the lateral tibial tuberosity, and a ligament bridging the two — and ends in three tendons: the intermediate to the ring digit, the outermost to the little toe, the innermost dividing for index and medius, with each lateral tendon sending a slip to strengthen that of the large ring digit.

occurrences.name: Extensor longus digitorum
occurrences.attachmentNote: Thylacinus cynocephalus. **The extensor longus hallucis is absent**, so this record carries the long digital extensor alone. Its origin is much more extensive than the cuscus's: the anterior aspect of the head of the fibula, the inner surface of the same bone in its upper two-thirds, and a corresponding portion of the interosseous membrane. Four tendons — the outermost to the minimus, the second dividing for annularis and medius, the third for medius and index, the fourth to the index alone.

occurrences.name: Long digital extensors of the pes
occurrences.divisionNote: **Gambaryan et al. say plainly that they cannot homologise the two digital extensors with the therian extensor digitorum longus**, and cannot say which of the two it would be. They keep Manners-Smith's names — extensor digitorum superficialis and profundus — on the argument that the four transverse ligaments of the echidna's ankle and the three of the platypus's carry the same tendons in the same relations, so the two animals' muscles correspond to each other even if neither corresponds to a therian muscle. They reject Haines's (1939) homologisation of the extensor digitorum superficialis with the peronei as contrary to its topography. The rows here are scored on the extensor field as a whole, which is what this record is.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Tachyglossus aculeatus, Gambaryan et al. (2002). Extensor hallucis longus in two bundles — a medial one from the tibia distal to the tibialis cranialis and reaching the fibular articulation, a lateral one from the processus articularis fibularis, the knee-joint bursa above the lateral femoral epicondyle and the medial edge of the fibula — to the ungual phalanx of the first toe, with a branch to the mediodorsal aspect of the ungual phalanx of the second. Extensor digitorum superficialis from the knee-joint bursa above the lateral femoral condyle and the proximal two-thirds of the fibula, by one tendon to the ungual phalanx of the second toe with a branch to the third. Extensor digitorum profundus from the knee-joint bursa lateral to the superficialis, down to a third of the fibula, sending three branches: to the laterodorsal first phalanx of the second toe, the lateral side of that toe's ungual phalanx, and into the superficialis tendon running to the third toe. **In the echidna the profundus is the most superficial muscle of the shin and in the platypus the deepest** — the same two muscles, inverted, which Gambaryan et al. explain by the platypus's functionally dominant muscles enlarging and overlaying the rest.

occurrences.name: Long digital extensors of the pes
occurrences.attachmentNote: Ornithorhynchus anatinus, Gambaryan et al. (2002). All three arise on the fibula here and none on the tibia. Extensor hallucis longus in two bundles from the processus parafibularis and the arched crest of the processus articularis fibularis, running along the medial edge of the first metatarsal to the medial side of the ungual phalanx of the first toe. Extensor digitorum superficialis in two independently arising bundles from the arched crest and the proximal seventh of the fibula, their tendons fusing at the ankle and then splitting into **five** tendons that pass through a ring-shaped ligament anchored on the naviculare, reaching the second metatarsal and the dorsal sesamoids of the second phalanges of toes II–V, each sending a branch on to the ungual phalanx; the fifth toe has no sesamoid so its tendon runs straight to the ungual phalanx. Extensor digitorum profundus from the processus parafibularis, its tendon running in the interosseous space, also splitting into five, the deep layer of each branch onto the dorsal proximal first phalanx and the superficial layer to the ungual phalanx by way of the dorsal sesamoid. **Every ungual phalanx in this animal has an extensor tendon reaching it from the medial and lateral side both**, which the echidna does not: there the profundus reaches only toes II and III laterally, and the superficialis only II and III medially. Two tendinous guys split off from the profundus tendon at the ankle, one into the lateral adipose pad and one to the plantar aponeurosis — the pad that broadens the swimming foot.

occurrences.name: Extensor digitorum longus
occurrences.attachmentNote: *Grus americana*, Fisher & Goodman (1955); anconal and palmar are dorsal and ventral in their usage. **M. extensor digitorum longus.** There is fleshy origin from the outer surface of the inner cnemial crest, from the distal edge of the outer cnemial crest, from the intervening area distal to the rotular crest, and from a triangular area on the upper one-third of the anterior face of the tibiotarsus. Below the middle of the belly there may be a small slip of origin coming from the overlying M. tib. ant. On its medial edge the belly is closely attached by aponeurosis to the intermuscular line. Insertion —The tendon is calcified above and below the intratarsal joint, but not across the joint itself; this is true for all tendons crossing this articulation. From its antero-lateral position at the region of its formatio *Insertion.* The tendon is calcified above and below the intratarsal joint, but not across the joint itself; this is true for all tendons crossing this articulation. From its antero-lateral position at the region of its formation, the tendon moyes distad and mediad to pass through a fibrous loop and then a bony canal just above the malleolar region. It crosses the medial edge of the intratarsal joint, goes down the antero-medial corner of the tarsometatarsus, and finally comes to lie in the middle of the anterior side of this bone. Nine centimeters above the metatarsal malleoli the tendon bifurcates, and the lateral ramus thus formed bi- furcates about 3 centimeters from **Scored on `tibia` rather than `tibiotarsus`**: the cnemial crest is a tibial landmark, and `fusedFrom` is deliberately not containment in this schema, so the crest is not reachable through the compound bone. That is the convention the other avian rows already use.

homology.notes: The muscle itself is straightforward; the interest is in its derivatives. The human fibularis tertius / rat fibularis digiti quinti case is one of Diogo & Molnar's cleanest demonstrations that shared name plus shared nerve still does not establish homology. Hattori & Tsuihiji (2021) propose that the classical homologies of the two anterior tibial muscles are swapped: on their reading the avian m. tibialis cranialis is homologous with the NON-AVIAN m. extensor digitorum longus, and the avian m. extensor digitorum longus with the non-avian m. tibialis anterior. Their argument is that this requires no drastic change in attachment sites between avian and non-avian homologues, whereas the classical scheme does. The classical scheme descends from Romer (1923-27) and, they note, had been used uncritically by palaeontologists for a century. Their method weights morphological and functional congruence over innervation, on the grounds that nerve-muscle specificity is itself variable across taxa — which is the reverse of the priority used elsewhere in this dataset, and worth noting as a genuine methodological disagreement rather than a detail. Allen et al. (2021) independently adopt the revised scheme in their crocodylian-to-avian homology table, equating the crocodylian extensor digitorum longus with the avian m. tibialis cranialis. That is a second line of support for Hattori & Tsuihiji's reading against the classical one, from authors working on moment arms rather than on homology, so the agreement is not circular.
homology.teaching: The rat double-fusion case is the single most economical illustration of parallelism masquerading as serial homology.

correspondences.note: Stated by Diogo & Molnar (2014) Table 13 as a "clear topological correspondence"; their forelimb name for it is the extensor digitorum.

muscles.name: Fibularis (peroneus) group
muscles.developmental: Somitic; lateral compartment of the crus, dorsal mass.
synonyms: peroneus longus / brevis / tertius / digiti quinti

consensus.insertion: Metatarsals and lateral tarsals.
consensus.action: Everts the foot; plantarflexes (longus, brevis) or dorsiflexes (tertius).
consensus.innervation: Superficial fibular nerve (longus, brevis); deep fibular nerve (tertius, digiti quinti).

occurrences.name: Fibularis longus + brevis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Scored from Zaaf et al.'s tables for Eublepharis macularius, with the Gekko gecko differences noted where they bear on the attachment. M. peroneus, partly tendinous proximally and partly muscular from almost the whole fibula, onto the fifth metatarsal. Gekko has two slips.

occurrences.name: Fibularis longus + brevis
occurrences.note: Both insert on the anterior surface of metatarsal V.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Fibularis longus arises on the fibular shaft distal to the iliofibular tubercle; brevis from the distal fibular shaft and the anterior tibial aponeurosis. Both insert on the anterior surface of metatarsal V.

occurrences.name: M. fibularis longus + brevis
occurrences.note: Names retained; longus plantarflexes, brevis dorsiflexes.

architecture.note: Values as modelled; maximum isometric force is derived, not measured.

occurrences.name: Fibularis longus, brevis (+ tertius in humans, digiti quinti in rats)
occurrences.action: Evert the foot; the longus also supports the transverse arch.
occurrences.innervation: Superficial fibular nerve for longus and brevis.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Galictis cuja. Fibularis brevis from the anterolateral and caudolateral surfaces of the middle of the fibula in two bellies, inserting on the dorsolateral tubercle of metatarsal V. Fibularis longus is the reason for the tibial and calcaneal rows: it arises tendinously from the CRANIAL HEAD OF THE FIBULA *and* from the lateral aspect of the LATERAL CONDYLE OF THE TIBIA with the adjacent tibial diaphysis, and it reaches a first insertion on the laterodistal CALCANEUS and the proximal margin of the metatarsal V tubercle before running internal to the long plantar ligament to a final attachment on the lateral surface of the plantar tubercle of metatarsal I. Both round the lateral malleolus. The tibial origin and the calcaneal insertion were missing while this note claimed the only omission was that the fibular fields were finer than one row could carry — a whole bone at each end, not a matter of granularity.

occurrences.name: Fibularis longus + brevis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Gekko gecko, from the differences column of Zaaf et al.'s tables. Zaaf et al. examined this muscle in both geckos and record no difference, so the Eublepharis rows stand for Gekko too. A blank in a differences column is an observation of sameness, not a gap, and scoring it as a row is what lets the clade rollup say the two species AGREE rather than say nothing.

occurrences.name: Peroneus longus + peroneus brevis
occurrences.origin: Longus from the lateral femoral epicondyle just distal to the flexor digitorum longus origin; brevis from almost the entire anterior, lateral and medial surfaces of the fibula, over nearly its whole length.
occurrences.insertion: Longus into a depression on the dorsolateral aspect of the shaft of metatarsal V; brevis onto the outer process on the proximolateral margin of metatarsal V.
occurrences.attachmentNote:
Iguana iguana. The longus insertion is a depression, against the 'lateral plantar tubercle' of Russell & Bauer (2008) — Hattori & Tsuihiji contradict them on the correlate itself, not on the muscle.

Iguana iguana, Russell & Bauer (2008). Russell & Bauer describe both members for *Iguana* and give the innervation argument this record turns on: the peronei are supplied by the same nerves as the tibialis anterior and the extensor digitorum communis (Jullien, 1967), and are therefore dorsal-division muscles despite lying on the lateral border of the crus. Peroneus longus from the lateral femoral epicondyle by a stout tendon that becomes inseparable from the knee capsule as it crosses, inserting on the proximal end of the lateral plantar tubercle of metatarsal V and held down by the lacinate ligament system; peroneus brevis from most of the fibular shaft for its whole length, inserting on the outer process of the head of metatarsal V.

occurrences.name: Peroneus longus + peroneus brevis
occurrences.origin: Longus from the lateral femoral epicondyle; brevis from almost the whole fibula.
occurrences.insertion: Longus into a depression on the dorsolateral shaft of metatarsal V; brevis onto the proximolateral margin of metatarsal V.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Varanus indicus. Hattori & Tsuihiji describe this animal together with its clade-mate and record no difference between the two for this muscle. A blank in a comparison is an observation of sameness, which is why both carry rows rather than one standing for the clade.

occurrences.name: Peroneus anterior + peroneus brevis
occurrences.origin: Peroneus anterior — the longus of this record — from the distal half of the dorsal aspect of the fibula, the origin marked by a slightly excavated surface; brevis from the distal end of the fibula.
occurrences.insertion: Peroneus anterior onto the dorsal aspect of the proximolateral margins of metatarsal V and phalanx IV-1; brevis onto the proximal margin of the dorsal aspect of metatarsal V.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Chelydra serpentina. The femoral origin the squamates give the longus is gone here — both heads are on the fibula, which is the condition crocodilians share and which Hattori & Tsuihiji use to group the two clades against lepidosaurs and birds.

occurrences.name: Peroneus longus + peroneus brevis
occurrences.origin: Longus from almost the entire laterodorsal aspect of the fibula, the surface between the longitudinal ridges on its dorsal and lateral aspects; brevis from the flat laterodorsal surface of the distal two-thirds of the fibular shaft.
occurrences.insertion: Longus merges with the brevis and inserts on the flat surface at its insertion site; brevis on the proximolateral margin of metatarsal V.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Paleosuchus palpebrosus. Both origins are bounded by ridges or are flat surfaces, so the fibula records the whole group.

occurrences.name: Peroneus longus + peroneus brevis
occurrences.origin: Longus from almost the entire laterodorsal aspect of the fibula; brevis from the laterodorsal aspect of the distal two-thirds of the fibular shaft.
occurrences.insertion: Longus onto the brevis insertion; brevis on the proximolateral margin of metatarsal V.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Crocodylus porosus. Hattori & Tsuihiji describe this animal together with its clade-mate and record no difference between the two for this muscle. A blank in a comparison is an observation of sameness, which is why both carry rows rather than one standing for the clade.

occurrences.name: Fibularis longus + fibularis brevis
occurrences.origin: Longus from the proximal margins of the cranial and lateral cnemial crests, the patellar tendon and associated fascia; brevis from most of the interosseal space between tibia and fibula — a narrow surface between two longitudinal ridges on the distal two-thirds of the tibial shaft, and the dorsal surface of the distal half of the fibula.
occurrences.insertion: Longus onto soft tissue, the sustentaculum tarsi and the insertion tendon of the flexor perforatus digiti III; brevis onto a proximal surface near the lateral margin of the hypotarsus, the tuberculum m. fibularis brevis.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Gallus gallus. **The insertion is different because the bone is gone.** In all three non-avian clades both heads end on metatarsal V; birds have lost it, and Hattori & Tsuihiji read the avian insertions — on the hypotarsus, on soft tissue and on another muscle's tendon — as the consequence. An attachment relocating because its element was lost, which is the same case as the therian supracoracoideus and the coracoid. The longus account is Fujioka's (1962) on Gallus rather than their own dissection.

occurrences.name: Fibularis longus + fibularis brevis
occurrences.origin: Longus from the proximal cnemial crests and the patellar tendon; brevis from the interosseal space between tibia and fibula.
occurrences.insertion: Longus onto soft tissue, the sustentaculum tarsi and the flexor perforatus digiti III tendon; brevis near the lateral margin of the hypotarsus.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Grus japonensis. Hattori & Tsuihiji describe this animal together with its clade-mate and record no difference between the two for this muscle. A blank in a comparison is an observation of sameness, which is why both carry rows rather than one standing for the clade.

occurrences.name: Fibularis longus and brevis
occurrences.action: Evert the foot and assist plantarflexion.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). Longus from the upper two-thirds of the lateral fibula, crossing the sole deep to the intrinsic muscles to reach the medial cuneiform and the first metatarsal; brevis from the lower third to the tuberosity of the fifth metatarsal. **Only the two superficial-fibular muscles are scored on this record.** Fibularis tertius carries the group's name and the extensors' nerve, and is scored with `extensor-digitorum-longus-hl` instead — this record's assessment already says the innervation cuts against the obvious grouping, and this is what acting on that looks like. Note also the longus tendon: it crosses the whole sole transversely, so a lateral muscle ends on the medial side of the foot.

occurrences.name: M. peroneus
occurrences.innervation: R. muscularis of the N. peroneus profundus.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Sphenodon punctatus, Osawa (1898), *Zur Muskellehre*. Günther's *peroneus longus*, Fürbringer's *fibulo-metatarsalis dorsalis*, Gadow's *peroneus anterior*, Perrin's *extenseur du cinquième tarsalien*. From the anterior and lateral surfaces of the lower three-quarters of the fibula, following on from the ilio-fibularis insertion, running almost straight down over the ankle to the proximal tarsal and the base of metatarsal V, with a thin tendinous strip also going to the base of metatarsal IV. **One muscle, where *Iguana* has a longus and a brevis** — and note that Osawa gives it the deep fibular nerve, which is the innervation Diogo & Molnar use to argue that the fibularis tertius and digiti quinti do not belong with the true peronei.

occurrences.name: Peroneus longus and peroneus brevis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Spilocuscus maculatus. The peroneus longus is very powerful, arising in both animals **by two heads separated by the anterior tibial nerve**. Here the superficial head is a broad flat band from the anterior and posterior prominences of the fibular head and the lateral collateral ligament of the knee; the deep head takes the outer aspect of the fibular shaft in its upper half. Its tendon runs behind the lateral malleolus to the outer margin of the foot, turns through a deep groove in the cuboid, crosses the sole and inserts into the base of the first metatarsal, confined on the way by two annular ligaments — behind the malleolus and on the outer aspect of the calcaneum — but with no complete sheath in the sole. The peroneus brevis comes off the anterior prominence of the fibular head by a narrow pointed tendon and takes fibres from the septum between it and the digital extensor, reaching the base of the fifth metatarsal. Ruge held that the inward insertion of the peroneus longus is not the original condition: the tendon began on the base of the fifth metatarsal and worked inwards as its fibres came into relation with the plantar ligaments, and he pointed to Monotremata — where the tendon is not free in a sheath in the sole and half its fibres still reach the fifth metatarsal — and to *Didelphis* and *Dasyurus hallucinatus*, which retain the fifth-metatarsal attachment. **Cunningham's two animals fall on either side of that sequence**: the thylacine's tendon is still slightly attached to the fifth metatarsal, the cuscus's lies quite free in its sheath with no attachment but the first metatarsal.

occurrences.name: Peroneus longus and peroneus brevis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Thylacinus cynocephalus. The peroneus longus is less strongly developed than the cuscus's but has a very similar two-headed origin. **Its tendon inserts into the ecto-cuneiform, and as it winds round the outer margin of the foot it is slightly attached by tendinous fibres to the base of the fifth metatarsal** — the primitive attachment the cuscus has lost. The peroneus brevis takes the fibular shaft in its upper half as well as the head, which Cunningham says is the usual rule and which Ruge describes in *Didelphis* and *Dasyurus hallucinatus*; it reaches the base of the fifth metatarsal. Ruge believed the peroneus brevis is itself derived from the outermost belly of the extensor brevis digitorum, which in this animal has not yet left the fibula. Ruge held that the inward insertion of the peroneus longus is not the original condition: the tendon began on the base of the fifth metatarsal and worked inwards as its fibres came into relation with the plantar ligaments, and he pointed to Monotremata — where the tendon is not free in a sheath in the sole and half its fibres still reach the fifth metatarsal — and to *Didelphis* and *Dasyurus hallucinatus*, which retain the fifth-metatarsal attachment. **Cunningham's two animals fall on either side of that sequence**: the thylacine's tendon is still slightly attached to the fifth metatarsal, the cuscus's lies quite free in its sheath with no attachment but the first metatarsal.

occurrences.name: Peroneus longus and peroneus digiti quinti
occurrences.divisionNote: **No separate peroneus digiti quarti.** In the echidna the peroneus digiti quinti tendon splits to reach the ungual phalanges of both the fourth and fifth toes, which Gambaryan et al. read as the quarti fused into it; in the platypus there is no fourth-toe tendon at all and they call the quarti totally lacking. Gambaryan et al. treat the identification of this group as beyond doubt in both animals, because its tendons lie lateral to all the other long extensors and pass with the peroneus longus under a transverse ligament of their own.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Tachyglossus aculeatus, Gambaryan et al. (2002). Peroneus longus from the lateral half of the distal end of the superior crest of the processus parafibularis, between the peroneus digiti quinti and the flexor digitorum fibularis, its origin running down two-thirds of the fibula; its tendon **turns through a groove of the tuber calcanei** onto the sole and crosses transversely, lateral to medial, to insert distal to all the tarsals on the plantolateral aspect of the first metatarsal. Peroneus digiti quinti from the processus parafibularis between the peroneus longus and the extensor digitorum profundus, its tendon splitting at the second phalanx of the fifth toe to reach the lateral surfaces of the ungual phalanges of both the fourth and fifth toes.
occurrences.action: Everts the foot; the peroneus longus turns it about its long axis.

occurrences.name: Peroneus longus and peroneus digiti quinti
occurrences.action: The peroneus longus is the principal muscle turning the foot about its long axis in swimming.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Ornithorhynchus anatinus, Gambaryan et al. (2002). Peroneus longus in three bundles — a medial one along the edge of a hook on the proximal cranial fibula, a lateral and deeper one from the lateral edge of the processus parafibularis running down the proximal quarter of the fibula — fusing into one belly whose tendon runs through the groove of the tuber calcanei to the middle of the medioplantar aspect of the first metatarsal. **Its synovial sheath is what has misled people.** The sheath fuses with the periosteum of the naviculare and the cuboid and is tightest on the proximal end of the fifth metatarsal, and Gambaryan et al. hold that this, and not a real tendon, is why Lewis, Szalay and others reported the muscle sending a slip to the fifth metatarsal. Peroneus digiti quinti from the processus parafibularis between the peroneus longus and the extensor digitorum profundus, two strong guys splitting off at the tuber calcanei — one into the tendon at the base of the lateral adipose pad, one onto the dorsolateral proximal first phalanx of the fifth toe — and the main tendon onto that toe's ungual phalanx. At 2.1 per cent of hind limb mass against the echidna's 0.8, the peroneus longus is nearly three times the muscle here, which is what rotating a webbed foot costs.

occurrences.name: Peroneus longus + peroneus brevis
occurrences.attachmentNote: *Grus americana*, Fisher & Goodman (1955); anconal and palmar are dorsal and ventral in their usage. **M. peroneus longus.** Fleshy from the space between the inner and outer cnemial crests, from the external face of the inner cnemial crest, and from the anterior surface of the outer cnemial crest. Part of this origin is inseparable from that of M. flex. perf. et perf. dig. I. All along the postero-medial edge of the belly there is aponeurotic origin from the intermuscular line on the medial surface of the tibiotarsus; this aponeurosis continues prox- imally on the anterior edge of the inner crest. On its lateral margin the muscle has both fleshy and tendinous origin from the muscles underlying its proximal two-thirds. Insertion —tThe calcified tendon formed in the middle of the shank’s length goes distally alo *Insertion.* tThe calcified tendon formed in the middle of the shank’s length goes distally along the postero-lateral corner of the tibiotarsus to the intratarsal joint. At the level of the external tibial condyle a vinculum 1.5 centimeters wide comes off posteriorly and passes medially to attach to the connective tissue sheath surrounding the extensor tendons as they pass through the intercondylar sulcus; this sheath is continuous from the proximal end of the sulcus to the proximal end of the hypotarsus, and it contains the tibial cartilage. The tendon that continues distally across the intratarsal joint is only 3 millimeters wide and much thinner than the tendon above the bifurcation. On the lateral su **M. peroneus brevis.** The origin is mixed fleshy and tendinous from the anterior and lateral faces of the fibula distal to the insertion of M. extens. ilio- fib. and continues on the tibiotarsus distal to the end of the fibular spine. Distal to the fibular crest of the tibia, in those dissections in which the belly extends this far, there is fleshy origin in a narrow area bordered anteriorly by an intermuscular line and posteriorly by the fibula. Insertion —The calcified tendon passes along the antero-lateral corner of the tibiotarsus. Just above the tibial condyles it passes through a strong loop of connective tissue. Here the tendon widens and thickens to pass across the lateral surface of the external tibia *Insertion.* The calcified tendon passes along the antero-lateral corner of the tibiotarsus. Just above the tibial condyles it passes through a strong loop of connective tissue. Here the tendon widens and thickens to pass across the lateral surface of the external tibial condyle and to insert on the proximo-lateral edge of the hypotarsus. We found no interconnections between this tendon and that of M. per. longus or the tibial cartilage. **Scored on `tibia` rather than `tibiotarsus`**: the cnemial crest is a tibial landmark, and `fusedFrom` is deliberately not containment in this schema, so the crest is not reachable through the compound bone. That is the convention the other avian rows already use.

homology.notes: Diogo & Molnar dwell on this group because the innervation is diagnostic and cuts against the obvious grouping. The fibularis tertius and fibularis digiti quinti are innervated by the DEEP fibular nerve — which supplies short extensors such as extensor digitorum brevis — not by the superficial fibular nerve that supplies the true lateral muscles fibularis longus and brevis. Deriving them from the lateral mass would require the innervation to have changed; deriving them from the extensor anlage does not.
homology.openQuestion: Diogo & Molnar state explicitly that a firm answer requires a much more extensive analysis including innervation and developmental data.
homology.teaching: Innervation as a decisive argument. Two muscles sit in the lateral compartment and carry a lateral-compartment name, but their nerve says they belong to the extensor group.

correspondences.note: Diogo & Molnar (2014) report that no pelvic or thigh muscle has a clear topological equivalent in the pectoral region or arm in any tetrapod clade they examine, which is the general result this particular absence sits under.

muscles.name: Popliteus
muscles.developmental: Somitic; derived from the interosseus cruris.

consensus.insertion: Posterior proximal tibia.
consensus.action: Unlocks the extended knee by rotating the tibia; medially rotates the leg.

occurrences.name: Popliteus
occurrences.attachmentNote: By a thick short tendon from the lateral femoral condyle and the aponeurosis over the distal lateral femur, to the medial and caudal aspects of the proximal two-thirds of the tibia. Some fibres insert onto flexor digitorum medialis rather than bone.

occurrences.name: Interosseus cruris
occurrences.attachmentNote: Scored from Zaaf et al.'s tables for Eublepharis macularius, with the Gekko gecko differences noted where they bear on the attachment. Scored from Zaaf et al.'s M. popliteus: from the proximal fibula, partly muscular and partly tendinous onto the anterolateral tibial shaft. This record's Lepidosauria occurrence is named 'interosseus cruris', the name Abdala & Diogo use for the same tibiofibular muscle.

occurrences.name: Interosseus cruris
occurrences.attachmentNote: Gekko gecko, from the differences column of Zaaf et al.'s tables. Zaaf et al. examined this muscle in both geckos and record no difference, so the Eublepharis rows stand for Gekko too. A blank in a differences column is an observation of sameness, not a gap, and scoring it as a row is what lets the clade rollup say the two species AGREE rather than say nothing.

occurrences.name: Popliteus
occurrences.action: Unlocks the extended knee by laterally rotating the femur on the tibia.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). Lateral femoral condyle to the posterior tibia above the soleal line. **A muscle that has moved to the other end of a bone.** Its ancestor is the interosseus cruris, a muscle running between tibia and fibula in the position an amniote fills with the interosseous membrane; the popliteus has left the fibula and climbed onto the femur, converting a leg muscle into a knee muscle. That is why `interosseus-cruris` is scored absent in a human on the next record and this one is present.

occurrences.name: M. popliteus
occurrences.attachmentNote: Iguana iguana, Russell & Bauer (2008). A thick triangular mass lying ventrally between tibia and fibula just distal to the knee, from the proximal third of the lateral side of the ventral crest of the tibia, in two bellies with a common insertion by parallel tendons on the mesial aspect of the proximal fibula. **Insertion proximal and lateral to its own origin** — the muscle runs backwards. This record derives it from the interosseus cruris, and *Iguana* has both, which is the observation the derivation rests on.

occurrences.name: M. fibulo-tibialis superior (popliteus)
occurrences.innervation: R. muscularis of the N. tibialis medialis.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Sphenodon punctatus, Osawa (1898), *Zur Muskellehre*. Fürbringer's name, and **Gadow called the same muscle the *M. interosseus cruris*** — which is this dataset's separate record, and the one this record is derived from. A small muscle from the tibial surface of the fibular head, from the tendinous sheet between it and the superior fibular head of the flexor digitorum profundus, and from the proximal interosseous membrane, running obliquely to the posterior surface of the proximal quarter of the tibia. Osawa scores a separate *fibulo-tibialis inferior* distally, so the tuatara has both members of the pair and Gadow's conflation is visible as such.

occurrences.name: Popliteus and pronator tibiae
occurrences.attachmentNote: Spilocuscus maculatus. **This muscle fills the entire interosseous space** — a continuous layer of oblique fibres running from the fibula downwards and inwards to the tibia, thick and fleshy in its upper and lower thirds and thin and largely tendinous in the middle. That is the ancestral `interosseus cruris` this record carries as a synonym, and here it dwarfs the popliteus proper: **a few very oblique superficial fibres from the lateral collateral ligament of the knee are all that Cunningham can identify as the popliteus, the rest being Humphry's pronator tibiae.** The upper mass is fixed to the posterior tibia and the antero-internal border of the fibula, the lower thickening to the antero-external tibial surface. Cunningham verifies Young's account of what it does: the tibiofibular joints admit only antero-posterior gliding, not pronation and supination, and the muscle's attachments in different planes throw the fibula obliquely across the tibia and draw it close. In this animal the two bones are separated at the lower tibiofibular joint by a fibrocartilage jutting up from the ankle, as in the koala.

occurrences.name: Popliteus and pronator tibiae
occurrences.attachmentNote: Thylacinus cynocephalus. The same interosseous sheet as the cuscus's, with the same upper and lower thickenings, but **the fibres are exceedingly short because the two bones lie so close together** — fibular movement on the tibia is extremely limited here, though of the same character. Below, the muscle is chiefly seen from the front of the limb, its tibial attachment lying so far forward on the bone. At the lower tibiofibular joint the two bones are in direct apposition, both surfaces coated with encrusting cartilage — where the cuscus has a fibrocartilage between them.

occurrences.name: Popliteus
occurrences.attachmentNote: Tachyglossus aculeatus, Gambaryan et al. (2002). Along the cranial border of the medial aspect of the proximal extremity of the processus parafibularis, to the proximal quarter of the medial aspect of the tibia, a short way from the insertions of the semimembranosus and the semitendinosus pars vertebralis. **This muscle arises from the fibula, not the femur.** In therians the popliteus takes the lateral femoral condyle; here both monotremes put it on a fibular process, which makes it a tibiofibular muscle rather than a knee muscle in the therian sense.

occurrences.name: Popliteus
occurrences.attachmentNote: Ornithorhynchus anatinus, Gambaryan et al. (2002). Along the medial edge of the processus parafibularis distal to the gastrocnemius lateralis, the origin running down the ligamentum parafibulopatellae to the patella and further onto the process articulating with the tibia, lateral to the joint bursa; inserting on the caudal aspect of the tibia medial to the semimembranosus and the semitendinosus pars ischiadica.

homology.notes: The popliteus derives from the interosseus cruris.
homology.teaching: The cleanest single case for separating topological correspondence from developmental correspondence. Worth teaching verbatim.

correspondences.note: Stated by Diogo & Molnar (2014) Table 14 as a "clear topological correspondence"; their forelimb name for it is the pronator teres, in Rattus and Homo.

muscles.name: Tibialis posterior
muscles.developmental: Somitic; deep ventral mass of the crus.

consensus.origin: Interosseous membrane and the adjacent tibia and fibula.
consensus.insertion: Navicular, cuneiforms and the bases of the middle metatarsals.
consensus.action: Inverts the foot; plantarflexes the ankle; supports the medial longitudinal arch.

occurrences.name: Tibialis posterior
occurrences.attachmentNote: Tibialis caudalis from the caudal tibial shaft and the cranial, medial and caudal aspects of the fibular head, through the sulcus of the medial malleolus, to the medial and ventral surfaces of the centrale and tarsal I and to the sesamoid between them.

occurrences.name: Tibialis posterior
occurrences.action: Inverts the foot and assists plantarflexion.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). Interosseous membrane and the facing surfaces of both leg bones, to the navicular tuberosity, the medial cuneiform and metatarsals 2-4 — the widest tarsal insertion of any muscle in the human foot, and the main dynamic support of the medial longitudinal arch.

occurrences.note: Iguana iguana, Russell & Bauer (2008). Not among the crural muscles Russell & Bauer describe for *Iguana*. Their ventral crural division is the two gastrocnemii, the flexor digitorum longus, the pronator profundus and the popliteus; the dorsal division is tibialis anterior, extensor digitorum longus and the peronei. There is no separate tibialis posterior in the lizard leg, which is the state this record's therian rows should be read against.
