occurrences.name: M. tibialis posticus
occurrences.innervation: Rr. musculares of the N. tibialis medialis.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Sphenodon punctatus, Osawa (1898), *Zur Muskellehre*. Fürbringer's *tibio-metatarsalis ventralis*, Perrin's *rotateur direct du pied*. A voluminous muscle from the whole posterior surface of the fibula and the proximal part of the interosseous membrane — **and Osawa says pointedly that it does not arise from the tibia, as is generally stated**, despite its name. It inserts by a flat tendon on the proximal tarsal and the bases of metatarsals I, II and III. Compare the *Iguana* row on this record, scored absent: Russell & Bauer's ventral crural division has no separate tibialis posticus at all.

occurrences.name: Tibialis posticus
occurrences.attachmentNote: Thylacinus cynocephalus. Small, lying between the flexor longus hallucis and the flexor longus digitorum. **It has apparently no direct bony attachment at its origin at all** — it springs from the fascia covering the popliteus, and on its outer side is inseparably connected with the flexor longus hallucis — so no origin is scored here. At the inner ankle its tendon passes under that of the flexor longus digitorum and runs along the inner margin of the foot to the internal cuneiform and the base of the first metatarsal.

occurrences.name: Tibialis posticus
occurrences.divisionNote: Cunningham suggests, and then argues against, reading the larger internal part as the flexor longus digitorum — which is absent in this animal — on the ground that its insertion is tarsal.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Spilocuscus maculatus. **Apparently double.** The larger, internal part occupies the place of the absent flexor longus digitorum and arises by two heads — a fibular one from the back of the head of the fibula, whose oblique fibres partly fuse with the upper popliteus, and a tibial one from the upper half of the posterior tibia — its tendon crossing a groove behind the medial malleolus to the inner aspect of the scaphoid. Cunningham raises the obvious possibility and declines it: this muscle *may* represent the flexor longus digitorum, but the tarsal insertion is hard to reconcile with that reading. The smaller external part is a minute belly deep under the huge flexor, from the head of the fibula and the fascia over the popliteus, its slender tendon crossing the same groove beneath the other to reach the plantar aspect of the scaphoid. Young found the tibialis posticus double in the koala too.

occurrences.name: Tibialis caudalis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Tachyglossus aculeatus, Gambaryan et al. (2002). From the caudal surface of the proximal end of the processus parafibularis lateral to the popliteus, and from three-quarters of the fibula lateral to the peroneotibialis; its tendinous sheet thickens to a broad flat tendon at the ankle, with raised margins carrying the synovial sheath of the flexor digitorum tibialis, and it inserts on the medial tubercle of the plantar surface of the astragalus. **This muscle arises entirely on the fibula in an animal that calls it the tibialis.** At 3.2 per cent of hind limb mass it is nearly twice the platypus's.

occurrences.name: Tibialis caudalis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Ornithorhynchus anatinus, Gambaryan et al. (2002). From the caudal aspect of the fibula between the flexor digitorum fibularis and the flexor digitorum tibialis, running along the fibula's medial edge for more than three-fifths of its length; the muscle's caudal surface is concave. Its broad tendon carries the synovial sheath of the flexor digitorum tibialis, as in the echidna, and both tendons run below the base of the spur — **the venomous crural spur is a landmark in this animal's ankle** — the tibialis caudalis ending on the distal end of the calcaneus rather than on the astragalus as it does in the echidna.

homology.teaching: The positive half of the popliteus lesson: this is what a developmentally supported correspondence looks like.

correspondences.note: Stated by Diogo & Molnar (2014) Table 14 as a "clear topological correspondence": the tibialis posterior ('pronator profundus') pairs with the flexor carpi radialis in Rattus and Homo, and with the palmaris profundus 1 — a deep urodele and lizard forearm muscle this dataset does not hold as a record — in Ambystoma and Timon.

Diogo & Molnar identify hindlimb tibialis posterior and forelimb palmaris profundus / pronator profundus (pronator quadratus) as the REAL ontogenetic counterparts — as against the popliteus/pronator teres pairing, which is topological only.
correspondences.caution: Demoted from basis "developmental" to "topological": nothing cited establishes a shared anlage, and CLAUDE.md reserves that value for cases where a source does. Diogo & Molnar (2014) Table 14 pairs the pronator quadratus with the interosseus cruris, and the tibialis posterior ('pronator profundus') with the palmaris profundus 1 in Ambystoma and Timon and with the flexor carpi radialis in Rattus and Homo. This edge crosses those two pairings and conflicts with them.

muscles.name: Flexor digitorum longus (pes)
muscles.developmental: Somitic; ventral mass of the crus.

consensus.insertion: Plantar surfaces of the distal phalanges.
consensus.action: Flexes the toes; plantarflexes the ankle.

occurrences.name: Flexor primordialis communis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Recorded as m. flexor primordialis communis. Five tendons, against four in the hand — the pes retains digit V. Its function is given as pressing the sole against the ground rather than flexing the digits.
occurrences.origin: Chiefly the posteroventral face of the fibula, with part arising by tendon from the fibular epicondyle of the femur.
occurrences.insertion: Plantar aponeurosis, which divides into five tendons to the proximal end of the terminal phalanx of each digit.

occurrences.name: Flexor digitorum longus
occurrences.attachmentNote: From the lateral femoral epicondyle; distally a stout tendon serving digits I-IV. Ankle plantarflexor, active in stance.

occurrences.name: Flexor digitorum longus
occurrences.note: Femoral origin; inserts on the proximoventral unguals I-III.
occurrences.attachmentNote: From the ventral distal femur and lateral condyle, which carries parallel striae aligned with the femoral long axis, onto the proximoventral unguals I-III.

occurrences.name: M. flexor digitorum longus
occurrences.note: Together with the flexor hallucis longus, forms the tendon system that produces automatic toe flexion when the ankle flexes — the mechanism of perching. Ankle plantarflexor.

architecture.note: Values as modelled; maximum isometric force is derived, not measured.

occurrences.name: Flexor digitorum longus
occurrences.attachmentNote: Flexor digitorum medialis from the caudal and caudomedial aspects of the fibular head, through the sulcus of the medial malleolus. It fuses with flexor digitorum lateralis at the distal tarsals into a tendinous sheet that divides into five tendons, which pass through the rings formed by flexor digitorum brevis and insert on the distal phalanges.

occurrences.name: Flexor digitorum longus and flexor hallucis longus
occurrences.action: Flex the toes and assist plantarflexion of the foot.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). Flexor digitorum longus from the middle half of the posterior tibia to the distal phalanges of digits 2-5; flexor hallucis longus from the lower two-thirds of the posterior fibula to the distal phalanx of the hallux. **The hand and the foot went opposite ways here.** In the hand the long flexor split into a superficial and a deep layer inserting at two levels on the same digits; in the foot it split by digit instead, one muscle for the hallux and one for the rest, both reaching the terminal phalanges as the ancestral single plate did. Compare the `flexor-digitorum-longus` human row.

occurrences.name: M. flexor digitorum longus
occurrences.attachmentNote: Iguana iguana, Russell & Bauer (2008). **The most compound muscle in the animal.** Three main heads — femoral from the lateral femoral epicondyle, fibular from the mesial proximal fibular shaft, and a calcaneal head from the ventrolateral astragalocalcaneum — and then a series of accessory heads that arise inside the sole: two metatarsal heads from the ventromesial fifth metatarsal, one from the distal calcaneal margin, and three aponeurotic heads from the dorsal face of the muscle's own aponeurosis. Several of those accessory heads insert not on bone but on the long flexor tendons of neighbouring digits. Two lumbricals are part of the same complex, one arising on the lateral margin of the digit III tendon and one from the aponeurosis between the digit II and III tendons. A muscle that repeatedly reattaches to itself on the way to the toes.

occurrences.name: M. flexor digitorum communis profundus
occurrences.innervation: Rr. musculares of the N. tibialis medialis, with the third head from the N. tibialis lateralis and the accessory heads from its Rr. plantares.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Sphenodon punctatus, Osawa (1898), *Zur Muskellehre*. **Four heads in the leg and two more picked up inside the sole.** Femorale from the lateral posterior surface of the fibular femoral condyle in common with the same-named head of the gastrocnemius; tibiale from the end tendon of the ischio-tibialis posticus lateralis; fibulare superius from the back of the fibular head and a tendinous sheet dividing it from the popliteus; fibulare inferius from the posterior and lateral surfaces of the distal third of the fibula. The first three unite into a tendinous mass near the ankle, the fourth joins it fleshily, and the whole fans into five slips to the terminal phalanges of all five toes **after passing through the slits of the flexor digitorum sublimis**. The two accessory heads arise from the proximal tarsal and from the volar prominence of metatarsal V and attach to the fourth and third tendons — a long flexor that recruits new heads from the bones it crosses, exactly as in *Iguana*.

occurrences.name: Flexor longus digitorum and flexor longus hallucis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Thylacinus cynocephalus. A small flexor longus digitorum and a large flexor longus hallucis. The digitorum arises from the posterior tibia in its upper two-thirds and by a separate pointed process from the back of the tibia's medial tuberosity and the posterior ligament of the knee; at the inner ankle it crosses the tibialis posticus tendon obliquely and, on entering the sole, **ends by joining the tendon of the hallucis rather than reaching a digit of its own**. The hallucis is very large, the outermost of the deep calf muscles, from the whole length of the posterior fibula; its thick rope-like tendon enters the sole in a groove on the back of the astragalus and, after receiving the digitorum, splits into four — one per toe.

occurrences.name: Flexor longus hallucis
occurrences.innervation: A twig from the internal popliteal nerve.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Spilocuscus maculatus. **The flexor longus digitorum is apparently absent** and the hallucis is huge, from the whole length of the posterior fibula and also from the fascia covering the popliteus. About mid-leg it divides into a small superficial and a large deep portion, and Cunningham's own comparison is the right one: they stand to each other as the flexor sublimis and profundus do in the forearm of the same animal. **The superficial portion is the flexor brevis digitorum, taking origin above the foot altogether** — its rows are on `flexores-breves-superficiales-pes` — and he settles the identification by nerve: it is supplied by a recurrent branch of the internal plantar nerve while the deep portion is supplied from the internal popliteal. The deep portion ends in a rope-like tendon grooved to receive the three delicate short-flexor tendons, and divides in the sole into five, one per toe.

occurrences.name: Flexor digitorum fibularis and flexor digitorum tibialis
occurrences.divisionNote: Both heads arise on the fibula and its parafibular process in this animal. The names record the courses of the tendons, not their origins.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Tachyglossus aculeatus, Gambaryan et al. (2002). Flexor digitorum fibularis from the proximal end of the processus parafibularis distal to the gastrocnemius lateralis, plus the lateral edge and more than two-thirds of the cranial surface of the fibula and a narrow strip of its caudal surface; its flat tendon runs along the medial aspect of the tuber calcanei and forms a plate splitting into five tendons to the ungual phalanges of all five toes. **Gambaryan et al. record a fifth-toe tendon that Lewis (1963) and Jouffroy et al. (1971) did not**, crediting Mivart with having seen it. Flexor digitorum tibialis from the laterocaudal and lateral aspects of the proximal processus parafibularis medial to the gastrocnemius lateralis, inserting by a broad aponeurosis on the medial edge of the first toe and sending guys to the tuber calcanei, the proximal laterodorsal fifth metatarsal, and the transverse tendinous ligaments of the fourth and fifth metatarsal joints. Because that insertion fuses with the deep layer of the plantar aponeurosis, **Mivart and Westling mistook this muscle for a plantaris**.
occurrences.action: Flexes the toes.

occurrences.name: Flexor digitorum fibularis and flexor digitorum tibialis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Ornithorhynchus anatinus, Gambaryan et al. (2002). Flexor digitorum fibularis by an aponeurosis below the broadening of the processus parafibularis and along its lateral edge, spreading over the whole caudal surface of the proximal fibula and part of its cranial surface down to the distal third; its tendon runs medial to the plantar eminences of the tuber calcanei, is held in a deepening of that surface by a strong ligament, broadens, and splits into five tendons to the ungual phalanges of all the toes. **The short muscles of the sole attach to both faces of that broadening**, which is what makes the tuber calcanei the organising landmark of this foot. Flexor digitorum tibialis from the proximal processus parafibularis between the popliteus and the tibialis caudalis, down to the distal end of the processus articularis fibularis; its thin round tendon lies in a sheath on the tibialis caudalis tendon, passes below the base of the crural spur, and ends by a broadening on the plantar surface of the medial sesamoid — **which Gambaryan et al. suggest is the prehallux**. At 3.5 per cent of hind limb mass the fibularis head is half again the echidna's.

occurrences.name: Flexor digitorum longus
occurrences.attachmentNote: *Grus americana*, Fisher & Goodman (1955); anconal and palmar are dorsal and ventral in their usage. **M. flexor digitorum longus.** The bifurcated head of origin is as figured by Fisher (1946: 682); his figure 21 is a posterior view, rather than anterior as labeled. Laterally the origin is fleshy from the postero-distal half of the fibular head and continues down to the last fourth of the fibular length. A narrow line on the tibiotarsus, adjacent and parallel to the fibular origin, also gives fleshy origin to this muscle. The most proximal part of the medial origin is beneath the distal end of M. popliteus and separated from the lateral head by tibial nerves and blood vessels. A longitudinal line on the proximal third of the postero-medial corner of the tibiotarsus provides further fleshy origin for the medial head. In *Insertion.* The calcified tendon, formed in the middle of the tibio- tarsal length, shortly crosses to a mid-posterior position on the shank. As it goes over the intratarsal joint it is in the most medial group and is the deepest of all tendons here, being immediately beneath that of M. plantaris. After passing through a bony canal in the hypotarsus, the tendon forms three rami about 5 centimeters above the tarsometatarsal malleoli. Before these branches are formed the tendon is joined by that of M. flex. hall. longus. The common branches characteristically perforate the other flexors as they pass to the digits. A fourth and extremely small ramus extends to the base of digit I, but we c

homology.teaching: The distal-greater-than-proximal similarity gradient is visible in a single salamander dissection.

correspondences.note: Stated by Diogo & Molnar (2014) Table 14 as a "clear topological correspondence"; their forelimb name for it is the flexor digitorum longus, and flexor digitorum profundus in mammals.

muscles.name: Flexores breves superficiales (pes)
muscles.developmental: Somitic; ventral intrinsic layer of the pes.

consensus.insertion: Middle phalanges.
consensus.action: Flexes the toes at the metatarsophalangeal and proximal interphalangeal joints.

occurrences.name: Flexores breves superficiales
occurrences.attachmentNote: Tripartite for every digit except the first, which lacks the phalangeal connection. The manus counterpart differs: there the slips flank the metacarpals of digits II and III but not I and IV.
occurrences.origin: Dorsal side of the plantar fascia.
occurrences.insertion: For digits II-V, the ventral side of the distal ends of the metatarsals and the ventral surface of the proximal end of the proximal phalanx; for digit I, the distal end of the metatarsal only.

occurrences.name: Mm. flexores breves superficiales
occurrences.note: A single muscular body in Triprion despite the plural name, on the lateroplantar tarsus beneath the aponeurosis plantaris.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Despite the plural name, a single muscular body in Triprion, on the lateroplantar tarsal surface and ventrally concealed by the aponeurosis plantaris.

occurrences.name: Flexores breves superficiales
occurrences.attachmentNote: Scored from Zaaf et al.'s tables for Eublepharis macularius, with the Gekko gecko differences noted where they bear on the attachment. Flexor digitorum brevis of the pes, from the proximal extremity of the fifth metatarsal onto the terminal phalanx. Gekko differs digit by digit, inserting at the distal end of metatarsal I on digit I, of the second phalanx on III and IV, and of the first phalanx on II and V.

occurrences.name: Flexor digitorum brevis superficialis
occurrences.note: Layer 1 of the seven-layer pedal scheme.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Flexor digitorum brevis superficialis, digits I-IV, from the ventral calcaneum with digit-specific variation. Layer 1 of the seven-layer pedal scheme Pereyra et al. set out.

occurrences.name: Flexor digitorum brevis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Flexor digitorum brevis, taking origin by an aponeurosis from the insertion of the flexor digitorum superficialis tendon at the plantar surface of the calcaneal tubercle. Its tendons split around those of flexor digitorum profundus, forming the rings the deep tendons pass through, and insert on the plantar and proximal aspects of the middle phalanges of II–V and the proximal phalanx of digit I.

occurrences.name: Flexores breves superficiales
occurrences.attachmentNote: Gekko gecko, from the differences column of Zaaf et al.'s tables. Digit by digit: the distal end of metatarsal I for digit I, of the second phalanx for III and IV, and of the first phalanx for II and V — where Eublepharis inserts on the terminal phalanx throughout.

occurrences.name: Flexor digitorum brevis
occurrences.action: Flexes the proximal interphalangeal joints of digits 2-5.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). Calcaneal tuberosity, plantar aponeurosis and intermuscular septa, to the bases of the middle phalanges of digits 2-5, splitting to let the long flexor tendons through. **The split tendon is inherited, not invented.** The same bifurcation is described for crocodylians, lepidosaurs and turtles in the hand, where the short flexor tendons divide to pass the long flexor, and Burch reconstructs it for *Tawa*. Humans kept it in the foot and lost the layer in the hand — see the `flexores-breves-superficiales` row, scored uncertain there for exactly that reason.

occurrences.name: Mm. flexores digitores breves
occurrences.attachmentNote: Iguana iguana, Russell & Bauer (2008). **All slips arise from the aponeurosis of the deep head of the femoral gastrocnemius**, not from bone — the deep femoral aponeurosis — with the slip to digit III also taking partial origin from the mesial plantar tubercle of metatarsal V. The system serves digits I, II and III only, and no fibres traverse the phalanges: the bellies stop at the metatarsophalangeal joint capsules and continue as tendons. Digit II's lateral belly splits around the long flexor tendon and rejoins above it; digit III's three tendons braid with a branch of the superficial femoral aponeurosis and with the third lumbrical before inserting on phalanx III.

occurrences.name: M. flexor digitorum communis sublimis
occurrences.innervation: Rr. superficiales plantares of the N. tibialis lateralis and medialis.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Sphenodon punctatus, Osawa (1898), *Zur Muskellehre*. A short muscle arising from the end of the femoral head of the gastrocnemius — from a tendinous arch, not from bone — and splitting into four slips that insert on both sides of the second phalanges of toes I to IV, **after forming a chiasma tendineum on the plantar side of the proximal phalanx for the deep flexor tendons to pass through**. The same perforated arrangement as in the hand, and as in *Iguana* and the human foot. Osawa notes that Perrin divided this one muscle into nine separately named flexors, which is the kind of subdivision this dataset's `parts` mechanism exists to hold rather than to reproduce.

occurrences.name: Flexor brevis digitorum
occurrences.attachmentNote: Thylacinus cynocephalus. A small muscle in the sole under the expanded plantaris tendon, from the inner aspect of the calcaneum close to its posterior extremity. Four delicate tendons issue from it, run a short way in a groove on the superficial surface of the great flexor tendon, then diverge to their digits. **This is the muscle in its expected place**; in the cuscus it has left the foot entirely.

occurrences.name: Flexor brevis digitorum
occurrences.innervation: A recurrent branch from the internal plantar nerve.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Spilocuscus maculatus, and **the muscle has left the foot**: it is the superficial portion of the great flexor mass, given off from the flexor longus hallucis while still in the leg, so its origin is the posterior fibula. Three tendons, to the minimus, annularis and medius, each pierced by the corresponding deep tendon in the usual way. Cunningham had already set out the general principle in his definition of an intrinsic foot muscle — that the flexor brevis digitorum is the homologue of the flexor sublimis of the forearm and may in some animals be seen taking origin beyond the limits of the foot — and this animal is his case. **He identifies it by nerve**: a recurrent branch from the internal plantar nerve, where the deep portion beside it is supplied from the internal popliteal.

occurrences.name: Flexor brevis digitorum
occurrences.innervation: Twigs from the internal plantar nerve in the sole; the outermost belly from the trunk of the external plantar.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Ornithorhynchus anatinus. **Four fleshy bellies with two different origins**: those for the index and medius arise from the plantar surface of the long flexor tendon as it enters the sole, those for the annularis and minimus by a common fleshy origin from the under surface of the outwardly directed calcaneal tuberosity. All insert into the bases of the first phalanges and partly into the flexor sheaths. The outermost belly is the one Ruge assigned to the plantar layer as an extra adductor of the minimus, and Cunningham's rebuttal — three special dissections — is on its origin being far from the plantar muscles, its continuity with the belly for the annularis, its lying superficial to the long flexor tendon of the minimus, and its insertion matching the other bellies. Meckel had taken all four bellies for lumbricals; Cuvier & Laurillard figure them together as the common short flexor.

occurrences.name: Flexor brevis digitorum
occurrences.innervation: A twig from the branch the internal plantar nerve sends round the calcaneal tuber — which Cunningham reads as standing in for the superficial division of the external plantar, absent in this foot.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Tachyglossus aculeatus. **One belly left of four**, and it survives for a reason: in Cunningham's specimen the flexor longus digitorum sent no tendon to the minimus, so the outermost short-flexor belly is retained for that digit. From the plantar fascia and the calcaneal tuber to the plantar surface of the base of the second phalanx of the little toe, partially fused with the flexor brevis minimi digiti beneath it — which, he warns, makes it very easy to mistake for an intrinsic muscle now that its three fellows are gone. **Mivart described a long flexor tendon to the minimus in *Echidna hystrix* and denied any part of the short flexor**; that disagreement is between two animals and is recorded, not resolved.

correspondences.note: Stated by Diogo & Molnar (2014) Table 15 as a "clear topological correspondence"; their forelimb name for it is the flexores breves superficiales.

muscles.name: Contrahentes digitorum (pes)
muscles.developmental: Somitic; ventral intrinsic layer of the pes.

consensus.insertion: Proximal phalanges.
consensus.action: Adducts the toes toward the foot's axis.

occurrences.name: Contrahentes digitorum
occurrences.attachmentNote: Passes from the tarsals along the ventral axis of the metatarsals. As in the hand, part of the origin is on the caput longum tendon rather than on bone.
occurrences.origin: The flat tendon of the caput longum musculorum contrahentium, and the tarsal bones.
occurrences.insertion: Proximal phalanx of each digit.

occurrences.name: Mm. contrahentes digitorum pedis
occurrences.note: Blotto et al. (2020) record a full contrahens series in the anuran foot, including one serving the prehallux — the pedal counterpart of the prepollex contrahens in the hand.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Blotto et al. record a full contrahens series in the anuran foot, including one serving the prehallux.

occurrences.name: Interdigiti dorsales + ventrales
occurrences.note: Running between successive metatarsals.
occurrences.attachmentNote: The interdigiti dorsales and ventrales of Pereyra et al., running between successive metatarsals; their origins are marked by longitudinally oriented fine striae on the proximolateral metatarsal surfaces.

occurrences.name: Adductor hallucis
occurrences.note: As in the hand, the contrahens layer is largely lost in mammals, with the adductor hallucis surviving as its principal representative.

occurrences.name: Adductor hallucis
occurrences.action: Adducts the great toe.
occurrences.innervation: Deep branch of the lateral plantar nerve.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). Oblique head from the bases of metatarsals 2-4, transverse head from the heads of metatarsals 3-5, both to the lateral side of the base of the proximal phalanx of the hallux. **The foot and the hand each kept exactly one contrahens, and it is the one to digit I in both.** Adductor hallucis here, adductor pollicis on `contrahentes-digitorum` — two limbs, the same survivor, the same two-headed arrangement, in an animal that uses the two limbs for completely different things.

occurrences.name: Mm. contrahentes
occurrences.attachmentNote: Iguana iguana, Russell & Bauer (2008). Small slips serving the first four digits, those to digits I-III from a common tendinous origin on the proximomesial shaft of metatarsal V and that to digit IV from the proximal ventrolateral border of metatarsal IV, each inserting by a small motor tendon on the proximolateral margin of the first phalanx of its digit, intimately associated with the metatarsophalangeal joint ligaments. **Four contrahentes, where a human has one** — the adductor hallucis, scored on this record from Gest.

occurrences.name: M. adductor digitorum communis and M. adductor digiti V
occurrences.innervation: Rr. plantares of the N. tibialis lateralis.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Sphenodon punctatus, Osawa (1898), *Zur Muskellehre*. Fürbringer's *tarso-digitalis ventralis medius* for the first, and he groups the adductor and flexor of digit V as *tarso-digitalis ventralis fibularis*. The adductor digitorum communis arises from the plantar prominence of metatarsal V and divides into three slips — one running almost transversely to the fibular side of the hallux's proximal phalanx and two to both sides of the second toe's. **A contrahens layer that reaches across the whole sole from the fifth metatarsal to the first toe**, which is the arrangement the human adductor hallucis is the survivor of.

occurrences.name: Plantar layer (three adductors)
occurrences.innervation: External plantar nerve — in this animal, which has no hallux, every intrinsic muscle of the foot is supplied by it.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Thylacinus cynocephalus. **The hallux is suppressed and the pes closely resembles a dog's**, but the three-layer plan is still plain. Three adductors, working towards a line through the medius: the adductor indicis and the adductor minimi digiti share a single pointed origin in the midline of the foot from the fibrous structures at the base of the metatarsus, then diverge to the fibular side of the index and the tibial side of the minimus, each inserting partly into a sesamoid and partly into the extensor tendon; the adductor annularis rises from the base of the middle metatarsal beneath them and swells into a fusiform belly. In some feet the adductor indicis was double. Cunningham's three-layer scheme is the frame for every row in this survey: each digit typically gets an adductor from the plantar layer, an abductor from the dorsal layer and a flexor brevis from the intermediate layer, and what varies between mammals is which of the three have fused, migrated or gone.

occurrences.name: Plantar layer (four adductors)
occurrences.attachmentNote: Dasyurus viverrinus. A long narrow foot whose metatarsals lie so close together that **not one intrinsic muscle can be seen from the dorsum** — all are crowded into the sole — and yet the three-layer plan survives crowding intact, which is the point Cunningham uses later against the carnivores, whose muscles fuse under the same conditions. The adductors of the index and minimus form one exceedingly thin triangular sheet, tendinous at its apex in the midline and arching over the bases of the annularis and medius, inserting by its angles into a sesamoid at each end; a faint fibrous raphe running from apex to base marks where the two muscles divide. The adductor annularis is a minute fusiform slip arising **from the deep surface of that raphe** and visible shining through the sheet. The adductor hallucis is a delicate muscle to the head of the rudimentary hallucal metatarsal. Ruge described a special adductor of the medius in *Dasyurus hallucatus*; Cunningham found none here and says it is rare for the digit that is the centre of adduction to have an adductor of its own.

occurrences.name: Plantar layer (four adductors)
occurrences.attachmentNote: Phascogale calura. **This animal has pes rows although it has no hindlimb rows** — the shot that destroyed its pelvis and thigh left the foot fit to dissect, and Cunningham describes it in full. Its foot closely resembles *Dasyurus viverrinus*'s outwardly, with a better-developed hallux that still has neither nail nor claw. The adductors of index, annularis and minimus share one tendinous origin from the base of the metatarsus in the midline, expanding into a thin fleshy sheet that lies on all the other intrinsic muscles and divides into three diverging slips near the roots of the toes; the adductor hallucis has an independent origin just inside their common tendon. **All four lie on one plane**, where in the thylacine and *Dasyurus* the adductors of index and minimus have pressed inwards and thrust the adductor annularis up above them.

occurrences.name: Plantar layer (three adductors and a raphe)
occurrences.divisionNote: The adductor indicis is absent as a muscle; Cunningham reads the distal end of the fibrous raphe, which attaches to the outer side of the base of the index's proximal phalanx, as that muscle converted into fibrous tissue.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Spilocuscus maculatus, and the most instructive foot in the marsupial series. The hallux is broad, clawless and set at right angles to the foot's axis, opposing the other toes; index and medius are bound in one sheath as far as the second joint and cannot move independently; the annularis is much the largest. **Adduction here is towards a line drawn through the index, not the medius** — an exception to the general rule, and the same exception the human foot makes. A median fibrous raphe accordingly lies over the index metatarsal, and the adductors arise from it. There is no adductor of the index at all: the raphe is attached to the outer side of the base of its proximal phalanx, and Cunningham reads its lower end as the missing muscle turned to fibrous tissue. The adductor hallucis is the most powerful and most complex — a double origin, from the base of the index metatarsal and the tibial side of the raphe and by a few fibres from the aponeurosis over the first dorsal interosseous, resolving into plantar, intermediate and dorsal slips that end respectively on the outer sesamoid, on the minute distal phalanx by a long tendon, and in the extensor tendon.

occurrences.name: Plantar layer (adductors on a raphe)
occurrences.divisionNote: Two specimens, two arrangements: adduction towards the index in one and towards the annularis in the other, with the adductor present in one specimen absent in the other and vice versa. Scored `variable` for genuine within-species variation seen by one worker in two animals.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Trichosurus vulpecula, Cunningham's *Phalangista vulpina*, **and his two specimens disagreed with each other.** In one, a median raphe ran from the base of the second metatarsal to the outer side of the base of the index's proximal phalanx, and adduction was towards the index as in the cuscus. In the other the raphe ran from the base of the middle metatarsal to the inner side of the base of the annularis, and the annular digit was the centre of the movement — with an adductor indicis present, which the cuscus lacks, and no adductor annularis. Cunningham then explains how a raphe acquires its distal attachment, using *Dasyurus*, where the raphe has no distal attachment at all and the adductor annularis arises from its deep surface: **let that muscle turn to fibrous tissue and you get the second specimen; let the adductor indicis turn instead and you get the cuscus and the first specimen.** One mechanism, two outcomes, both in one species.

occurrences.name: Plantar layer (four adductors)
occurrences.innervation: The muscular branch of the deep division of the external plantar nerve, which supplies all the intrinsic muscles except the abductor ossis metatarsi minimi digiti and the flexor brevis hallucis.
occurrences.attachmentNote:
Ornithorhynchus anatinus, from **both feet of four specimens** — the largest sample in Cunningham's survey, and he says why he needed it: the plantar layer is always distinct but the intermediate and dorsal layers are usually more or less fused. Four adductors, all from the plantar surface of the external and middle cuneiforms, drawing the toes towards the index. The adductor minimi digiti is the largest and lies very obliquely, chiefly on the tibial side of the minimus's first phalanx but sending a slender fleshy process forward to the second. In one very large specimen a delicate extra fasciculus went to the outer side of the medius, and Cunningham could find it in no other. **He disagrees with Ruge twice here.** Ruge described an extra adductor for the index: Cunningham looked for it in vain and could not use the deep external plantar nerve to help, because in this animal that nerve cannot be traced inward past the muscles of the index — it breaks up into terminal twigs, quite unlike Ruge's figure. Ruge also described an extra plantar muscle for the minimus: Cunningham made three special dissections and pronounces it the outermost belly of the flexor brevis digitorum, on four grounds, the last being that it is inserted like the other bellies of that muscle. He concedes Ruge's point that it takes an external plantar twig, and says a nerve alone is not enough to separate a muscle from the one it plainly belongs to.

**Gambaryan et al. (2002) count three, not four, and call them contrahentes.** They arise by a common aponeurosis on the plantar tubercle of the naviculare: the contrahens of digit V from the most superficial layer, onto the medial sides of the distal fifth metatarsal and the first and second phalanges of that toe; the contrahentes of digits III and IV from the second and third layers, onto the medial sides of the metatarsals, the first phalanges and the proximal second phalanges of their toes. **The contrahens of the second toe is absent in this animal** — where Cunningham's four include an adductor hallucis and Gambaryan et al. treat the hallucal muscle as a separate abductor–flexor–adductor set. The two counts are not reconciled here.

**Their nomenclature argument belongs to this record.** They hold that 'contrahentes' should name the group inserting on the *medial* sides of all the toes, which in a sprawling animal keeps the foot from turning laterally during the support phase. As therian limbs become parasagittal that lateral force disappears and the requirement becomes preventing the toes from spreading; the contrahens of digit III drops out and muscles appear on the *lateral* sides of digits I and II. The muscles serving digits IV and V they call homologous with the reptilian and monotreme contrahentes without reservation; those on the lateral sides of I and II they derive from the interossei instead, using the platypus's own elaborate interossei as the model of that transformation. Hence their recommendation: **`adductores` for therians, `contrahentes` for reptiles and monotremes** — against Ribbing (1938), Jouffroy & Lessertisseur (1959) and Kyou-Jouffroy (1971), who homologised the therian adductors with the reptilian contrahentes entire. This record is the union of both readings and does not adopt either name.

occurrences.name: Plantar layer (five adductors)
occurrences.innervation: Muscular branches of the external plantar nerve, which supplies all the intrinsic muscles except the abductor and flexor brevis of the hallux.
occurrences.attachmentNote:
Tachyglossus aculeatus, Cunningham's *Echidna setosa*. **The best-represented layer in a foot whose intrinsic muscles are mostly going or gone** — every digit has an adductor and the annularis has two, and they draw the toes towards the interval between index and hallux rather than towards a digit. The adductors of hallux and index share an origin from the under surface of the calcaneum near the outer margin and cross the sole obliquely, superficial to the rest; the other three arise together from the ligaments under the tarsus and diverge as thin bands ending in flat aponeurotic tendons on the tibial sides of the **ungual** phalanges of medius, annularis and minimus. The annularis also has a very delicate extra fasciculus, which Cunningham matches to the unaccountable extra adductor he found in one large platypus. **The adductors are so thin as to be semi-transparent**, and he says plainly that these muscles are undergoing retrograde change.

**Gambaryan et al. (2002) find four here and call them contrahentes**, arising on the deep plantar aponeurosis at the level of tarsale III and inserting on the medial sides of the **second** phalanges of digits II–V. Cunningham has five, reaching the ungual phalanges of medius, annularis and minimus. The two dissections agree that the group is present and that it inserts medially, and disagree on the count and on how far down the toe it goes; neither is preferred here. Their reason for the name is the reptilian comparison: in reptiles the contrahentes lie superficial to the interossei — closer to the plantar surface — and insert on the medial sides of the first phalanges of all the toes, which is the arrangement this foot repeats.

occurrences.name: Plantar layer (two or three adductors) and opponens
occurrences.attachmentNote: Canis lupus familiaris. **The adductors survive as a distinct plantar layer in every carnivore Cunningham examined**, even where the layers behind them have fused — generally two of them, the adductor indicis and the adductor minimi digiti, working towards a line through the medius, with a common origin in the midline from the ligamentous textures at the base of the metatarsus. An adductor annularis turns up occasionally in the dog, feeble and fused with the tibial head of that toe's short flexor, which Cunningham uses to argue the muscle is lost here by fusion and not by suppression. **An opponens minimi digiti belongs with this layer**, arising with the adductor of the little toe and inserting on the plantar face of the distal third of the fifth metatarsal shaft; he found it in all four tetradactylous cats and both dogs.

occurrences.name: Plantar layer (two or three adductors) and opponens
occurrences.attachmentNote: Felis catus. **The adductors survive as a distinct plantar layer in every carnivore Cunningham examined**, even where the layers behind them have fused — generally two of them, the adductor indicis and the adductor minimi digiti, working towards a line through the medius, with a common origin in the midline from the ligamentous textures at the base of the metatarsus. An adductor annularis turns up occasionally in the dog, feeble and fused with the tibial head of that toe's short flexor, which Cunningham uses to argue the muscle is lost here by fusion and not by suppression. **An opponens minimi digiti belongs with this layer**, arising with the adductor of the little toe and inserting on the plantar face of the distal third of the fifth metatarsal shaft; he found it in all four tetradactylous cats and both dogs.

occurrences.name: Plantar layer (two or three adductors) and opponens
occurrences.attachmentNote: Puma concolor. **The adductors survive as a distinct plantar layer in every carnivore Cunningham examined**, even where the layers behind them have fused — generally two of them, the adductor indicis and the adductor minimi digiti, working towards a line through the medius, with a common origin in the midline from the ligamentous textures at the base of the metatarsus. An adductor annularis turns up occasionally in the dog, feeble and fused with the tibial head of that toe's short flexor, which Cunningham uses to argue the muscle is lost here by fusion and not by suppression. **An opponens minimi digiti belongs with this layer**, arising with the adductor of the little toe and inserting on the plantar face of the distal third of the fifth metatarsal shaft; he found it in all four tetradactylous cats and both dogs.

occurrences.name: Plantar layer (two or three adductors) and opponens
occurrences.attachmentNote: Panthera pardus. **The adductors survive as a distinct plantar layer in every carnivore Cunningham examined**, even where the layers behind them have fused — generally two of them, the adductor indicis and the adductor minimi digiti, working towards a line through the medius, with a common origin in the midline from the ligamentous textures at the base of the metatarsus. An adductor annularis turns up occasionally in the dog, feeble and fused with the tibial head of that toe's short flexor, which Cunningham uses to argue the muscle is lost here by fusion and not by suppression. **An opponens minimi digiti belongs with this layer**, arising with the adductor of the little toe and inserting on the plantar face of the distal third of the fifth metatarsal shaft; he found it in all four tetradactylous cats and both dogs.

occurrences.name: Plantar layer (two or three adductors) and opponens
occurrences.attachmentNote: Panthera leo. **The adductors survive as a distinct plantar layer in every carnivore Cunningham examined**, even where the layers behind them have fused — generally two of them, the adductor indicis and the adductor minimi digiti, working towards a line through the medius, with a common origin in the midline from the ligamentous textures at the base of the metatarsus. An adductor annularis turns up occasionally in the dog, feeble and fused with the tibial head of that toe's short flexor, which Cunningham uses to argue the muscle is lost here by fusion and not by suppression. **An opponens minimi digiti belongs with this layer**, arising with the adductor of the little toe and inserting on the plantar face of the distal third of the fifth metatarsal shaft; he found it in all four tetradactylous cats and both dogs.

occurrences.name: Plantar layer (three adductors)
occurrences.attachmentNote: Meles meles. **A plantigrade pentadactyl foot that comes nearer Cunningham's three-layer type than the digitigrade carnivores do** — though he is careful to add that plantigrady itself has no effect on where the intrinsic muscles sit: they are as plantar in the badger as in the otter or the cats. Three adductors — hallucis, indicis, minimi digiti — arising side by side in one plane from the bases of the second and third metatarsals and radiating to adduct towards the medius. **No adductor annularis and no opponens minimi digiti could be found.** Ruge's figure of the adducting muscles in *Meles* agrees except that his arise on different planes.

occurrences.name: Plantar layer (three adductors) and opponens
occurrences.attachmentNote: Lutra lutra. Five digits in a common web that nevertheless move freely, so the intrinsic muscles are well developed — and **with one or two minor exceptions this foot meets every requirement of Cunningham's three-layer type**, the closest any carnivore in his survey comes to it. The adducting layer matches the badger's in number and character, with the addition of an opponens minimi digiti of the kind found in the tetradactylous carnivores, inserted on the plantar face of the distal third of the fifth metatarsal.

occurrences.name: Plantar layer (three adductors) and opponens
occurrences.attachmentNote: Mustela putorius, and **the only row this animal should ever carry from this source**. Cunningham says his observations do not extend beyond the adducting muscles: the specimen was so putrid that dissecting the deeper layers was impossible. What he did make out with certainty is that the adductors are identical in number and disposition with the otter's and the badger's, and that like the otter it has an opponens minimi digiti developed in the same way. The deeper layers of this foot are unrecorded, not absent.

occurrences.name: Plantar layer (adductor hallucis alone)
occurrences.divisionNote: The adductor minimi digiti is present only as a fibrous band in the muscle's position, with the muscle's connections and none of its tissue.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Odobenus rosmarus, a very young specimen long in spirit. **The adductor hallucis is the only member of this layer left, and it is already double** — an adductor obliquus from the plantar base of the fourth metatarsal and an adductor transversus from the fascia over the flexor brevis minimi digiti, coalescing over the flexor brevis indicis into one long narrow tendon that reaches the extensor tendon on the fibular side of the hallux's first phalanx. That oblique-plus-transverse split is the same one the human foot makes and the one Cunningham sees beginning in the tamandua. A slender **fibrous band** occupies the position of the adductor minimi digiti, from the fourth metatarsal base to the tibial side of the minimus. Murie figured two slips here as a superficial layer of interossei, did not figure the transverse head at all, and put both origins on the middle metatarsal; Cunningham's specimen differs and he says so.

occurrences.name: Plantar layer (three adductors)
occurrences.attachmentNote: Tamandua tetradactyla. **Adduction here is towards the annularis while abduction is away from the index** — the two halves of the apparatus referred to different digits, which Cunningham says he has seen nowhere else. Three adductors. The minimi digiti is a narrow slip from the base of the fourth metatarsal and the sheath of the peroneus longus tendon. The hallucis and indicis are fan-shaped and arise largely from a strong fibrous raphe running from the head to the base of the fifth metatarsal — the hallucis from its proximal half and the ligaments over the third and fourth metatarsal bases, the indicis from its distal half. In the left foot an extra adducting slip for the index ran transversely across the roots of annularis and medius from the base of the minimus's proximal phalanx: **Cunningham reads it as the beginning of the split into an oblique and a transverse part that is complete in the apes and in man**, and which the walrus's adductor hallucis has already made.

occurrences.name: Plantar layer (four adductors)
occurrences.attachmentNote: Euphractus sexcinctus. **The best-preserved layer in a foot where most of the rest has turned to ligament.** Four adductors working towards the medius, the first three from a common origin on the fibrous textures at the bases of the second and third metatarsals. The adductor indicis has an extra head from the base of the third metatarsal shared with the adductor annularis, which Cunningham suggests may represent a transversus indicis — the same oblique-and-transverse split he traces in the tamandua and the walrus. He disputes Galton's naming of two muscles in this foot and rejects his identification of the adductor minimi digiti as an opponens outright: an opponens must insert on the metatarsal, and this muscle reaches the distal phalanx.

occurrences.name: Plantar layer
occurrences.attachmentNote: Bradypus tridactylus. **Absent, along with every other intrinsic muscle in the sole of this foot.** The proximal phalanges of the three functional digits are square nodules a quarter of an inch long that coalesce early with the metatarsal heads, abolishing the metatarsophalangeal joints; since the primary office of an intrinsic pedal muscle is to act at those joints, Cunningham found not a vestige of one on dissecting the sole. He reads the adductors and the marginal abductors as suppressed, and the flexores breves as having wandered to the dorsum and joined the dorsal interossei — a conclusion he draws from the hand of the same animal, where the migration is caught in progress and a palmar layer of adductors still survives, though largely tendinous and, he thinks, going the same way.

occurrences.name: Plantar layer (two adductors)
occurrences.innervation: The adductor indicis from a deep branch of the internal plantar nerve, the adductor annularis from the deep division of the external plantar.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Procavia capensis. A tridactyl foot — hallux and minimus absent — in which **only the index has all three of its typical muscles**, the medius and annularis each lacking an abductor. Two adductors: the indicis from the fibrous structures on the plantar surface of the scaphoid, the annularis from the ligamentous tissue under the cuboid. Murie & Mivart had described these as the second and fourth single interossei and figured them arising far apart on the same plane as the other muscles; Cunningham corrects that — proximally they are in contact and superficial, and diverge only towards their insertions.

occurrences.name: Plantar layer
occurrences.attachmentNote: Bathyergus suillus. **Absent, and Cunningham declines to say why.** He records the total absence of both the plantar adducting and the dorsal abducting muscles and states that whether this is suppression or fusion with the flexores breves is impossible to make out — if fusion, there are certainly no traces of it to be found. Compare the echidna, where he does commit to suppression, and the tetradactylous carnivores, where he commits to fusion and gives his evidence.

occurrences.name: Adductor hallucis, and an adductor annularis in fibre
occurrences.attachmentNote: Castor fiber. A putrid specimen, both feet carefully dissected. **The only muscular element of this layer is the adductor hallucis** — a very minute belly followed by a long slender fibrous tendon, from the deep surface of the middle cuneiform to the outer aspect of the base of the hallux's first phalanx. The adductor annularis is present as a distinct fibrous band beside it, running to the inner aspect of the base of the annularis: **it contains no muscular fibres, and its position and connections alone tell its history.** The same substitution of fibrous band for muscle runs through this foot, as it does through the armadillo's.

occurrences.name: Plantar layer (two adductors on a raphe)
occurrences.attachmentNote: *Pteropus* sp. A pentadactyl foot with four outer toes of nearly equal length and a slightly smaller hallux, all clawed. **Only two adductors, and they form one thin triangular sheet** spread over the flexores breves and separated from them by the deep division of the external plantar nerve — arising by its apex from the plantar tarsus nearer the inner than the outer margin, and divided into its two muscles by a distinct fibrous raphe running apex to base. **The raphe's distal end is unattached**, ending close to the inner side of the root of the medius, which is the condition Cunningham uses in the brushtail possum to explain how such a raphe acquires an attachment at all. The adductor minimi digiti is much the larger and reaches the inner sesamoid of the minimus; the adductor hallucis reaches the outer sesamoid of the hallux.

correspondences.note: Stated by Diogo & Molnar (2014) Table 15 as a "clear topological correspondence"; their forelimb name for it is the contrahentes digitorum.

muscles.name: Flexores breves profundi (pes)
muscles.developmental: Somitic; deepest ventral intrinsic layer of the pes.

consensus.insertion: Proximal phalanges and metatarsophalangeal sesamoids.
consensus.action: Flexes the metatarsophalangeal joints; abducts and adducts the toes.

occurrences.name: Mm. flexores breves profundi
occurrences.note: Includes slips serving the prehallux.

occurrences.name: Flexor digitorum brevis profundus
occurrences.note: Deep flexor layer; metatarsal origins marked by fine striae.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Flexor digitorum brevis profundus, digits I-IV, from metatarsals I-III and V and the distal calcaneum. The metatarsal origins are marked by fine striae — the pedal correlates Pereyra et al. identify for the first time.

occurrences.name: Interossei (plantar and dorsal)
occurrences.innervation: Deep branch of the lateral plantar nerve.

occurrences.name: Interossei and the short flexors of the hallux and fifth digit
occurrences.action: Flex the metatarsophalangeal joints; the interossei abduct and adduct the digits about the axis of digit II.
occurrences.innervation: Lateral plantar nerve, deep branch; flexor hallucis brevis by the medial plantar nerve.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). Four dorsal interossei from adjacent metatarsal shafts, three plantar interossei from the bases and medial sides of metatarsals 3-5, flexor hallucis brevis from the cuboid and lateral cuneiform, flexor digiti minimi brevis from the base of metatarsal V. **Scored on this record's own mammalian synonymy**, which names the interossei plantares and dorsales as its mammalian representatives. The same carve-up is contested in the hand and is handled the same way there. Note the axis: the human hand abducts about digit III and the foot about digit II, so the two sets of interossei are arranged around different rays.

occurrences.name: Mm. interossei plantares
occurrences.attachmentNote: Iguana iguana, Russell & Bauer (2008). Three bellies, the deepest muscles of the sole, from the ventrolateral margins of metatarsals IV, III and II, crossing the intermetatarsal spaces distomesially to insert fleshily on the distal ventromesial aspect of the metatarsal lying mesial to each origin. **Metatarsal to metatarsal, never reaching a phalanx** — and Russell & Bauer note their dorsal border marks the boundary between the dorsal and ventral muscle masses of the foot, which is what makes them a useful landmark rather than just a small muscle.

occurrences.name: Mm. interossei plantares
occurrences.innervation: Rr. interossei of the N. tibialis medialis and lateralis.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Sphenodon punctatus, Osawa (1898), *Zur Muskellehre*. **Four muscles, for toes I to IV, and none for the fifth** — Osawa says so explicitly. Each arises from the facing sides of the bases of two metatarsals and inserts on the plantar and slightly the fibular side of the proximal phalanx of its toe. Compare *Iguana*, where Russell & Bauer find three, from metatarsals IV, III and II, inserting metatarsal-to-metatarsal without reaching a phalanx.

occurrences.name: Intermediate layer and dorsal interossei
occurrences.attachmentNote: Thylacinus cynocephalus. Four flexores breves, one on the plantar surface of each metatarsal, each of two slips embracing the base of the proximal phalanx and inserting one into each sesamoid, sometimes into the extensor tendon as well. **Whether the two slips arise separately or in common follows no rule at all** — Cunningham found the muscle of a given digit two-headed in one foot of an animal and one-headed in the other foot of the same animal. Acting together the slips flex; acting singly they abduct or adduct, according to which is used. The four dorsal interossei are more plantar than dorsal, reaching only a short way up between the bones; the first, being marginal in a foot with no hallux, is the largest and has two parts, one from the metatarsal base with the flexor brevis and one that **wanders backwards to the scaphoid for its origin** — the tendency of a marginal muscle. In the small female's feet the flexores breves and interossei showed a slight tendency to fuse; in the large male they were quite distinct.

occurrences.name: Intermediate layer and dorsal interossei
occurrences.attachmentNote: Dasyurus viverrinus. Each of the four outer toes has a flexor brevis, **quite distinct from the dorsal interossei and showing no tendency to fuse with them** despite the intermetatarsal spaces being nearly obliterated. Each arises from the base of its own metatarsal and divides into two slips embracing the root of the toe, one to each sesamoid — differing from the thylacine's only in that the two heads always share a common origin here. The four dorsal interossei are plantar in position, one-headed, from the bases of the four outer metatarsals, abducting from a line through the medius, which therefore has two of them.

occurrences.name: Intermediate layer and dorsal interossei

parts.name: Flexores breves of the four outer toes

occurrences.attachmentNote: Phascogale calura. The four outer toes each have a double-headed flexor brevis arranged as in *Dasyurus*. **The hallux also has one, and here it is quite distinct from the abductor** — the observation on which Cunningham's reading of the fused hallucal slip in *Dasyurus* rests — though only its tibial head is present. Four dorsal interossei, arranged as in *Dasyurus*.

occurrences.name: Intermediate layer, dorsal interossei and opponens minimi digiti
occurrences.divisionNote: The second dorsal interosseous is not separable: index and medius share one skin sheath and act as one digit, and the muscle is completely amalgamated with the inner head of the flexor brevis medii. Cunningham infers it rather than dissects it.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Spilocuscus maculatus. Five flexores breves, one per toe, each of two slips ending one on each sesamoid; the flexor brevis hallucis, set apart by the hallux's position, comes off the under surface of the scaphoid by a single tendon and divides. **The dorsal interossei are the interesting layer.** The first, the abductor indicis, is the most powerful, by two heads from the internal cuneiform and the first metatarsal. The second cannot be found as an independent muscle at all — index and medius share one integumental sheath and function as a single digit, and the second interosseous is completely amalgamated with the inner head of the flexor brevis medii, the first interosseous serving as abductor for both digits. **The third and fourth each consist of two slips with different jobs**: one with the ordinary abducting insertion, the other taking origin by two delicate heads on the dorsum and ending in a tendon that bifurcates into the adjacent sides of two digits, so that it approximates them. Cunningham reads this as a fourth layer of muscles forming by fission of the dorsal layer, with a new function — and notes the same splitting in the thylacine's hand. A strong quadrate opponens minimi digiti runs obliquely from the outer margin of the plantar cartilage to the whole fibular margin of the fifth metatarsal.

occurrences.name: Intermediate layer, dorsal interossei and opponens minimi digiti
occurrences.attachmentNote: Trichosurus vulpecula. Five flexores breves, all two-slipped except that of the little toe, which has a fibular head only — Cunningham suspects its missing inner head is fused into the fourth dorsal interosseous, which projects further into the sole than its neighbours. The flexor brevis hallucis is more powerful than the cuscus's. The second dorsal interosseous is again absent as an independent muscle and again inside the inner head of the flexor brevis medii — and here Cunningham can show it, because that slip runs up between the metatarsals to the dorsum, so that **the same fleshy slip looks like the missing interosseous from above and like the flexor from below.** The fourth dorsal interosseous is the remarkable one: two slips, one inserted into the summit of a powerful tendinous arch slung between the adjacent bases of the annularis and minimus, the other into that arch's inner end. Cunningham lines the arch up with two other solutions to the same problem — the transverse band tying the tendon to the neighbouring metatarsal head in the cuscus's hand, and the bifurcating tendon in the cuscus's foot — and quotes Young's description of a third in the wallaby's hand.

occurrences.name: Intermediate layer and dorsal interossei
occurrences.attachmentNote: Ornithorhynchus anatinus. **A complicated foot, and Cunningham's point is that the two layers are in the act of merging.** Every digit but the minimus has a flexor brevis, generally two-headed but often looking single until cleaned, with insertions more plantar than usual; the flexor brevis hallucis is single-bellied from the internal cuneiform and, taking a more proximal origin than its neighbours, probably holds the fibres of the absent abductor hallucis in its midst — Ruge calls the whole muscle the abductor, Cunningham calls it both. The dorsal interossei must be dissected from above before the flexores breves are touched. The fourth is single-headed and inseparably united with the outer head of the flexor brevis annularis. **The second and third are two-headed and end in fibrous arches slung between the sesamoids of adjacent digits, so they approximate the toes rather than abduct them** — which Cunningham reads as the first stage of the process completed in the cuscus, where the interossei have split into separate approximators and abductors; here the two parts exist but have not gained separate insertions. The first is fused with the inner head of the flexor brevis indicis, and beside it lies a strong fibrous cord from the base of the second metatarsal splitting distally across to the sesamoids of index and hallux — which Cunningham identifies as that muscle's missing inner head, turned to fibre. In a young male there was little fusion between the two layers but the two heads of each flexor brevis were closely united, which he takes to mean the usual two slips derive from a single mass. Ruge figured all the interossei as single-headed with simple insertions; Cunningham saw that in none of his specimens.

occurrences.name: Intermediate layer and the second dorsal interosseous
occurrences.divisionNote: The flexores breves of the medius and annularis and three of the four dorsal interossei are absent. Cunningham could find no trace of them in any neighbouring muscle and reads them as suppressed rather than fused — the opposite of his reading for the tetradactylous carnivores.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Tachyglossus aculeatus. **Only three flexores breves and one dorsal interosseous survive.** The flexor brevis hallucis is minute but complete, two heads from a common origin on the plantar fibrous structures of the middle cuneiform, diverging to the sides of the second phalanx. The flexor brevis indicis has two heads of which only the tibial is fleshy — the fibular is a short fibrous cord. The flexor brevis minimi digiti is **the best-developed intrinsic muscle in this foot and the only one not visibly degenerating**, represented by its outer head alone, from the anterior aspect of the calcaneal tuber to the outer side of the second phalanx. The second dorsal interosseous is the sole survivor of its layer, detectable only from the plantar side, its tendon splitting into a hair-like slip for the medius and a stronger one for the index — so it is chiefly an abductor of the index but has an approximating action too. **Cunningham finds no clue as to where the absent muscles went and concludes they were lost by suppression** — and notes the oddity that the stunted hallux, the least mobile digit of all, is the only one keeping its full complement.

occurrences.name: Flexores breves and dorsal interossei, amalgamated
occurrences.divisionNote: Partially or completely amalgamated. Cunningham keeps them as two parts because tendinous intersections mark the boundary even where dissection cannot, not because he could separate them in every case.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Canis lupus familiaris. Cunningham examined ten carnivore feet — dog, dingo, cat, puma, leopard, lion, otter, badger, polecat and walrus — and his general finding for the four tetradactylous cats and the two dogs is that **the crowding of the metatarsals has cost the layers their definition**: no muscle is suppressed, but the flexores breves and dorsal interossei have partly or wholly amalgamated, so that muscles usually described as bicipital are really tricipital, and quadricipital for the medius. He rejects crowding as the cause, because *Phascogale* and especially *Dasyurus* have metatarsals as closely packed and every intrinsic muscle still separate. In the dog the bones are so close that a knife point can barely be introduced between them. **Not a trace of any abductor of the little toe is present as a distinct muscle**; in one specimen the fibular head of the short flexor showed a slight tendency to split at its insertion, which Cunningham takes as a sign that it has absorbed the abductor. An adductor annularis is occasionally found in the dog, feeble and more or less fused with the tibial head of that toe's short flexor — which he reads as evidence that in the other cats the muscle is lost by fusion rather than by suppression. Where no natural separation can be made, Cunningham says tendinous intersections running through the muscle usually still betray its composite character, and he warns that the mode of insertion will not distinguish the components: the dorsal interossei almost always reach the extensor tendon, but one slip of a flexor brevis frequently does too. In no case do the dorsal interossei arise from the metatarsal shafts.

occurrences.name: Flexores breves and dorsal interossei, amalgamated
occurrences.divisionNote: Partially or completely amalgamated. Cunningham keeps them as two parts because tendinous intersections mark the boundary even where dissection cannot, not because he could separate them in every case.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Felis catus. occurrences.attachmentNote: Panthera pardus. occurrences.name: Flexores breves and dorsal interossei
occurrences.attachmentNote: Meles meles. **Certain heads of the flexores breves have been lost to fusion with the dorsal layer.** Hallux, index and minimus each keep a double-headed short flexor; the flexores breves of the annularis and medius are reduced to tibial heads. Cunningham can trace the annularis's missing fibular head — partially united with the fourth dorsal interosseous, separate at its origin and completely fused just beyond it — but for the medius no indication survives, and he suspects the bulky third dorsal interosseous holds its fibres. Four dorsal interossei abduct from a line through the medius, which therefore has two.

occurrences.name: Flexores breves and dorsal interossei
occurrences.attachmentNote: Lutra lutra. **Only a very slight tendency to fusion between the flexores breves and the dorsal interossei** — the least of any carnivore here. Every digit but the hallux has a double-headed short flexor; the flexor brevis hallucis is represented by a single inner head. The dorsal muscles are as in the badger.

occurrences.name: Flexores breves and the third dorsal interosseous
occurrences.attachmentNote: Odobenus rosmarus. **The intermediate layer is almost complete while the other two are barely represented** — the reverse of most feet in this survey. Every digit has a short flexor, two-headed except the hallux, whose fibular head alone is in place while its inner head lies displaced deep in the sole as a separate oblique bundle from the middle cuneiform joining the abductor hallucis tendon. **Only the third dorsal interosseous survives as a distinct muscle**; the fourth and second are presumed to be inside the outer head of the flexor brevis annularis and the inner head of the flexor brevis medii, both of which run a long way up between the metatarsals, and for the first not even that clue exists. Murie called these muscles the double or deep interossei. Cunningham disagrees with him about the deep oblique bundle: Murie thought it and its neighbour might be a double adductor hallucis, and Cunningham answers that the nerve settles it — his was single and supplied by the internal plantar — and that the true adductor is present anyway.

occurrences.name: Flexores breves and dorsal interossei
occurrences.attachmentNote: Tamandua tetradactyla. The flexores breves are poorly developed except at the margins, and are told from the dorsal interossei by lying on a more plantar plane and being invisible from the dorsum. Only the little toe has a two-headed one; the three middle digits have single delicate tibial slips and the hallux a strongly marked tibial head with a more proximal origin. Four powerful single-headed prismatic dorsal interossei, one per space, abducting from a line through the index — so **the index has two of them, one on each side, plus an adductor and a flexor brevis: four intrinsic muscles on one digit, which Cunningham says is unique so far as he is aware.** He also reads the tibial-only short flexors of medius and annularis as doing the work of the human first and second plantar interossei, antagonising the third and fourth dorsal interossei.

occurrences.name: Flexores breves and dorsal interossei, mostly fibrous

parts.name: Flexores breves of the middle digits

occurrences.divisionNote: The middle digits' short flexors and the dorsal interossei are present as fibrous bands in the muscles' own positions, not as muscles. Macalister found two of them fleshy in another *Dasypus*, so the state varies.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Euphractus sexcinctus, and **the most remarkable thing in this foot: the muscles that have gone are still there as fibrous bands with precisely their own positions and connections.** Only two members of the intermediate layer remain fleshy — the flexor brevis hallucis, well developed and properly bicipital though its tibial head shares a common tendon with the abductor far back in the sole, and the flexor brevis minimi digiti, so minute it can have almost no action. Everything else, flexores breves and dorsal interossei together, is ligament, and Cunningham can find it no function beyond preventing over-extension at the metatarsophalangeal joints; the digits are bound together and can hardly move independently, which he offers as the cause. **He says no author had noticed these bands before**, and notes that Macalister describes as muscles in *Dasypus* two that were fibrous in his own specimen — so the transformation is reversible, or at least not uniform. Galton describes similar bands in *Orycteropus*, which he called metacarpal ligaments in the hand.

occurrences.name: Dorsal interossei
occurrences.divisionNote: Cunningham reads the flexores breves as having joined the dorsal interossei rather than been suppressed. In the pes he infers it; in the manus of the same animal he can still see the five short flexors turning back through the interosseous spaces to reach them.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Bradypus tridactylus. **The only intrinsic muscles left in this foot, and they survive for a secondary reason.** With the metatarsophalangeal joints abolished by ankylosis the interossei have no abducting action; but through their usual connection with the extensor tendons they act, as Duchenne had pointed out, as extensors at the joints between the phalanges — and the extensor apparatus here is very weak, the extensor brevis sending only two small tendons. So they are retained on the merits of that action and must be studied with the extensor brevis rather than with the sole. Four of them. The second and third are the strongest, arising from the adjacent metatarsals **and from the sides of the proximal phalanges**, each dividing distally so that slips from both build a fleshy-margined expansion over the second phalangeal joint of the medius around the extensor brevis tendon. **The annular digit depends on this group entirely for extension.** In the hand the arrangement is nearly identical, with the common extensor tendons replacing the extensor brevis, and there the flexores breves can still be seen doing the migrating: five small muscles under cover of the adductors, each turning backwards through an interosseous space to join its dorsal interosseous — converted from flexors into extensors by the route they take. The short flexor of the medius has already disappeared.

occurrences.name: Flexor brevis medii (suspensory ligament) and the second and third dorsal interossei
occurrences.divisionNote: Authors disagreed about which muscles the ligament contains: Stubbs (1766) made it five, Meckel added the lumbricals — though two lumbricals are present as independent muscles in this foot — and Flower called it the homologue of the interossei. Cunningham reads it as the flexor brevis medii alone, from the arrangement of the surviving fibres.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Equus caballus. Cunningham's horse–ox–sheep series is one argument in three animals: **the suspensory ligament of the fetlock is a short flexor turned to ligament, and each animal shows the transformation at a different stage.** He made thin transverse microscopic sections of all three and looked at them against a black ground. In the horse only the middle digit is developed and it keeps exactly the three intrinsic muscles that belong to a medius: the flexor brevis medii and the second and third dorsal interossei. The flexor brevis is the suspensory ligament — nearly twice the thickness of a human tendo Achillis, from the plantar base of the large metatarsal and the lower tarsals, dividing below to embrace the fetlock and inserting partly into the sesamoids and partly into the extensor tendon. **It bears its history on its face**: two thin streaks of striated muscle almost invariably run down its superficial surface, and two distinct strands of pink fleshy tissue run its whole length on the deep surface, showing in section as two crescentic outlines of transversely divided muscle embedded in tendon, broken by fat cells with cut nerves and vessels among them. Cunningham is explicit that the muscle left is far too little to do anything. The second and third dorsal interossei survive as rudiments — a two-inch belly and a long delicate tendon each, one on either side of the ligament, from the rudimentary second and fourth metatarsals — and **their interest is as a link in the soft parts between the modern horse and its three-toed ancestor.** He corrects the veterinary anatomists, who take them for the interossei of the lateral digits: those went with the digits. He also records that in a horse dissected at Dick's Royal Veterinary College in 1880-81 these bellies were several inches long, each exceeding a human plantaris.

occurrences.name: Flexores breves medii and annularis (suspensory ligament)
occurrences.attachmentNote: Bos taurus. Cunningham's horse–ox–sheep series is one argument in three animals: **the suspensory ligament of the fetlock is a short flexor turned to ligament, and each animal shows the transformation at a different stage.** He made thin transverse microscopic sections of all three and looked at them against a black ground. **The ox's ligament shows its muscular origin more strikingly than the horse's and is built from two short flexors rather than one.** Two digits remain, medius and annularis, their metatarsals fused into a single bone still marked by a furrow in front, a groove behind and a notch below. The ligament divides into five slips — two to each digit, ending one on each sesamoid with a marginal band forward to the extensor tendon, and a fifth central slip that passes forward through the notch and splits to join both extensor tendons. In section the muscle shows as **four small thick-outlined rings side by side**, and Cunningham reads each ring as the head of a flexor brevis: the ligament is both heads of the flexor brevis medii and both of the flexor brevis annularis, fused and degenerated, with the central slip made of the outer head of one and the inner head of the other. He finds no evidence that any other intrinsic muscle is in it. Two thick tendinous cords also leave its superficial surface to join the perforatus tendons; **he denies these any muscular origin** and derives them from the dense fascia over the intrinsic muscles — a claim the sheep then proves.

occurrences.name: Flexores breves (suspensory ligament)
occurrences.attachmentNote: Ovis aries. Cunningham's horse–ox–sheep series is one argument in three animals: **the suspensory ligament of the fetlock is a short flexor turned to ligament, and each animal shows the transformation at a different stage.** He made thin transverse microscopic sections of all three and looked at them against a black ground. **The end of the series: not a vestige of muscular tissue is left.** The same four rings appear in section, nearer the deep surface, with delicate white outlines — and under the microscope they are fat cells with occasional vessels and nerves among them and no muscle at all.
