Cunningham draws the mechanism from this: the fibrous change proceeds by fatty degeneration of the muscle fibres with a concurrent increase in the muscle's connective tissue, is always further advanced on the superficial surface, and spares the vessels and nerves. **The sheep also settles the ox's tendinous cords**: here the ligament is covered by a dense aponeurosis attached to each margin of the metatarsus which has no anatomical union with it — the ligament glides freely beneath — and which joins the perforatus by a flat ribbon-like band. That aponeurosis is the deep layer of fascia spread over the intrinsic muscles in other animals, which is why the ox's cords are fascia and not muscle.

occurrences.name: Flexores breves and the first two dorsal interossei
occurrences.attachmentNote: Procavia capensis. Every digit has a two-headed flexor brevis on the plantar aspect of its own metatarsal, with the usual connections — Murie & Mivart's double interossei. Of the dorsal layer only the first two survive: the abductor indicis, powerful, from the inner and dorsal surface of the second metatarsal, and a weaker second interosseous from the plantar base of the middle metatarsal under the adductor indicis. **The third and fourth are presumed inside the outer heads of the flexores breves of medius and annularis.** This foot is also one of the few exceptions Cunningham finds to the usual plantar nerve pattern: the internal plantar sends a deep branch to all the muscles of the index and on to the second interosseous, and he found the same peculiarity in the hand of the same animal, where the median nerve supplies the index's muscles and ends in the outer head of the flexor brevis medii.

occurrences.name: Flexores breves and dorsal interossei
occurrences.divisionNote: The two interosseous bands flanking the medius–annularis pair contain no muscle; they are scored as a part because Cunningham identifies them as those muscles by position and connection, and because they now do the suspensory ligament's job in an animal that arrived at it from the other layer.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Elephas maximus. The feet of a foetal Indian elephant long preserved in Edinburgh, checked against Miall & Greenwood, whose results Cunningham says his differ from only slightly. **The foot is peculiar for the absence of most of the plantar adducting and dorsal abducting muscles**, and he gives the reason directly: digits encased in tough integument and a thick plantar cushion have no room to be separated or approximated, so such muscles would have been almost functionless. In the largely developed annularis and medius, between which lateral movement is impossible, the muscles that would have done that work have changed function instead — **the dorsal interosseous on each side of the double digit is converted into a strong ligamentous band, and the two act together exactly as the suspensory ligament of the horse, ox or sheep does**, preventing over-extension at the metatarsophalangeal joints. Of the four short-flexor bellies typical for those two digits only the two marginal ones are kept, and they act together as one short flexor for what is functionally one digit.

occurrences.name: Flexores breves
occurrences.attachmentNote: Bathyergus suillus. Cunningham's *Bathyergus capensis*, one of the six feet the Challenger Commission gave him. Pentadactyl, and **the flexores breves are the only intrinsic muscles it has** — five of them, each of two strong slips. There is a total absence of the plantar adducting and the dorsal abducting layers, and he says plainly that he cannot tell whether they were suppressed or fused: if fused, no trace of the fusion is discoverable. The same arrangement holds in the hand of the same animal. He groups the Cape mouse with it, and adds the crested agouti and the guinea pig on Mivart & Murie's authority as further cases in which flexores breves alone are developed.

occurrences.name: Flexores breves and dorsal interossei

parts.name: Flexores breves of the middle digits
Flexor brevis minimi digiti, outer head

occurrences.attachmentNote: Castor fiber. The three middle digits each have a well-marked two-headed flexor brevis with the usual connections. **The inner head of the flexor brevis hallucis is an aponeurotic band with a few fleshy fibres left near its origin, and the outer head of the flexor brevis minimi digiti is a slender fibrous cord** — two more of this foot's muscles caught partway to ligament. Two dorsal interossei survive of four.

occurrences.name: Flexores breves
occurrences.innervation: The deep part of the external plantar nerve supplies both heads of the four outer short flexors and ends in the outer head of the flexor brevis hallucis; the internal plantar sends three twigs to that muscle's large inner head.
occurrences.attachmentNote: *Pteropus* sp. **Typically complete, and the most complete intermediate layer in Cunningham's survey**: a flexor brevis for every digit, each of two heads, all eight slips separate along their entire length and lying in one plane, from the fibrous textures at the base of the metatarsus to the sesamoids alone. **Not a trace of the dorsal interossei is to be found** — the outer head of the flexor brevis minimi digiti and the inner head of the flexor brevis hallucis are considerably larger than the rest, and Cunningham suggests the missing marginal abductors have coalesced with them. So a foot with a perfect flexor layer and no abductors at all.

correspondences.note: Stated by Diogo & Molnar (2014) Table 15 as a "clear topological correspondence"; their forelimb name for it is the flexores breves profundi.

muscles.name: Pubotibialis
muscles.developmental: Somitic; ventral (flexor) muscle mass of the hindlimb bud.

consensus.origin: Anterior edge and anterior ventral face of the pelvis.
consensus.insertion: Anterior face of the proximal tibia.
consensus.action: Supports the body during walking and flexes the knee.
consensus.innervation: Ventral division of the lumbosacral plexus.

occurrences.name: Pubotibialis
occurrences.note: Described here from Taricha torosa; not yet scored in other taxa in this dataset, so its absence elsewhere is unsampled rather than observed.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Its parallel fibres pass anterior to the puboischiotibialis to a proximal tibial insertion. Function attributed on the strength of Ashley-Ross (1995) electromyography in Dicamptodon, not inferred from geometry.

occurrences.name: M. pubotibialis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Iguana iguana, Russell & Bauer (2008). Ventral head from the pubic tubercle and the dorsal aspect of the puboischiotibialis aponeurosis; dorsal head in common with the ambiens. The two join loosely a third of the way down and insert by a common tendon on the proximolateral tibia. **Its motor tendon is also a muscle origin**: one of the six tendons of origin of the femorotibial gastrocnemius is a band from this tendon just before it inserts. This record's own note says its relation to the amniote 'ambiens' is not established here, and the *Iguana* row does not settle it — the two share a head.

occurrences.name: M. pubo-tibialis posticus
occurrences.innervation: R. pubo-tibialis posticus of the N. obturatorius and short branches of the N. femoralis.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Sphenodon punctatus, Osawa (1898), *Zur Muskellehre*. Fürbringer's *ileo-pectineo-tibialis profundus*, Gadow's *pubi-ischio-tibialis*, Perrin's *rotateur inverse de la cuisse*. A slender muscle from the pubic tubercle, running first along the medial thigh then entering its posterior side, to the lateral proximal corner of the tibia — **and Osawa corrects Gadow explicitly**, who had put the insertion on the back of the neck of the fibula facing the tibia. He also argues that Günther's poorly described *M. gracilis* corresponds to this muscle rather than to the puboischiotibialis, quoting Günther's text to show the origin on the uncinate process of the pubis does not fit.

occurrences.name: Pubo-tibialis (PT)
occurrences.attachmentNote: Prestosuchus chiniquensis, Liparini & Schultz (2013). **Reconstructed as absent, and that is a claim rather than a gap.** The pubo-tibialis is rare among living archosaurs and residual where it survives at all; no evidence of it was found in this specimen and the authors did not restore it. Schachner et al. (2011) likewise left it out of *Poposaurus* for want of muscle scars, and Carrano & Hutchinson did not consider it for *Tyrannosaurus*. Were it present, Liparini & Schultz expect it would have arisen from the lateral surface of the pubis and inserted on the first head of the adductor femoris — muscle to muscle, so it would carry no bony insertion even then.

homology.notes: A pelvis-to-tibia muscle anterior to the puboischiotibialis. Its relation to the amniote ambiens is not established here.

muscles.name: Femorofibularis
muscles.developmental: Somitic; ventral (flexor) muscle mass of the hindlimb bud.

consensus.origin: Ventral face of the distal end of the femur.
consensus.insertion: Posterolateral face of the fibula.
consensus.action: Flexes the knee.
consensus.innervation: Ventral division of the lumbosacral plexus; branches of the same nerve serve the distal ischioflexorius.

occurrences.name: Femorofibularis
occurrences.note: Robust in Taricha, against the thin narrow muscle usual in salamanders. Ashley-Ross (1992) found a size trade-off with the ischioflexorius: Dicamptodon and newly metamorphosed Ambystoma have a large ischioflexorius and a slender femorofibularis, older Ambystoma the reverse, and Darevsky & Salomatina (1989) report the same trade-off in Paramesotriton. Francis (1934) noted that branches of one nerve supply the distal ischioflexorius and the femorofibularis, which is the basis for treating them as alternative solutions to one mechanical demand. Described here from Taricha torosa; not yet scored in other taxa in this dataset, so its absence elsewhere is unsampled rather than observed.
occurrences.attachmentNote: A short femur-to-fibula strap crossing only the knee, against the ischioflexorius which runs from the pelvis to the sole. Two muscles of very different span substituting for one another in size is a caution against reading function from length.

homology.teaching: A reciprocal size relationship between two muscles that share a nerve branch but not a span. The trade-off shows up across species and within one species across ontogeny.
homology.notes: Diogo & Molnar (2014) follow the consensual view that this is a thigh muscle and, on two grounds, treat it as a derived urodele muscle rather than part of the tetrapod leg bodyplan that gave rise to the amniote leg muscles: it is innervated by the sciatic nerve alone (Francis 1934), and anurans have neither the muscle nor any apparent derivative of it. They keep two alternatives open without adopting either. Howell (1938) described a tibial-innervated avian 'femorocruralis' that appears to be part of the gastrocnemius complex migrated proximally, which would make the femorofibularis correspond to part of the reptilian gastrocnemius complex; and Humphry's (1872) proposal that it corresponds to at least part of the short head of the mammalian biceps femoris cannot be discarded. Shared innervation with the distal ischioflexorius is the strongest evidence bearing on its identity.

muscles.name: Caudalipuboischiotibialis
muscles.developmental: Somitic; caudal hypaxial series recruited to the hindlimb.

consensus.origin: Transverse process of the fourth caudal vertebra.
consensus.insertion: The tendinous inscription dividing the puboischiotibialis.
consensus.action: Assists the puboischiotibialis in limb retraction and flexes the tail laterally.
consensus.innervation: Ventral rami of the anterior caudal spinal nerves.

occurrences.name: Caudalipuboischiotibialis
occurrences.note: Coactive with the puboischiotibialis during walking (Ashley-Ross 1995). Described here from Taricha torosa; not yet scored in other taxa in this dataset, so its absence elsewhere is unsampled rather than observed.
occurrences.attachmentNote: A muscle with a skeletal origin and no skeletal insertion: it ends on another muscle's tendinous inscription. Salamandra and Cryptobranchus lack that inscription altogether, so in those genera the insertion has nothing to attach to.

homology.notes: One of three tail-to-pelvis muscles. Its insertion on a tendinous inscription rather than bone means it cannot be reconstructed from a skeleton. Diogo & Molnar (2014) separate it from the caudal-pelvic muscles it is usually grouped with on topology: where the ischiocaudalis connects the pelvis to the tail, this one connects the tail to the puboischiotibialis, so it bears on limb retraction as well as tail flexion. They report Gadow's (1882) suggestion that part of the lizard flexor tibialis externus derives from it, without adopting it.

muscles.name: Iliocaudalis
muscles.developmental: Somitic; caudal epaxial series reaching the pelvic girdle.

consensus.insertion: Ilium.
consensus.action: Draws the tail laterally.
consensus.innervation: Dorsal rami of the anterior caudal spinal nerves.

occurrences.name: Iliocaudalis
occurrences.note: Its fibres run parallel to the epaxial muscles and it is distinguishable from them only by its insertion. Described here from Taricha torosa; not yet scored in other taxa in this dataset, so its absence elsewhere is unsampled rather than observed.
occurrences.attachmentNote: A muscle identified by where it ends rather than by any visible boundary — the clearest case in this source of an attachment doing the work of delimiting a muscle.

occurrences.name: Iliococcygeus
occurrences.action: Supports the pelvic viscera; draws the coccyx forward.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). **The human pelvic floor is tail musculature that stayed behind.** Iliococcygeus is one of the three parts of levator ani, running from the tendinous arch over the obturator internus fascia to the coccyx and the anococcygeal body. In a lizard the same muscle moves the tail; in an animal whose tail is a coccyx it has become a sling supporting the viscera, without changing either attachment in kind. Gest also lists pubococcygeus, puborectalis, pubovaginalis and levator prostatae, which are the pubic-origin members of the same sheet.

occurrences.name: M. coccygeo-iliacus
occurrences.innervation: Dorsal rami of the caudal spinal nerves.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Sphenodon punctatus, Osawa (1898), *Zur Muskellehre*. Gadow's *pars ilio-caudalis* of the ilio-ischio-caudalis. The forward continuation of the dorsal muscle mass of the tail, inserting on the caudal border and inner surface of the dorsal end of the ilium. **Osawa reads it as homologous with the longissimus dorsi and ileo-lumbalis** — a tail-to-pelvis muscle he places in the epaxial series, and its dorsal-ramus supply is why.

homology.teaching: Where a muscle has no visible border with its neighbours, its insertion is the only thing that makes it a muscle at all.

muscles.name: Ischiocaudalis
muscles.developmental: Somitic; caudal hypaxial series reaching the pelvic girdle.

consensus.origin: Transverse process of the fourth caudal vertebra.
consensus.insertion: Posterior border of the ischium.
consensus.action: Draws the tail laterally.
consensus.innervation: Ventral rami of the anterior caudal spinal nerves.

occurrences.name: Ischiocaudalis
occurrences.note: The most medial of the three ventral muscles connecting tail and pelvic girdle. Described here from Taricha torosa; not yet scored in other taxa in this dataset, so its absence elsewhere is unsampled rather than observed.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Flat, thin and strap-like. With the caudalipuboischiotibialis and caudofemoralis it forms a series of three, all from the anterior caudal transverse processes, differing in where they end.

occurrences.name: Coccygeus
occurrences.action: Supports the pelvic viscera; draws the coccyx forward.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). Ischial spine to the lateral coccyx and the lowest sacrum — the ischiococcygeus under its clinical name. With [[iliocaudalis]] it is the second half of the answer to what happened to the caudal musculature in an animal with no tail: it did not disappear, it took over the pelvic outlet.

occurrences.name: M. coccygeo-ischiadicus
occurrences.innervation: N. coccygeo-ischiadicus from the second postsacral nerve.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Sphenodon punctatus, Osawa (1898), *Zur Muskellehre*. Gadow's *pars ischio-caudalis*, Perrin's ischio-caudal. The forward continuation of the ventrolateral superficial tail mass, inserting by a very thin tendon on the tuber ischii. **A thin muscle overlies its insertion and becomes the posterior lip of the cloaca** — the M. sphincter cloacae posterior — which Osawa suggests is a splitting-off from this one. The tail musculature turning into a sphincter, in an animal that still has a tail; compare the human rows on this record and on `iliocaudalis`, where the same field became the pelvic floor.

muscles.name: Extensor tarsi tibialis
muscles.developmental: Somitic; dorsal (extensor) muscle mass of the hindlimb bud.

consensus.insertion: Ventral surface of the tibiale.
consensus.action: Supinates the foot.
consensus.innervation: Dorsal division of the lumbosacral plexus.

occurrences.name: Extensor tarsi tibialis
occurrences.note: Described here from Taricha torosa; not yet scored in other taxa in this dataset, so its absence elsewhere is unsampled rather than observed.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Crosses knee and ankle to reach a proximal tarsal. Function presumed from geometry, not measured.

homology.notes: Diogo & Molnar (2014) derive both the anuran 'tibialis anticus brevis' and the human tibialis anterior from this urodele muscle, which is what puts the three on one anlage rather than merely in one position.

muscles.name: Extensor cruris et tarsi fibularis
muscles.developmental: Somitic; dorsal (extensor) muscle mass of the hindlimb bud.

consensus.insertion: Posterodorsal and posteroventral faces of the fibula, with a portion on the fibulare.
consensus.action: Extends the knee.
consensus.innervation: Dorsal division of the lumbosacral plexus.

occurrences.name: Extensor cruris et tarsi fibularis
occurrences.note: The postaxial complement of the extensor cruris tibialis: the two wrap the tibia and fibula respectively from the two femoral epicondyles. Described here from Taricha torosa; not yet scored in other taxa in this dataset, so its absence elsewhere is unsampled rather than observed.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Three rows on two bones for one muscle, because it wraps the fibula from dorsal to ventral and continues onto the proximal tarsus.

homology.notes: Diogo & Molnar (2014) derive the anuran 'peroneus' and the human fibularis (peroneus) longus and brevis from this muscle. The anuran peroneus corresponds to part or all of it, lying on the fibular side of the dorsal leg and inserting on the fibula. They note the name 'tibialis anticus longus' would suggest the tibial anlage instead, and argue against that reading.

muscles.name: Interosseus cruris
muscles.developmental: Somitic; deep layer between the zeugopodial elements.

consensus.insertion: Distal portion of the tibia.
consensus.action: Stabilises the two long bones of the crus against one another.
consensus.innervation: Dorsal division of the lumbosacral plexus.

occurrences.name: Interosseus cruris
occurrences.note: Described here from Taricha torosa; not yet scored in other taxa in this dataset, so its absence elsewhere is unsampled rather than observed.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Joins the medial sides of tibia and fibula. Its serial counterpart in the forelimb is the pronator profundus, which in salamanders runs the other way — from the ulna across to the radial side — and acts as a pronator rather than a strut.

occurrences.note: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). Not listed, and the structure in its position is the interosseous membrane — a ligament where a salamander has a muscle. It is not simply lost: the popliteus derives from it, and is scored on that record. One ancestral muscle here becomes a ligament and a knee rotator in the same animal.

occurrences.name: M. interosseus cruris
occurrences.attachmentNote: Iguana iguana, Russell & Bauer (2008). From the lateral face of the distal end of the tibia, ventral to the inferior tibiofibular ligament, its fibres running at right angles to the long axes of both bones to insert on the distal end of the mesial surface of the fibula. **This record occupies the position of the amniote interosseous membrane as a muscle**, and *Iguana* has it distally while the popliteus — which derives from it — occupies the proximal end of the same interosseous space. One ancestral sheet, in this animal, still present at one end and already a separate knee muscle at the other. Compare the human rows, where the muscle is gone and the space is ligament.

occurrences.name: M. fibulo-tibialis inferior
occurrences.innervation: R. muscularis of the N. tibialis medialis.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Sphenodon punctatus, Osawa (1898), *Zur Muskellehre*. Fürbringer's name, Perrin's *interosseux de la jambe*. A small, almost rectangular muscle from the tibial surface of the distal half of the fibula, running nearly horizontally to the fibular side and slightly the extensor side of the distal third of the tibia. **Gadow did not notice it at all**, Osawa says, and it is overlain dorsally by a strong tendinous band running obliquely from mid-tibia to the distal fibula, which Osawa names the *ligamentum interosseum obliquum*. This record occupies the position of the amniote interosseous membrane as a muscle, and the tuatara has muscle and ligament side by side in the same space.

occurrences.name: Peroneotibialis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Tachyglossus aculeatus, Gambaryan et al. (2002). Fills nearly the whole interosseous space, separated from the popliteus by a branch of the popliteal nerve; the origin reaches the distal quarter of the fibula and the insertion the distal sixth of the tibia. **A mammal with a muscle where the interosseous membrane should be**, which is what this record exists to hold — the same arrangement as the tuatara's fibulo-tibialis inferior and the lizard's interosseus cruris. Gambaryan et al. say they placed this muscle and the popliteus in the jumping group artificially, so the grouping is a convenience of theirs and not a claim about function.

occurrences.name: Peroneotibialis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Ornithorhynchus anatinus. **Found only in Tachyglossus** — Gambaryan et al. dissected both genera and state the muscle could be found in the echidna alone. The two species disagree inside one order, so whether Monotremata has this muscle is a species-level fact and the clade rolls up as variable rather than present.

homology.notes: Occupies the position of the amniote interosseous membrane as a muscle rather than a ligament.

correspondences.note: Stated by Diogo & Molnar (2014) Table 14 as a "clear topological correspondence"; their forelimb name for it is the pronator quadratus.

muscles.name: Pronator profundus (pes)
muscles.developmental: Somitic; deep ventral intrinsic layer of the pes.

consensus.insertion: Lateral face of the distal tibia, the tibiale, and the base of the first metatarsal.
consensus.action: Pronates the foot.

occurrences.name: Pronator profundus
occurrences.note: Described here from Taricha torosa; not yet scored in other taxa in this dataset, so its absence elsewhere is unsampled rather than observed.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Roughly triangular, converging from the postaxial to the preaxial side of the ankle — the same crossing course as its counterpart in the hand.

occurrences.note: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). Not listed. The human leg has no pronator: the tibia and fibula do not rotate on each other the way the radius and ulna do, and the interosseous membrane between them is a strut rather than an axis. Compare the forearm, where three separate pronators and a supinator are scored.

occurrences.name: M. pronator profundus
occurrences.attachmentNote: Iguana iguana, Russell & Bauer (2008). From the distal two-thirds of the ventral and mesial fibular shaft, its fibres crossing the limb distomesially to a stout aponeurosis over the ventral astragalocalcaneum, from which tendons run to the ventromesial proximal metatarsal I, the mesial borders of metatarsals II and III, and the proximoventral fourth distal tarsal. **The whole aponeurosis forms a sling covering the ventral aspect of the mesotarsal joint** — a pronator that has become a strap across the ankle. The hand muscle of the same name is a separate record, which is the convention Walthall & Ashley-Ross's shared naming forced.

homology.notes: Walthall & Ashley-Ross give the same name to this muscle and to its counterpart in the hand, which is why the two are separate records here.

correspondences.caution: Diogo & Molnar (2014) use 'pronator profundus' as the alternative name for the leg muscle tibialis posterior, which Table 14 pairs with the palmaris profundus 1 or the flexor carpi radialis, not with the pronator quadratus. Whether this record is that muscle needs settling before the edge can be sourced.

muscles.name: Contrahentium caput longum (pes)
muscles.developmental: Somitic; deep ventral intrinsic layer of the pes.

consensus.insertion: A flat tendon attaching to the distal tarsal bones.
consensus.action: Flexes the tarsus.

occurrences.name: Caput longum musculorum contrahentium
occurrences.note: Described here from Taricha torosa; not yet scored in other taxa in this dataset, so its absence elsewhere is unsampled rather than observed.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Thin, lying deep to the plantar fascia. Its insertion tendon is in turn the origin of the contrahentes digitorum, the same chained arrangement the hand shows.

occurrences.name: Contrahentium caput longum
occurrences.attachmentNote: A single muscle from the medial ligamentum calcanei, inserting fleshily along the distal three-quarters of the ventral tibiale, independent of the tibialis posterior.
occurrences.note: Moved here from the forelimb record of the same name, where it had been filed for want of a pes counterpart.

Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). Not listed, as in the hand. The one contrahens the human foot retains is the adductor hallucis, scored on [[contrahentes-digitorum-pes]]; the long head of the contrahens layer is gone from both limbs.

homology.notes: Separated from the forelimb record of the same name because Blotto et al. (2020) and Walthall & Ashley-Ross (2006) both describe hand and foot muscles under this one name.

correspondences.note: Stated by Diogo & Molnar (2014) Table 14 as a "clear topological correspondence"; their forelimb name for it is the contrahentium caput longum, in Ambystoma.

muscles.name: Flexor accessorius lateralis (pes)
muscles.developmental: Somitic; deep ventral intrinsic layer of the pes.

consensus.insertion: Dorsal side of the plantar fascia.
consensus.action: Pronates the foot.

occurrences.name: Flexor accessorius lateralis
occurrences.note: Described here from Taricha torosa; not yet scored in other taxa in this dataset, so its absence elsewhere is unsampled rather than observed.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Fibres run diagonally toward the anterior side of the foot. The forelimb counterpart takes the distal ulna as well as the carpals; this one is confined to the tarsus.

occurrences.name: Quadratus plantae
occurrences.action: Redirects the pull of the long digital flexor along the axis of the foot.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). Anterior calcaneus and the long plantar ligament, inserting not on bone but on the flexor digitorum longus tendons. **The hand lost this muscle and the foot kept it**, which is the opposite of the digital-extensor case and the reverse of what a strict serial reading of the two limbs would predict. Its job is purely mechanical: the long flexor enters the sole obliquely from the medial side, and this muscle pulls its tendons straight before they reach the toes.

occurrences.name: Musculus accessorius
occurrences.attachmentNote: Thylacinus cynocephalus. **Absent.** Cunningham states it in a footnote and states it for both animals at once: there is no musculus accessorius in the foot of either the thylacine or the cuscus. The human row on this record is the quadratus plantae, so this is a muscle the placental column has and these two marsupials do not.

occurrences.name: Musculus accessorius
occurrences.attachmentNote: Spilocuscus maculatus. **Absent.** Cunningham states it in a footnote and states it for both animals at once: there is no musculus accessorius in the foot of either the thylacine or the cuscus. The human row on this record is the quadratus plantae, so this is a muscle the placental column has and these two marsupials do not.

occurrences.name: Accessorius
occurrences.innervation: A twig from the trunk of the external plantar nerve.
occurrences.attachmentNote:
Ornithorhynchus anatinus. Cunningham (1882) records it only through its nerve: the trunk of the external plantar gives twigs to the abductor ossis metatarsi minimi digiti, the outermost belly of the flexor brevis digitorum **and the accessorius** before dividing. The thylacine and the cuscus are scored `no` on this record, so the two monotremes have a muscle both marsupials have lost.

**Gambaryan et al. (2002) supply the attachments Cunningham did not**, and with them an argument about the heel. Here the muscle arises on the **dorsal** surface of the tuber calcanei, at its distal edge, and inserts on the dorsal surface of the common tendon of the flexor digitorum fibularis — it ends on another muscle's tendon and never reaches bone distally, which is why only the origin is scored. In therians the quadratus plantae arises on the lateral aspect of the tuber calcanei as it does here, **but from that process's plantar surface**. Gambaryan et al. take the discrepancy as evidence that the dorsal surface of the monotreme tuber calcanei answers to the plantar surface of the therian one — an inversion of the whole heel, argued from where one small muscle sits.

occurrences.name: Accessorius
occurrences.innervation: A twig from the trunk of the external plantar nerve.
occurrences.attachmentNote:
Tachyglossus aculeatus. Cunningham (1882) records it only through its nerve: the trunk of the external plantar runs down over the accessorius, undivided, and supplies it. The thylacine and the cuscus are scored `no` on this record, so the two monotremes have a muscle both marsupials have lost.

**Gambaryan et al. (2002) give it attachments.** From the lateral edge of the tuber calcanei, proximal to the abductor metatarsi V, the belly lying closer to the plantar surface of the foot than the tubercle does; its fibres insert on the plantolateral side of whichever tendon of the flexor digitorum fibularis runs to the fifth toe, then pass deeper to reach the tendon of the fourth. **It ends on tendon, not bone**, which is why only the origin is scored — the same thing Gest's human row records for the gemelli, and a reminder that a muscle with no distal osteological correlate is invisible to a fossil.

correspondences.note: Stated by Diogo & Molnar (2014) Table 14 as a "clear topological correspondence"; their forelimb name for it is the flexor accessorius lateralis, in Ambystoma.

homology.notes: Diogo & Molnar (2014) treat the flexor accessorius complex as a distinct amphibian structure corresponding to the distal bundle of the flexor digitorum longus in lizards, Sphenodon, turtles and crocodylians, and to the quadratus plantae of monotremes, rats and humans. Their evidence for the mammalian half is developmental and topological: in human ontogeny the quadratus plantae arises near the flexor digitorum and hallucis longus and migrates distally, so it is a leg muscle that moves into the foot, and both it and the urodele complex run distomedially onto the flexor digitorum communis derivatives. **They explicitly leave open whether the medial/lateral division is ancestral.** It is usual in urodeles and frequent in some mammals but absent in anurans, turtles, squamates and humans, and they raise it as possible parallel differentiation of one ancestral complex in urodeles and in mammals independently — so holding this and the medial muscle as two records follows the urodele condition and is not a claim about the tetrapod ancestor.

muscles.name: Flexor accessorius medialis (pes)
muscles.developmental: Somitic; deep ventral intrinsic layer of the pes.

consensus.origin: Distal fibula, the fibulare and the intermedium.
consensus.insertion: Plantar fascia.
consensus.action: Pronates the foot.

occurrences.name: Flexor accessorius medialis
occurrences.note: Described here from Taricha torosa; not yet scored in other taxa in this dataset, so its absence elsewhere is unsampled rather than observed.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Parallel to the lateral accessory and sharing its insertion, differing only in taking a more proximal origin that reaches the fibula.

occurrences.note: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). Not listed. Only the lateral member of the pair survives in a human foot, as the quadratus plantae; see [[flexor-accessorius-lateralis-pes]].

correspondences.note: Stated by Diogo & Molnar (2014) Table 14 as a "clear topological correspondence"; their forelimb name for it is the flexor accessorius medialis, in Ambystoma.

homology.notes: Diogo & Molnar (2014) treat the flexor accessorius complex as a distinct amphibian structure corresponding to the distal bundle of the flexor digitorum longus in lizards, Sphenodon, turtles and crocodylians, and to the quadratus plantae of monotremes, rats and humans, which is itself often differentiated into medial and lateral bundles and is often called 'flexor accessorius' in the literature. **Whether the medial/lateral division is ancestral is left open** — usual in urodeles, frequent in some mammals, absent in anurans, turtles, squamates and humans, and possibly differentiated in parallel rather than inherited. See the lateral record.

muscles.name: Intermetatarsales
muscles.developmental: Somitic; ventral intrinsic layer of the pes.

consensus.insertion: Metatarsal of the adjacent digit.
consensus.action: Adducts the metatarsals and the digits attached to them.

occurrences.name: Intermetatarsales
occurrences.note: These muscles form the web-like structures between the digits. Described here from Taricha torosa; not yet scored in other taxa in this dataset, so its absence elsewhere is unsampled rather than observed.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Extend further distally on the fibular side of each metatarsal — an asymmetry the intermetacarpales of the hand do not show.

occurrences.note: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). As in the hand, the human interossei of the foot are scored once — on [[flexores-breves-profundi-pes]] — and the claim this record has on them is recorded rather than acted on. Howell (1936) found the relationship between Interossei, Intermetacarpales, Dorsometacarpales and Contrahentes digitorum unclear across tetrapods, and nothing in a human table resolves it.

occurrences.name: Mm. intermetatarsales
occurrences.attachmentNote: Iguana iguana, Russell & Bauer (2008). **Only two slips**, occupying the spaces between metatarsals II and III and between III and IV. Each arises from the proximal two-thirds of the mesial face of the shaft of the lateralmost metatarsal of its pair and runs distomesially to insert on the lateral aspect of the mesialmost of the pair for almost its entire length. Compare the manus, where Russell & Bauer treat McMurrich's Mm. intermetacarpales as intermetacarpal *ligaments* and this dataset scores the forelimb record absent for the same animal — the foot keeps as muscle what the hand has as ligament.

correspondences.note: Stated by Diogo & Molnar (2014) Table 15 as a "clear topological correspondence"; their forelimb name for it is the intermetacarpales.

muscles.name: Extensores digitorum breves (pes)
muscles.developmental: Somitic; dorsal intrinsic layer of the pes.

consensus.origin: Distal tarsals at the base of each digit.
consensus.insertion: Dorsal surface of the proximal end of the terminal phalanx, by long tendons.
consensus.action: Extends the digits.

occurrences.name: Extensores digitorum breves
occurrences.note: Five slips, one per digit. The muscular part reaches only about two-thirds along the metatarsal; the tendon continues to the terminal phalanx. Described here from Taricha torosa; not yet scored in other taxa in this dataset, so its absence elsewhere is unsampled rather than observed.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Five slips against three in the manus, which serves digits II-IV only. The difference is the salamander hand's missing digit V, not a difference in the muscle layer.

occurrences.name: Extensores digitorum breves
occurrences.attachmentNote: Extensor digitorum brevis superficialis arises from the astragalar hollow and lateral calcaneum; the deep layer arises from the proximodorsal metatarsals, whose fine striations run parallel to the metatarsal long axis.
occurrences.note: Moved here from the forelimb record of the same name, where it had been filed for want of a pes counterpart.

occurrences.name: Extensores digitorum breves
occurrences.origin: Two proximal heads from the dorsal depression on the astragalus; the hallucal slip from the dorsal aspect of metatarsal I; the digit II, III and IV slips from the dorsal or dorsolateral aspects of metatarsals II, III and the astragalocalcaneum lip respectively.
occurrences.insertion: Proximodorsal lip of each phalanx of digits III and IV from the tarsal heads; the proximodorsal lips of phalanges I-1 and I-2 from the hallucal slip; the proximodorsal lips of the phalanges of digits II and III from their own slips; the ungual of digit IV with accessory insertions on IV-2 to IV-4.
occurrences.attachmentNote:
Iguana iguana. Hattori & Tsuihiji's separation of the interossei dorsales out of this complex is what makes the remainder countable; the slips left here are the ones arising from the tarsus or from the digit's OWN metatarsal, and those arising from the metatarsal medial to the digit are on `interossei-dorsales-pes`.

Iguana iguana, Russell & Bauer (2008). Russell & Bauer describe the system belly by belly, and it is not the same in each digit — which is the point. Digit I has one belly from the proximodorsal shaft of metatarsal I; digit II one, from metatarsal III, the oblique intermetatarsal ligament and the distal half of metatarsal II; digit III three, one from a small pit in the dorsal astragalocalcaneum and two from metatarsals II and IV; digit IV a long head from an adjacent pit plus two more; digit V three, from the astragalocalcaneum and the head of metatarsal V. Insertions run to the distalmost phalanx with accessory branches to the proximal ends of intervening phalanges. Read against the manus row, where all five superficial slips arise from the ulnare alone.

occurrences.name: Extensores digitorum breves
occurrences.origin: Dorsal depression on the astragalus, with two additional slips beyond the Iguana condition; the digit II and III slips from the dorsal and dorsolateral aspects of metatarsals II and III.
occurrences.insertion: Proximodorsal lips of the phalanges of digits III and IV, and — unlike Iguana — of digits I and II as well; in Varanus an additional tendinous insertion on the medial margin of the distal metatarsal III.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Varanus indicus. **Two more slips than the iguana**, serving digits I and II, which is the second scored difference between Hattori & Tsuihiji's two squamates.

occurrences.name: Extensor digitorum brevis + abductor hallucis
occurrences.origin: Depression on the dorsal aspect of distal tarsal IV; the hallucal member (m. abductor hallucis) from the dorsal aspect of metatarsal I with an additional origin on phalanx I-1.
occurrences.insertion: Merging distally with the interossei dorsales and inserting with them on the proximodorsal lips of the distal phalanges of digits III and IV; the hallucal member on the proximodorsal lips of I-1 and I-2.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Chelydra serpentina. The tarsal origin is on distal tarsal IV rather than on the astragalus as in squamates and crocodilians — the one place Hattori & Tsuihiji concede the turtle origin is 'slightly different', while still following Gadow (1882) in calling it homologous. Trachemys adds an origin from DT III and an insertion on digit II (Walker 1973). The additional hallucal origin on I-1 is this animal's; Trachemys has it on DT I instead.

occurrences.name: Extensor digitorum I, II et III
occurrences.origin: Depression on the dorsal aspect of the astragalus; the hallucal slip from the dorsal aspect of metatarsal I; the digit II, III and IV slips from the dorsal surfaces of metatarsals II, III and IV.
occurrences.insertion: Dorsally on digits I-III through the dorsal aponeurosis; the hallucal slip on the proximodorsal lips of I-1 and I-2; each digital slip on the proximodorsal lip of every phalanx of its digit.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Paleosuchus palpebrosus. Suzuki et al. (2011) kept this muscle separate in crocodilians as m. extensor digitorum I, II et III; Hattori & Tsuihiji propose extensor digitorum brevis as the standard name for it and its homologues, because the digit I-II bellies are sometimes missing in lepidosaurs and the digit IV belly in crocodilians, so a name fixed to a digit list does not travel. In Caiman the origin is not on the astragalus but on soft tissue between it and the calcaneum.

occurrences.name: Extensor digitorum I, II et III
occurrences.origin: Depression on the dorsal aspect of the astragalus, plus the dorsal surfaces of metatarsals I-IV for the digital slips.
occurrences.insertion: Dorsally on digits I-III by the dorsal aponeurosis, and on the proximodorsal lips of the phalanges of each digit served.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Crocodylus porosus. Hattori & Tsuihiji describe this animal together with its clade-mate and record no difference between the two for this muscle. A blank in a comparison is an observation of sameness, which is why both carry rows rather than one standing for the clade.

occurrences.name: Extensores breves digitorum III et IV
occurrences.origin: Dorsal aspect of the distal half of the tarsometatarsus, the digit III origin marked by a slightly depressed rugose surface and the digit IV origin by a sulcus lateral to it.
occurrences.insertion: Proximodorsal lip of phalanx III-1, and the medial aspect of IV-1 — the latter tendon running through the canalis interosseus distalis and its insertion marked by a tuber.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Gallus gallus. **Two members left of five.** The extensor digitorum brevis and the extensor hallucis brevis are both absent in birds, and only the digit III and IV slips survive, both now arising from the tarsometatarsus. Hattori & Tsuihiji use the digit III member as a test case for their metatarsal-identity reasoning: its origin on the middle of the distal half of the tarsometatarsus corresponds to metatarsal III, not to metatarsal II, which is why they refuse it as the homologue of the non-avian interosseous dorsalis digiti III.

occurrences.name: Extensores breves digitorum III et IV
occurrences.origin: Dorsal aspect of the distal half of the tarsometatarsus.
occurrences.insertion: Proximodorsal lip of III-1 and the medial aspect of IV-1.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Grus japonensis. Hattori & Tsuihiji describe this animal together with its clade-mate and record no difference between the two for this muscle. A blank in a comparison is an observation of sameness, which is why both carry rows rather than one standing for the clade.

occurrences.name: Extensor digitorum brevis and extensor hallucis brevis
occurrences.action: Extend the metatarsophalangeal joints of digits 1-4.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). Both from the superolateral surface of the calcaneus; brevis to the extensor expansions of toes 1-4, hallucis brevis to the dorsum of the proximal phalanx of the hallux. **The hand lost this layer and the foot kept it** — see the `extensores-digitorum-breves` row, scored absent for the human hand. Both limbs of one animal, one retaining the ancestral short extensor sheet and the other not, which is a caution against reading the two limbs as versions of each other.

occurrences.name: M. extensor digitorum communis brevis, M. extensor hallucis brevis and M. extensor digiti minimi proprius
occurrences.innervation: Rr. musculares of the N. peroneus profundus medialis and lateralis.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Sphenodon punctatus, Osawa (1898), *Zur Muskellehre*. The communis brevis from the proximal tarsal and partly the ankle capsule, dividing into three small bellies whose slender tendons pass into the dorsal aponeuroses of toes II to IV; the hallucis brevis from the base of metatarsal I to the dorsum of the hallux's proximal phalanx, which Osawa says **can be regarded as the interosseus of the first toe**; and the digiti minimi proprius from the ankle capsule and the lateral proximal tarsal, in two bellies, one to the base of metatarsal V and one to the proximal phalanx of toe V with a slip to metatarsal IV.

occurrences.name: Extensor brevis digitorum

parts.name: Fibular belly to the index and medius

occurrences.attachmentNote: Thylacinus cynocephalus. **This is a muscle caught in the middle of a migration.** Ruge traced its history: it belongs originally to the peroneal group, in Monotremata it arises entirely from the fibula, and through the mammalian series its bellies descend to the dorsum of the foot one at a time until, as in the human row on this record, the whole muscle is pedal. Cunningham's two marsupials are two steps of that sequence in two animals he dissected himself. **The entire muscle still arises from the fibula** here, under cover of the two peronei, as three separate fleshy bellies: the largest from the upper third of the shaft, its tendon joining the dorsal expansion of the little toe; the other two side by side from the middle third, the posterior giving a tendon that divides for index and medius, the anterior sending its tendon to the ring toe. All of them accompany the peroneal tendons behind the lateral malleolus — so this animal's short extensors of the toes reach the foot by going round the ankle with the peronei.

occurrences.name: Extensor brevis digitorum

parts.name: Pedal portion, to the index and medius

occurrences.attachmentNote: Spilocuscus maculatus. **This is a muscle caught in the middle of a migration.** Ruge traced its history: it belongs originally to the peroneal group, in Monotremata it arises entirely from the fibula, and through the mammalian series its bellies descend to the dorsum of the foot one at a time until, as in the human row on this record, the whole muscle is pedal. Cunningham's two marsupials are two steps of that sequence in two animals he dissected himself. **Here the migration is half done**: the part belonging to the medius and index has reached the dorsum of the foot, while that belonging to the two outer digits still shows a fibular origin. The two fibular bellies are a good-sized one from the outer aspect of the fibular head under the superficial head of the peroneus longus, its tendon passing behind the lateral malleolus to the dorsal expansion of the minimus, and beneath it a second from the middle third of the inner aspect of the shaft, reaching the ring digit by the same route. The pedal portion is a very minute band arising by a narrow tendon from the outer aspect of the calcaneum and ending in two delicate tendons for index and medius. The koala's arrangement is the same; Ruge found two fibular bellies plus a pedal portion for hallux and index in *Didelphis*.

occurrences.name: Extensor digitorum brevis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Tachyglossus aculeatus. **Absent.** Gambaryan et al. open their account of the short muscles of the hind foot by stating that the extensor digitorum brevis is lacking in the Monotremata, and describe only flexor groups thereafter. The dorsal intrinsic layer of this foot is therefore empty, and every extensor tendon reaching a monotreme toe comes from the crus. Set beside the marsupials on this record, which all have a pedal portion however minute, this is a loss inside Mammalia and not a retained primitive state — the record is scored `yes` from *Taricha* through the crocodilians and birds to the marsupials and humans.

occurrences.name: Extensor digitorum brevis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Ornithorhynchus anatinus. **Absent**, on the same statement covering both monotremes. What the platypus has instead is a long extensor system of extraordinary reach: the extensor digitorum superficialis and profundus each split into five tendons at the foot, so every toe receives extensor tendons from both sides. A short extensor would have nothing left to do.

correspondences.note: Stated by Diogo & Molnar (2014) Table 13 as a "clear topological correspondence"; their forelimb name for it is the extensores digitorum breves.

muscles.name: Abductor et extensor digiti I (pes)
muscles.developmental: Somitic; dorsal intrinsic layer of the pes, preaxial margin.

consensus.origin: Proximal tarsals of the preaxial ankle.
consensus.insertion: Lateral face of the first metatarsal and its phalanx.
consensus.action: Abducts and extends the first metatarsal and its digit.

occurrences.name: Abductor et extensor digiti I
occurrences.note: The paper's text calls these 'bones of the wrist' in the hindlimb section, evidently a slip for the ankle; the muscle is figured in the pes. Described here from Taricha torosa; not yet scored in other taxa in this dataset, so its absence elsewhere is unsampled rather than observed.
occurrences.attachmentNote: The preaxial counterpart of the abductor digiti minimi at the other margin of the foot. Its forelimb equivalent takes the radiale and intermedium.

occurrences.name: Adductor et extensor hallucis et indicus
occurrences.origin: A broad, flat or slightly depressed surface on the dorsolateral aspect of the distal fibula, and the medial half of a slight convex lip at the proximolateral margin of the tarsal facet of the astragalocalcaneum.
occurrences.insertion: Medial margin and laterodistal shaft of metatarsal I, and metatarsal II.
occurrences.attachmentNote:
Iguana iguana. The record's name comes from Russell & Bauer's for this muscle, so this is the animal it was named from.

Iguana iguana, Russell & Bauer (2008). Russell & Bauer give this muscle as two parallel-fibred slips from the dorsal aspect of the distal fibula and the astragalocalcaneum, closely associated at origin with the short digital extensor of digit I. The slip to digit I passes dorsal to that extensor and bifurcates halfway along metatarsal I, one branch to its mesial margin and one to its lateral margin distally; the slip to digit II inserts fleshily on the proximodorsal shaft of metatarsal II. Corroborates and extends the row Hattori & Tsuihiji (2021) scored from correlates.

occurrences.name: Adductor et extensor hallucis et indicus
occurrences.origin: Dorsolateral aspect of the distal fibula and the proximolateral margin of the tarsal facet of the astragalocalcaneum.
occurrences.insertion: Metatarsal I only, the insertion marked by rugosity on the bone.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Varanus indicus. **The insertion is narrower than the iguana's** — MT I alone, where Iguana takes MT I and MT II, and Chamaeleo takes only MT II (Russell & Bauer 2008). Three squamates, three different digits for one muscle, which is the position-versus-identity question asked inside a clade.

occurrences.name: Extensor hallucis proprius
occurrences.origin: Distal end of the fibula, the origin marked as a clear depression on the distodorsal margin of the bone, and the dorsal aspect of the astragalocalcaneum.
occurrences.insertion: Lateral sides of the distal third of metatarsal I and the proximal half of phalanx I-1, and the medial side of the mid-shaft of I-1.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Chelydra serpentina. The tarsal origin is absent in Trachemys (Walker 1973), so it varies within turtles.

occurrences.name: Adductor hallucis dorsalis
occurrences.origin: Dorsal aspect of the distal fibula.
occurrences.insertion: Dorsal aspect of the proximal third of the shaft of metatarsal I, just proximal to the tibialis anterior insertion; the distal border of the insertion is marked by a transverse ridge on metatarsal I.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Paleosuchus palpebrosus. No tarsal origin here, unlike the squamates and the turtle.

occurrences.name: Adductor hallucis dorsalis
occurrences.origin: Dorsal aspect of the distal fibula.
occurrences.insertion: Dorsal aspect of the proximal third of metatarsal I, bounded distally by a transverse ridge.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Crocodylus porosus. Suzuki et al. (2011) described the insertion as divided into two sites in this species; Hattori & Tsuihiji dissected the same species and did not find the division, and read the disagreement as intraspecific variation rather than error.

occurrences.name: Adductor hallucis dorsalis
occurrences.note: Gallus gallus. Absent. Hutchinson (2002) treated this muscle as the homologue of the avian m. extensor hallucis longus; Hattori & Tsuihiji reject that and place the avian muscle with the extensor hallucis brevis instead, on `extensores-digitorum-breves-pes`. So the absence here is a positive claim about where the avian muscle went, not silence.

occurrences.name: Adductor hallucis dorsalis
occurrences.note: Grus japonensis. Absent, as in Gallus.

occurrences.name: Abductor hallucis
occurrences.action: Abducts and flexes the great toe.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). Medial side of the calcaneal tuberosity to the medial side of the base of the proximal phalanx of the hallux — the preaxial marginal muscle of the sole, in the position its forelimb counterpart the abductor pollicis brevis occupies in the palm.

occurrences.name: M. abductor et extensor hallucis proprius longus lateralis
occurrences.innervation: R. muscularis of the N. peroneus profundus tibialis and medialis.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Sphenodon punctatus, Osawa (1898), *Zur Muskellehre*. Gadow's *extensor hallucis proprius*, Perrin's *extenseur superficiel du premier doigt*. Osawa carves it out of Fürbringer's *fibulo-tarso-digitalis dorsalis*, taking the part destined exclusively for the first toe and treating the rest with the muscles of the dorsum of the foot. It lies deep among the extensors, arises from the anterior surface of the distal fibula, from the ligamentum interosseum obliquum and from the interosseous membrane, and divides into a medial abductor and a lateral extensor before reaching the dorsum and medial side of metatarsal I. The short abductor hallucis proprius, from the medial part of the proximal tarsal to the medial side of the hallux's proximal phalanx, is scored here as a third part.

occurrences.name: Abductor hallucis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Thylacinus cynocephalus. **Absent, because the hallux is.** Cunningham's pes description opens by saying the hallux is suppressed, and the consequence runs through the whole foot: this animal is the one case in his marsupial series where every intrinsic muscle takes the external plantar nerve, the internal plantar having no hallucal muscles left to supply.

occurrences.name: Abductor and flexor brevis hallucis, fused
occurrences.attachmentNote: Dasyurus viverrinus, and **a muscle Cunningham cannot name, for a reason he sets out**. The rudimentary hallux carries a small fleshy slip from the scaphoid to the inner side of its metatarsal head. Is it the abductor or the flexor brevis? The nerve does not decide it — both usually take the internal plantar, and this does. Ruge, figuring the same slip in *Dasyurus hallucatus*, called it the abductor hallucis. Cunningham argues it is both fused into one, and his evidence is the next animal: in *Phascogale*, whose hallux is slightly better developed, the two lie in close proximity but are distinct. **A homology settled by looking at a relative rather than at a nerve.**

occurrences.name: Abductor hallucis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Phascogale calura, and **the row that decides the *Dasyurus* question**. From the base of the first metatarsal to the outer side of the base of the proximal phalanx, lying in close contact with the flexor brevis hallucis but easily separable from it. Because the two are separable in this animal, whose hallux is slightly better developed, Cunningham reads the single hallucal slip in *Dasyurus viverrinus* as the two fused rather than as the abductor alone, which is what Ruge had called it.

occurrences.name: Abductor hallucis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Spilocuscus maculatus. A strong muscle rising **from the plantar cartilage and from a sesamoid bone gliding on the plantar surface of the scaphoid** — that cartilage being the plate which in this animal replaces the plantar fascia and takes the place of a heel, described on the `gastrocnemius` row. It inserts chiefly by fleshy fibres into the tibial sesamoid of the hallux, is prolonged by a slender tendon to the tibial side of the distal phalanx, and gains the extensor tendon by a third slip. **Its nerve is unlike the others': the abductor hallucis appears to be supplied by a special branch to the hallux**, where in Cunningham's other marsupials it takes the internal plantar with the flexor brevis hallucis.

occurrences.name: Abductor hallucis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Trichosurus vulpecula. Present but **very poorly developed compared with the cuscus's, and largely tendinous in composition** — a muscle on its way out in an animal whose foot otherwise closely resembles the cuscus's.

occurrences.name: Abductor hallucis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Ornithorhynchus anatinus. **Absent as a separate muscle, and Cunningham says where it has gone**: the flexor brevis hallucis is single-bellied and takes a more proximal origin than its neighbours — from the internal cuneiform — which he reads as that muscle holding the abductor's fibres in its midst. Ruge applied the name abductor hallucis to the whole muscle; Cunningham thinks it better to regard it as a combination of both, and the row is scored on his reading with Ruge's recorded. He could trace no nervous filament to it at all, and only supposes it takes the internal plantar.

occurrences.name: Abductor hallucis
occurrences.innervation: A minute twig from the innermost digital branch of the internal plantar nerve, which supplies the abductor and flexor brevis of the hallux.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Tachyglossus aculeatus. **Very rudimentary**: from the fascia at the root of the hallux to the tibial aspect of the ungual phalanx by a minute thread-like tendon. It is one of only two muscles left in this foot's dorsal layer, and one of the three that the stunted hallux — the least mobile digit in the foot — keeps in full when better digits have lost theirs.

occurrences.name: Abductor hallucis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Meles meles. **Absent, and Cunningham says which muscle contains it**: the inner head of the flexor brevis hallucis, on the same reasoning he uses for the missing abductor of the little toe in the same foot — bulk, and an origin more proximal than its neighbours'. Compare the otter, in which a small abductor hallucis is present and quite separate from that head.

occurrences.name: Abductor hallucis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Lutra lutra. **Present, small, and quite separate from the inner head of the flexor brevis hallucis** — which is exactly what it is not in the badger, whose arrangement is otherwise the same. Two closely related pentadactyl carnivores on either side of one fusion.

occurrences.name: Abductor hallucis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Odobenus rosmarus. From a sesamoid gliding on the tibial side of the internal cuneiform to the inner side of the base of the hallux's first phalanx, and **in this specimen almost entirely fibrous — a strong rounded tendinous cord with a few muscular fibres at its proximal end.** Murie describes a fleshy belly three quarters the length of the hallucal metatarsal, and notes that in the sea-lion and the seal tendinous fascia replaces the muscle while in *Ursus americanus* a representative is found. Cunningham's animal sits with the seal rather than with Murie's walrus, and he offers the youth of the specimen as the reason.

occurrences.name: Abductor hallucis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Tamandua tetradactyla. A wide origin **from a cartilaginous process attached to the inner margin of the sole** and from the plantar fascia, to the inner sesamoid at the root of the hallux. Supplied by the internal plantar nerve with the flexor brevis hallucis, in the usual way — this foot's nerve arrangement is ordinary however unusual its muscles are.

occurrences.name: Abductor hallucis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Euphractus sexcinctus. Shares a common tendon far back in the sole with the tibial head of the flexor brevis hallucis, from the ligaments about the calcaneum and astragalus, then separates and runs by a long narrow tendon to the tibial side of the **ungual** phalanx of the hallux — past the joint the intrinsic muscles usually stop at.

occurrences.name: Abductor hallucis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Bradypus tridactylus. **Absent**, with the hallux, which like the minimus is reduced to a metatarsal carrying no phalanges. See the `flexores-breves-profundi-pes` row for what survives in this foot and why.

occurrences.name: Abductor hallucis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Castor fiber. Well developed, from the inner and under surface of the internal cuneiform to the inner sesamoid at the root of the hallux — **one of the few muscles in this foot that has not begun turning into a fibrous band.**

occurrences.name: Abductor hallucis
occurrences.attachmentNote: *Pteropus* sp. **Absent**, with the whole dorsal layer bar the abductor of the fifth metatarsal. Cunningham accounts for it by the size of the inner head of the flexor brevis hallucis, which is considerably larger than its fellows — the same argument he makes for the badger and, in the other direction, for the platypus.

correspondences.note: Stated by Diogo & Molnar (2014) Table 13 as a "clear topological correspondence"; their forelimb name for it is the abductor pollicis longus, in Timon.

muscles.name: Abductor digiti minimi (pes)
muscles.developmental: Somitic; intrinsic layer of the pes, postaxial margin.

consensus.insertion: Fibulare, the postaxial distal tarsal, and the base of the fifth metatarsal.
consensus.action: Abducts the fifth metatarsal and its digit.

occurrences.name: Abductor digiti V
occurrences.note: Basale V is scored as a distal tarsal; the paper's more specific term is kept here rather than given its own element. Described here from Taricha torosa; not yet scored in other taxa in this dataset, so its absence elsewhere is unsampled rather than observed.
occurrences.attachmentNote: An extensive fleshy insertion across three skeletal elements. The manus counterpart serves digit IV, because the salamander hand has lost digit V — the same muscle at the same margin, on a differently numbered digit.

occurrences.name: Abductor digiti minimi
occurrences.attachmentNote: A large muscle with fleshy origin over almost the whole dorsolateral fibulare, inserting by short tendon on the dorsal and proximal metatarsal V.
occurrences.note: Moved here from the forelimb record of the same name, where it had been filed for want of a pes counterpart.

occurrences.name: Abductor digiti minimi
occurrences.action: Abducts the fifth digit.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). Medial and lateral sides of the calcaneal tuberosity to the lateral base of the proximal phalanx of digit V — the postaxial marginal muscle, the mirror of the abductor hallucis across the sole. In the hand the equivalent muscle arises from the pisiform, a sesamoid the foot has no counterpart for, so the two limbs reach the same arrangement from different bones.

occurrences.name: M. abductor digiti quinti
occurrences.attachmentNote: Iguana iguana, Russell & Bauer (2008). Fleshy origin from the distal aspect of the ventrolateral margin of the astragalocalcaneum, deep to the distal head of the flexor digitorum longus and mesial to the peroneus brevis motor tendon, the small belly fanning slightly to insert fleshily across the proximal end of metatarsal V, chiefly on the mesial and lateral plantar tubercles and spanning the gap between them. In the hand the corresponding muscle arises from the pisiform, a bone the foot has no counterpart for, so the two limbs reach the same marginal position from different elements.

occurrences.name: Abductors of the little toe
occurrences.attachmentNote: Thylacinus cynocephalus. **Two, and sometimes three.** The abductor ossis metatarsi minimi digiti and the abductor minimi digiti share an origin on the outer aspect of the calcaneal tuber, the first reaching the base of the fifth metatarsal and the second running as a long narrow tendon to the extensor tendon on the fibular side of the first phalanx. In the large male's foot a third, exceedingly minute fasciculus ran from the metatarsal base to the outer sesamoid. Cunningham reads the split as the muscle's three usual insertions — metatarsal, sesamoid, extensor expansion — each pulling away a set of fibres of its own; **the abductor of the metatarsal is very constant across Mammalia and the other two are rarely separate**, and this animal, *Dasyurus* and the cuscus are three steps of that separation in one family.

occurrences.name: Abductors of the little toe
occurrences.attachmentNote: Dasyurus viverrinus. Three, as in the thylacine, but with the sesamoid slip arising further back — from the under surface of the projecting base of the fifth metatarsal — and **constant here where in the thylacine it was occasional**. Cunningham makes it out partly because the deep division of the external plantar nerve passes under cover of it as it turns inwards, which is the one exception in his whole marsupial series to that nerve running between the plantar layer and everything deeper. Ruge found the same slip in *Dasyurus hallucatus* but without an independent insertion, blended with the outer head of the short flexor.

occurrences.name: Abductors of the little toe
occurrences.attachmentNote: Phascogale calura. Two, not three: the abductor ossis metatarsi minimi digiti with exactly the connections it has in the thylacine and *Dasyurus*, and **a single abductor minimi digiti** where those two animals have it split.

occurrences.name: Abductors of the little toe

parts.name: Third abductor, to the extensor tendon

occurrences.attachmentNote: Spilocuscus maculatus. **Three, arising side by side from the outer and under surface of the calcaneal tuber, and inserted into the metatarsal, the outer sesamoid and the extensor tendon respectively — the muscle's three usual insertions, each with its own belly.** This is the full development of a separation the thylacine shows only occasionally and feebly, from the metatarsal base, and *Dasyurus* shows constantly but from further back. Cunningham's conclusion is that the abducting apparatus on the outer side of this foot is more differentiated than in any of the other animals he had examined.

occurrences.name: Abductors of the little toe
occurrences.attachmentNote: Trichosurus vulpecula. Two, not the cuscus's three: one to the base of the fifth metatarsal, the other partly to the outer sesamoid and partly to the extensor tendon at the base of the minimus — the two insertions that in the cuscus have each taken a belly of their own.

occurrences.name: Abductor ossis metatarsi minimi digiti and abductor digiti quinti
occurrences.attachmentNote:
Ornithorhynchus anatinus. **The only abductor of the little toe in this foot** — a short powerful muscle from the outer side of the calcaneal tuberosity to the fibular aspect of the base of the fifth metatarsal, supplied directly from the trunk of the external plantar rather than from either of its divisions (Cunningham 1882). Cunningham notes that the outermost belly of the flexor brevis digitorum, inserting on the outer side of the first phalanx, must add a considerable abducting action to its flexing one, **and that this helps spread the integumental web between the digits** — a swimming foot using a short flexor as an abductor.

**Gambaryan et al. (2002) find two abductors here, not one**, and neither takes its origin from bone. Their abductor metatarsi V arises from a branch of the insertion tendon of the semitendinosus pars vertebralis and the adjacent edge of the tuber calcanei, ending on the lateral edge of the proximal fifth metatarsal; their abductor digiti quinti arises from the same tendon superficial to it and inserts on the lateral edges of the first and second phalanges of the fifth toe and the distal fifth metatarsal. **So the muscle that spreads this web hangs off the tendon of the muscle that rotates the metatarsals** — the semitendinosus pars vertebralis, the largest muscle in the platypus hind limb. Cunningham's single calcaneal origin and their tendinous one are not reconciled here.

occurrences.name: Abductor digiti quinti and abductor metatarsi V
occurrences.attachmentNote:
Tachyglossus aculeatus. **Two dissections of this animal disagree about whether these muscles exist, and the row records both rather than choosing.**

**Cunningham (1882): absent, both of them.** The dorsal layer of this foot is down to two muscles, the abductor hallucis and the second dorsal interosseous, and neither an abductor minimi digiti nor an abductor ossis metatarsi minimi digiti is among them. He reads the echidna's missing intrinsic muscles as suppressed, finding no trace of them fused into anything. Set that against the platypus, where the abductor ossis metatarsi is the only abductor of the little toe but is short and powerful, and against every marsupial in his survey, all of which have two or three.

**Gambaryan et al. (2002): both present, and both on the tuber calcanei.** The abductor metatarsi V from the lateral aspect of the tuber calcanei and the inner surface of the tendinous plate underlying the heel callosity, to the lateral side of the distal part of the fifth metatarsal; the abductor digiti quinti from close beside it, on the upper point of the tuber calcanei and the same tendinous sheet, to the lateral edge of the first phalanx of the fifth toe. The attachments scored are theirs.

An attachment is an observation and does not age, so the later date does not decide this. What can be said is that the two accounts differ in where they looked: Cunningham enumerates the layers of the sole, and Gambaryan et al. describe a group defined by its connection to the tuber calcanei, which is the region Cunningham treats least.

occurrences.name: Abductors of the little toe
occurrences.attachmentNote: Canis lupus familiaris. **Absent as a distinct muscle of any kind.** Cunningham states it flatly for the dog, and gives his one piece of positive evidence for where it went: in a single specimen the fibular head of the short flexor of the little toe showed a slight tendency to split at its insertion. He is tracking a graded series across the carnivores — three separate slips in the leopard, two in the puma, two coalescing and re-separating in the lion, none in the dog — and the dog is its end.

occurrences.name: Abductors of the little toe
occurrences.attachmentNote: Felis catus. The abductor ossis metatarsi minimi digiti and the abductor minimi digiti share an origin on the proximal outer aspect of the calcaneum and separate, the first to the projecting base of the fifth metatarsal and the second by a long narrow tendon to the outer face of the base of the first phalanx. Cunningham is reading these animals as a graded series in which this apparatus disappears by fusion with the outer head of the short flexor, and the dog is its far end, with no abductor left at all.

occurrences.name: Abductors of the little toe
occurrences.attachmentNote: Puma concolor. The abductor ossis metatarsi minimi digiti and the abductor minimi digiti share an origin on the proximal outer aspect of the calcaneum and separate, the first to the projecting base of the fifth metatarsal and the second by a long narrow tendon to the outer face of the base of the first phalanx. Cunningham is reading these animals as a graded series in which this apparatus disappears by fusion with the outer head of the short flexor, and the dog is its far end, with no abductor left at all.

occurrences.name: Abductors of the little toe

parts.name: Third slip, fused with the short flexor

occurrences.attachmentNote: Panthera pardus. The abductor ossis metatarsi minimi digiti and the abductor minimi digiti share an origin on the proximal outer aspect of the calcaneum and separate, the first to the projecting base of the fifth metatarsal and the second by a long narrow tendon to the outer face of the base of the first phalanx. A small third slip from the base of the fifth metatarsal, above the level of the short flexor, joins that muscle's outer head after a short independent course. Cunningham is reading these animals as a graded series in which this apparatus disappears by fusion with the outer head of the short flexor, and the dog is its far end, with no abductor left at all.

occurrences.name: Abductors of the little toe
occurrences.attachmentNote: Panthera leo. The abductor ossis metatarsi minimi digiti and the abductor minimi digiti share an origin on the proximal outer aspect of the calcaneum and separate, the first to the projecting base of the fifth metatarsal and the second by a long narrow tendon to the outer face of the base of the first phalanx. Cunningham is reading these animals as a graded series in which this apparatus disappears by fusion with the outer head of the short flexor, and the dog is its far end, with no abductor left at all.

occurrences.name: Abductor ossis metatarsi minimi digiti
occurrences.attachmentNote: Meles meles. **Only the abductor of the metatarsal survives**, with the usual attachments. The abductor minimi digiti proper is accounted for by the outer head of the little toe's short flexor: it is unusually bulky and takes origin further back than its neighbours, from the surface of the long plantar ligament, and Cunningham concludes the lost muscle has coalesced with it.

occurrences.name: Abductors of the little toe
occurrences.divisionNote: Cunningham reads the third slip as an abductor; Murie reads it as the proximal belly of a digastric short flexor. Both readings are of the same walrus foot and both are recorded.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Odobenus rosmarus. The abductor ossis metatarsi minimi digiti with its usual attachments, and an abductor minimi digiti arising **not from bone but from the fascia covering the outer surface of that muscle**. A third slip runs from the under surface of the anterior border of the calcaneum to the fibrous textures at the base of the fifth metatarsal, and Cunningham and Murie disagree about it: Murie points out that if those fibrous textures are lifted the slip passes straight into the outer head of the short flexor, making a digastric muscle, and classes it with that flexor. Cunningham calls it a third abductor of the minimus — common enough in the marsupials — and supports himself from Murie's own drawing of *Otaria jubata*, where the same muscle reaches the first phalanx on its own account.

occurrences.name: Abductors of the little toe
occurrences.attachmentNote: Tamandua tetradactyla. Both present: the abductor ossis metatarsi with its usual attachments, and a narrow abductor minimi digiti from the outer side of the calcaneal tuber ending in a long slender tendon on the outer sesamoid at the base of the minimus.

occurrences.name: Abductors of the little toe
occurrences.attachmentNote: Euphractus sexcinctus. Both from the calcaneum: the abductor minimi digiti by a long tendon to the **fibular side of the distal phalanx**, the abductor ossis metatarsi to the base of the metatarsal. Cunningham disagrees with Galton over exactly these two, Galton having called the calcaneum-to-metatarsal muscle the abductor minimi digiti and the calcaneum-to-ungual-phalanx muscle the flexor brevis; Cunningham names them by their insertions and assigns the true flexor brevis to the minute fasciculus Galton left unnamed.

occurrences.name: Abductors of the little toe
occurrences.attachmentNote: Bradypus tridactylus. **Absent.** The minimus itself is a rudimentary metatarsal supporting no phalanges, and Cunningham reads the marginal abductors of this foot as suppressed along with the marginal digits they belonged to.

occurrences.name: Abductor ossis metatarsi minimi digiti
occurrences.attachmentNote: Procavia capensis. **The minimus is absent from this foot, and what is at issue is whether its abductor has moved to the annularis.** Murie & Mivart found muscular fibres arising from a fascia on the outer surface of the calcaneum and inserted into the head of the ligamentous fourth metatarsal, and suggested this might be the abductor ossis metatarsi minimi digiti transferred to the annular digit. Cunningham found the thick ligamentous fascia in his specimen but could detect no muscular fibres in it. He takes the fascia, and the fibres where they exist, to be that muscle in retrograde change — so the row is scored uncertain, which is the state of the evidence rather than a hedge: two workers, two specimens, one with muscle in it and one without.

occurrences.name: Abductors of the little toe
occurrences.attachmentNote: Bathyergus suillus. **Absent**, with the whole dorsal layer. See the `contrahentes-digitorum-pes` row for why Cunningham does not choose between suppression and fusion here.

occurrences.name: Abductor ossis metatarsi minimi digiti
occurrences.attachmentNote: *Pteropus* sp. **The only member of the dorsal layer present in this foot**, well developed and with the usual connections, supplied by one or two twigs from the external plantar nerve before it divides. The abductor minimi digiti proper is absent, and Cunningham suggests it is inside the unusually large outer head of the short flexor.

homology.teaching: Postaxial position and digit number disagree between hand and foot in salamanders. Matching by number would pair this muscle with nothing; matching by position pairs it with the manual extensor lateralis digiti IV.

correspondences.note: Stated by Diogo & Molnar (2014) Table 15 as a "clear topological correspondence"; their forelimb name for it is the abductor digiti minimi.

muscles.name: Interossei dorsales (pes)
muscles.developmental: Somitic; deep dorsal mass of the pes.
synonyms: mm. interossei dorsales digiti II-IV (Hattori & Tsuihiji 2021)
part of mm. extensores breves (Russell & Bauer 2008, for lepidosaurs)
part of mm. interossei dorsales (Walker 1973, for turtles)
m. abductor digiti II (Aves; Vanden Berge & Zweers 1993)

consensus.origin: Dorsal or lateroplantar aspect of the metatarsal one position medial to the digit of insertion.
consensus.insertion: Proximodorsal lip of the phalanges of that digit, largely through the dorsal aponeurosis.
